The Big Idea: Curtis C. Chen
Posted on November 4, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi Leave a Comment
It may be getting cooler as we fully embrace fall, but things are heating up in space! Author Curtis C. Chen is here with not only his Big Idea, but a science lesson that he says will better help you understand his newest novel, Kangaroo Forth, the fourth installment of his Kangaroo series.
CURTIS C. CHEN:
Hashtag shameless cross promotion: if you want to know about the very specific references to twentieth-century pop culture in the fourth Kangaroo book, Kangaroo Forth, go read the “My Favorite Bit” that I wrote for Mary Robinette Kowal’s journal yesterday.
Today, I’m going to talk about the real-world inspiration for the “heat lock” situation that occurs in K4. Don’t worry, this isn’t really a spoiler—think of it as watching the safety video before you board an amusement park ride. Good to know just in case anything happens, let’s hope it doesn’t, fingers crossed, wink emoji!
(Disclaimer: I am not a professional space scientist or science communicator by training, so please excuse any errata below.)
Now, we all know that “it is very cold in space,” as Ricardo Montalban famously said in Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan, but it can also get very hot in space. On Earth’s Moon, for example, surface temperatures can climb to more than 250 degrees Fahrenheit in direct sunlight (with local variations depending on terrain like craters, and other factors). The lunar surface retains a lot of heat because there’s no atmosphere, and therefore no medium for natural convection. It takes considerably more time for that accumulated heat from the Sun to radiate away in vacuum as infrared energy.
In May of 2013, astronauts aboard the International Space Station (ISS) performed an unscheduled spacewalk to replace a leaking Pump Flow Control Subassembly (PFCS) module that was part of the cooling system for the station’s solar panels. The photovoltaic panels that turn sunlight into electricity for the station generate considerable heat during normal operation, and the system is kept within operating temperatures by ammonia “cooling loops” that circulate through radiator panels outside the station. This particular malfunction prompted the ISS crew to shut down one-eighth of the station’s power generation capacity until the problem was fixed.
So what happens in Kangaroo’s science-fictional future, where multitudes of spacecraft and off-planet habitats are powered by “ionwell” nuclear reactors that generate even more waste heat than solar panels? Well, if the cooling modules for those power systems ever fail, the ship or station running the reactor will heat up real fast, and if you can’t control the temperature, that’s a critical life support emergency for the people on board. Hence the need for “thermal regulation lockdown,” or “heat lock” in their military jargon. Power down any nonessential systems, limit personnel activity, keep an eye on the thermostat, and hope you don’t have to do anything more drastic.
By the way, heat retention in vacuum is also why a human body won’t immediately freeze to death in outer space, despite what you may have seen in many science-fiction-y shows over the years . . . but that’s another podcast!
Kangaroo Forth: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|iBookstore|Vintage Books (signed paperbacks)

OpenAI Acquires Pierre Computer to Supercharge Codex
			
		 	
				OpenAI has acquired developer tools startup Pierre Computer Company to strengthen Codex. "The deal, announced today, signals OpenAI's aggressive push into the developer tools market as the AI arms race intensifies," reports The Tech Buzz. Financial terms weren't disclosed. From the report: 
Pierre Computer Company had been building specialized tools for code analysis and review, capabilities that complement Codex's existing strength in code generation. For developers, this could mean a more seamless experience -- using AI not just to write initial code snippets, but to understand legacy codebases, spot potential bugs, and conduct thorough reviews before deployment. That's a workflow improvement that enterprise engineering teams have been demanding.
[...] For Pierre Computer Company, the acquisition likely provides the resources and distribution that startups in this space desperately need. Building AI developer tools requires massive compute infrastructure and access to cutting-edge models -- both of which OpenAI has in abundance. Pierre's team will now have access to OpenAI's latest models, including the technology behind ChatGPT and the recently announced Shepherd model for AI research validation.
The integration timeline remains unclear, but developers using Codex should expect to see Pierre's capabilities rolling out in the coming months. OpenAI has been moving quickly to ship new features -- it just launched Dots, transforming its coding tools into an always-on AI assistant. Adding Pierre's code review and analysis features could make Codex a genuine end-to-end solution for software development teams.

DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google’s AI policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
19:29:52 UTC
04:29:52 KST

DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine. On Tuesday, Google told schools they could turn off Gemini, but it said shutting off its other AI features would cost schools Google Search, as well.
DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated. According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves over 150 million users globally.
On X, DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s online documentation, explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.”
Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement, writing, “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong.”
In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to.
The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives. As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they don’t want AI data centers built in their towns. But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion.
Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “Guided Learning” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer. But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether.
After the backlash on Tuesday, Google defended its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback. It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually.
The problem, of course, is that Google Search now heavily uses AI, through AI Overviews and a conversational AI Mode that answers users’ queries.
DuckDuckGo isn’t anti-AI, to be clear — it offers its own set of AI features, including a chat interface called Duck.ai and an AI search assistant.
However, unlike Google, it provides options to disable these features in both its search and browser settings, the company says. It also offers a dedicated website, noai.duckduckgo.com, where AI-assisted answers, AI-generated images, and AI feature suggestions are all turned off.
That flexibility may be driving demand for its services, as the company reported earlier this year that its app installs were up 30% as users rejected being force-fed Google’s AI Search.

Xbox previews two new ways to control cloud games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
19:01:51 UTC
04:01:51 KST

I revealed yesterday that the new Xbox Nano controller supports a Wi-Fi connection directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming, and now Microsoft is making it official today. Two new Xbox previews will let players try out using a phone as a controller on smart TVs, as well as cloud connect on the Xbox Nano to connect directly to cloud servers.
Xbox previews two new ways to control cloud games
Xbox Cloud Gaming is getting a phone controller and new direct Wi-Fi connectivity for the Xbox Nano.
“Instead of a Bluetooth connection to your TV, cloud connect uses your Wi-Fi to connect directly to the cloud server running your game,” says the Xbox team. “That can help reduce input latency, so gameplay may feel more responsive.”
Players in the US will be able to preview the new cloud connect option for the Xbox Nano controller starting today. If you’re not in the US you will be able to preview a new phone controller option on smart TVs. The controller is available on the Xbox Cloud Gaming website, allowing people to use the streaming service without a dedicated Bluetooth controller.
Microsoft says “both experiences are still being tested” and that “availability and supported games or devices may be limited” during this beta phase. You’ll need to use the Xbox beta app for Android or the Xbox Accessories app on PC to set up cloud connect on the Nano controller, and the smart TV phone controller just requires a toggle of preview features from the Settings > Account section of Xbox Cloud Gaming.

"Several regional facilities of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems," the health ministry said in a statement.
The incident had no impact on blood supplies, EFS spokesperson Charley Dubois said. "We have staff round the clock since blood can be needed at any time. They were warned about the problems by alerts and moved the blood to other refrigerators that were not connected," she said. [...] Investigations are under way into how the attack was carried out, what equipment may have been affected and when systems can safely return to service. The attack followed a similar incident in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses.

Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:53:29 UTC
03:53:29 KST

Introducing Ripple-65B Preview,
a Frontier Open-Weight Model
Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model.
To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains.
Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview, a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4).
Ripple’s dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The model’s small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators.
Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud, and OpenRouter. Fireworks goes live later today.
Achieving U.S. Open-Weight Frontier at One-Tenth Cost
LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million. In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone.
In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding, as estimated to the best of our knowledge.¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run.
Steep Ascent Reinforcement Learning
Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics.
Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling, score centering, and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved.
The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA.
A Co-Designed Model Architecture
Ripple-65B Preview’s architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization.
Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added FFN activation clipping, gated attention, global NoPE, and value residuals.
Careful Model Laddering Led to Large Improvements
We optimized Ripple’s pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments.
Our starting point was Olmo 3’s model ladder, from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention. Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals. In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code.
Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with 16x less compute. Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale.
Conclusion
We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier.
We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors.
At Ricursive, we are selectively hiring exceptional researchers and engineers as we push the frontier of full-stack AI from model to silicon. If you’re interested, check out https://www.ricursive.com/careers.
¹ U.S. open-weight players like Reflection were reported to commit to $150M per month for compute at SpaceX Colossus to train their models. Reflection reported that Beam took 4 weeks to pretrain and 4 weeks to posttrain.

Have I Befriended a Murderer?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:40:54 UTC
03:40:54 KST

Thoughtful stories for thoughtless times.
Longreads has published hundreds of original stories—personal essays, reported features, reading lists, and more—and more than 14,000 editor’s picks. And they’re all funded by readers like you. Become a member today.
Edward Abel Smith | Longreads | November 3, 2026 | 5,962 words (21 minutes)
On a sunny Saturday morning earlier this year, I was driving my two daughters to the playground through patchy phone signal when a voicemail notification appeared. Pressing play impatiently, an upbeat voice with a north of England accent bellowed through the car’s loudspeaker: “Hi Ed. I’ve just been flicking through The Times, and I’ve seen you’ve been chosen as their book of the week. Bloody well done, my friend! I am super proud.”
I was stunned. My book, A Hateful Decision, about Churchill’s attack on the French navy during the Second World War, had just been published. Being named The Times Book of the Week was, without question, the highlight of my writing career. But the way this news was delivered felt profoundly weird. The man who had congratulated me—referring to me as his “friend” with such sincerity—was Robin Garbutt, and he’d called from Wealstun Prison, where he was, and still is, serving a life sentence for the murder of his wife, Diana. She was killed in her bed, beaten so brutally that her face was barely recognizable by the time the police got there.
In 2021, I was researching a possible sequel to my first book, a biography of Ian Fleming, the creator of James Bond. While at the National Archives in West London, partly through a filing error and partly through my own boredom, I found myself looking at recent criminal case files rather than the wartime naval intelligence records I had come for. One caught my eye immediately: Diana Garbutt, a woman murdered in the flat above the post office she ran with her husband Robin in the North Yorkshire village of Melsonby.
The only available document for her murder was the judge’s summing up, and it was damning. Robin had called the emergency services on the morning of March 23, 2010, saying their post office had been robbed at gunpoint. After the perpetrators left, he claimed he had run upstairs to find Diana dead. But no one in the village had seen any evidence of the robbery, even though it was a busy morning. The paramedics who first attended Diana noted that she had rigor mortis—a sign she had died many hours before Robin claimed the robbery took place. It appeared Robin had invented the robbery to cover his own murderous tracks. The descriptions of the wounds she had sustained in her final moments of life were horrific. As I read on, I felt nothing but contempt for her husband. The judge made it clear to the jury that he believed Robin to be a killer. Ten of the 12 jurors agreed, and Robin was found guilty by a majority verdict.
When I got home from the archives, I looked up the case online, curious to know what had become of Robin. There was a strange sense of relief to learn he was still behind bars. But as I scanned through the search results, something made me double-take: a website dedicated to Robin Garbutt. What kind of convicted murderer has his own website? It turned out his family had set one up, maintaining throughout that he was innocent of killing his wife. I was, of course, skeptical; a lot of people in prison claim they should never have been convicted. But what struck me about Robin’s website was the list of supporters: family, childhood friends, and a remarkable number of Melsonby residents, a village of fewer than 800 people.
Getting in touch with Robin was surprisingly straightforward. The “contact us” section of his website directed me to his friend Jane Metcalfe—a proud woman from the same part of the country as Robin, and someone who would rather use ten words when one would suffice. She was desperate for more media attention for the case. A new author was hardly what she had in mind, but she graciously stuck with me, suggesting I write to Robin directly. We started to exchange letters through a system called eMates. I would type a letter to Robin, which would be printed and delivered to his cell. For an extra 26 pence, I could include a response sheet, on which he would write a reply by hand.
Over the next six months of writing to each other, Robin would instruct Jane to send me documents from his case. I started to build up my own archive of police reports, trial transcripts, and witness statements, all arriving in hard copy through the post. Thanks to years of reading and watching fictional detectives like Sherlock Holmes and Miss Marple, a surprising amount of the prosecution documents made sense to me. But there was one element I still couldn’t understand: What type of person could murder their wife in such a merciless way? For someone painted as so gentle by those who knew him, it just did not add up. Perhaps he was a psychopath? That possibility scared me the most. At the same time, I was desperate to find out more—to the point I thought I might scrap Ian Fleming and write a book about the murder instead.
When I broached the topic with Robin in one of my many letters to him, he suggested we should meet. I jumped at the chance, due to curiosity as much as anything else. As far as I was aware, I had never met a convicted murderer. I had certainly never set foot in a prison. As a director in a large corporation, it was a far cry from the air-conditioned London offices I was used to.
Jane was instrumental in the coordination, kindly collecting me from York Station, where she brushed aside my outstretched hand in favor of a warm bear hug. The half-hour drive to Wealstun Prison was conducted at such speed I was no longer frightened by the prospect of entering a high-security prison so much as making it there in one piece. Jane did not look at the road nearly as much as I would have liked, either, but in fairness maybe she did not need to—she had made this journey so many times before. Her red Ford Fiesta told its own story: a flyer tucked in the windscreen declaring Robin’s conviction the country’s worst miscarriage of justice, the back seat buried under the paperwork of his various appeals. By the time we pulled up outside the prison, I had been given the full case for Robin’s innocence at considerable volume. Then Jane drove off and left me alone in front of a great fence that seemed to swallow the sky.
Visiting a prison for the first time is not unlike catching a flight. There are the same queues, the same searches, the same surrendering of your belongings, the same slow procession through a series of checkpoints, each one deeper into the complex than the last. Eventually, I was shown into the visiting room—a vast, gymnasium-sized space of plastic chairs and laminate tables, with a small canteen in one corner and a children’s play area in the other. I bought two cheese toasties and two coffees and sat down to wait.
When Robin walked in, my first thought was how little he matched what I had expected. He was tall and trim, calm in a way that seemed entirely unperformed. The man who had been photographed entering court looking gaunt and hollow-eyed had filled out; more than a decade of prison routine seemed, paradoxically, to have done him good.
He sat down, thanked me for the sandwich and drink, let me flounder through some small talk about the weather, and then, with the patience of someone who has had a great deal of practice at waiting, he broke in gently. “If you write a book about me,” he said, “it’s important that you feel you can ask me anything, even if it might seem really insensitive. You need to make up your own mind about who you think killed Diana. I’ll tell you the facts. Anything you want to know, I will tell you. But I won’t try to persuade you either way.”
It was a disarming thing to say. I noticed, as he spoke, that he twisted the wedding ring on his finger—slowly, almost unconsciously, as though it were a habit he was no longer aware of.
I liked Robin immediately. He was warm, he put me at ease, and there was a tiredness about him—heavy bags under his eyes, a particular quality of sadness—that felt, even then, at odds with the version of him the prosecution had described. But underneath the warmth of the visit was a thought I couldn’t quite shake: that this was precisely how a guilty man would want to come across. There was an uneasy feeling that I was being played. I wrote in my notebook on the train back to London, “Can I imagine R standing over his wife’s bed with a metal pole, brutally beating her to death while she slept?”
After my first visit, Robin began calling me. Usually once a week, at lunchtime, when he and his fellow inmates were locked in their cells, a quiet hour that became, for both of us, a kind of fixed point in the week.
He had only been at Wealstun for a few months when we first made contact. Before that, he had spent over a decade at HMP Frankland, one of Britain’s highest-security prisons, nicknamed “Monster Mansion.” Wealstun brought an important change: a telephone in his cell, rather than a queue for the communal phones. For Robin, it meant a small measure of privacy. For me, it meant he could call any day. If I missed a call, he couldn’t try again for another hour, and I had no way of calling him back. So whenever his number appeared on my screen, I stopped whatever I was doing and answered. I found myself ducking into storerooms, or stepping out of meetings with a vague excuse, or pressing the phone to my ear in empty corridors while colleagues walked past, entirely unaware of who I was talking to.
Our conversations had a rough structure. We would begin with pleasantries—how the week had been, what we had each been doing. And it was here, every time, that I would catch myself. I found myself talking down my own life: glossing over a weekend away, understating the dinner with friends, mentioning my newborn daughter only briefly and moving on. Because on the other end of the line was a man who had spent the weekend sitting in a cell. There is no natural way to bridge that distance. Instead, I minimized it, which came across as guarded and standoffish. But despite my awkwardness, Robin always stayed interested in my life; I found myself touched.
We would then move on to his case. Robin’s life is consumed by the process of trying to overturn his conviction through an arduous, complicated, and deeply flawed system that moves at a snail’s pace. I had never heard of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) before I started speaking to Robin. It is now a body I could lecture on at length, should anyone be foolish enough to listen. In brief, the CCRC is an independent organization that screens claims of miscarriage of justice, deciding which cases merit referral to the Court of Appeal and which are rejected before they can get there. Robin refers to his dealings with the CCRC as a game of Whac-A-Mole: Each time a prosecution pillar is addressed, the CCRC pulls up another point to dismiss his application.
The motive the police gave for Diana’s murder was financial: Robin had been stealing from the Post Office and murdered his wife when she found out, inventing the robbery to cover both the killing and the missing money. But when Robin first applied to the CCRC in 2015, he pointed out that Post Office records for the six years he had worked there—which the Post Office had previously failed to disclose—showed that the spending patterns the prosecution used to indicate theft were entirely normal for their branch throughout his and Diana’s tenure. The CCRC accepted this was significant. They rejected the application anyway.
My own research into their finances has done little to simplify the picture. The Garbutts lived on the premises of their business, making it almost impossible to draw a clean line between personal and company expenditure. By all accounts, they were just getting by, though with some exceptions: over £5,000 spent on weekend retreats, a holiday to America, and tickets to Glastonbury. Such expenses weren’t impossible on their income, but they sat uneasily against the broader picture of a couple living hand to mouth. What impressed me when discussing this with Robin was his ability to never come across as bitter toward those who implicated him. His arguments were never personal against anyone—even though he was accusing them of causing his wrongful conviction.
The fraud motive still never quite added up, especially when I considered a separate scandal surrounding the Post Office’s Horizon computer system. In 2019, investigations and a campaign by a handful of wrongfully convicted individuals revealed a huge miscarriage of justice: hundreds of subpostmasters in Britain wrongly prosecuted for financial discrepancies caused by faulty Horizon software—the same software used to generate the financial records for Robin’s post office. I am not suggesting Horizon exonerates Robin. But it raises the possibility that the prosecution’s motive is built on data from deeply unreliable software. For me, that’s important.
Robin applied to the CCRC again in 2017, this time targeting the question of opportunity. The expert who analyzed Diana’s stomach contents had placed Diana’s time of death between 2:30 a.m. and 4:30 a.m.—a window that made Robin the only person who could have killed her. But Robin’s legal team argued to the CCRC that an independent pathologist found this expert’s methodology to be flawed.
This timeline had other issues, too. Robin had been running the village shop within his post office branch since 4:30 a.m. on the morning of the murder—supposedly with his dead wife upstairs—serving a steady stream of around 70 locals and commuters from Scotch Corner, one of the busiest junctions in the north of England. David Harper, the milkman, was among the first, arriving at around 5:15 a.m. “I had a nice chat with Robin as I always would,” he recalled. “He was his usual friendly, affable, and personable self.” At around 6:45 a.m., Robin’s friend Brian Hird came in for his copy of The Northern Echo. “He was just his normal cheery self,” Brian told me. As Brian was paying, he heard something from behind the counter. “It sounded like a woman’s voice coming from the stairs behind the shop,” he explained in Robin’s trial. “I think she just said one word, ‘Robin.’ I was sure it had come from their apartment.” If Brian was right, then Diana was alive at 6:45 a.m.—over an hour and a half after the prosecution’s suggested window closed. For reasons that have never been fully explained, the jury did not accept his account. Robin has never understood why. Brian remains a friend and still sometimes visits Robin in prison, along with dozens of others who have stood by him all these years.
But if Diana was not killed before 4:30 a.m., when did she die? I have spent much of the last five years obsessing over 79 seconds. That is the window between the post office safe being remotely unlocked at 8:35:54 a.m. on March 23, 2010, and Robin’s 999 emergency call being received at 8:37:13 a.m. In that time, according to Robin, a man in a balaclava appeared, pointed a gun at him, and said, “Don’t do anything stupid. We have your wife.” Robin then had to bolt the front door, fill a holdall bag from the safe and the till, let the robber leave through the back, run upstairs to find Diana, and call the emergency services.
I have put the timeline to investigators, criminologists, and former police officers. The broad consensus is that it was possible, but only just. Measuring the dimensions of the shop to the stairs and up to the bedroom, I have recreated the steps at home several times, and in the allotted time. But “if Robin had killed her,” one of his friends from the village asked me, “why would he have given himself such a short window of time?” It is the same kind of question I hear time and again, no matter which side of the argument someone is on. If they believe Robin is guilty, then they say, “That does not make sense; he is lying.” And if they believe Robin is innocent, then they say, “Robin would make up something more believable to cover his tracks.” For me, 79 seconds is tight. But it is not impossible, and impossibility is the only thing that would have settled it for me.
The CCRC accepted that the initial pathologist’s evidence should be removed from the prosecution case. They rejected Robin’s application anyway.
The third CCRC application, submitted in 2019, added grounds related to the murder weapon. The pole used to beat Diana to death was found on a wall near the post office a few days after the crime. But footage from a local television crew, time-stamped from the day after the murder, showed that the wall was empty—meaning the pole could not have been placed there by Robin on the night of the murder, as the prosecution had claimed. DNA analysis also revealed that the officer who had spotted the murder weapon had left his DNA not only on the bar itself, but at the crime scene, in a property he maintained he had never entered. None of Robin’s DNA was found on the murder weapon. The CCRC accepted these points. The application was rejected anyway.
It has been suggested to me that there was something nefarious going on with the policeman whose DNA was discovered at the scene. He was on holiday for the week of the murder, but he decided to return to work several days early, at which point he found the murder weapon. He didn’t explain his premature return. And he could not recollect what he had been doing at the time of the murder. No alibi. No attempt at an alibi. My efforts to track him down for an explanation, or to obtain a comment from North Yorkshire Police, have so far been unsuccessful.
But having learned so much about this case, I feel the DNA can be explained by simple incompetence. There is plenty of evidence for that. The judge in Robin’s trial described North Yorkshire Police’s investigation as having a “regrettable lack of professionalism.” When investigators compared crime scene photographs taken on the day of the murder to ones taken afterward, they noticed discrepancies: bedside table lamps that had mysteriously disappeared, later found to have been moved to the back of the wardrobe. A clump of hair on the bed—matching neither Robin’s short gray nor Diana’s dark brown—bagged as evidence, then subsequently lost. An investigation riddled with errors like these is also one where a police officer’s DNA ending up on a murder weapon is, at least, explicable.
Until learning all this, I had been working from a position of skepticism about Robin’s innocence, looking for reasons to doubt the verdict. I soon found myself doing the opposite: looking for reasons to trust the investigation. I struggled to find them.
By the time I first met him, Robin was working on his fourth CCRC application with his pro bono legal team. He described it as his “last chance,” although I wondered whether he had said the same about the previous three. At the time of writing, that application has been sitting with the CCRC for two years. Every three months, Robin receives an update letter. Each one contains a variation of the same sentence: that his case officer is “familiarising myself with the issues in your case.” Robin will often talk very calmly, in a measured way, about the CCRC, and end with the same sentence: “Anyway, sorry to rant, Ed.”
Something kept catching, like a loose thread. I did not trust the investigation. But the CCRC might still know something I did not—with their unfettered access to police databases, internal memos, and forensic evidence. A flawed institution is not automatically a wrong one.
After his fourth application was submitted, I did something I had been avoiding for a long time. I put it to Robin directly: Perhaps the CCRC, for all its faults, had looked at the full picture and reached the right conclusion. That perhaps he was guilty. That perhaps he had murdered his wife. I had been dancing around the question since the moment I first walked into Wealstun Prison. Asking it out loud felt like a betrayal—of the connection we had built, of the hours he had given me, of the trust he had extended to a stranger. But I also knew that if I never asked it, I would always wonder.
The disappointment in his voice surprised me, not because I expected him to react any differently, but because it was the first time he had not been his deliberately optimistic self.
“Ah, um,” he stuttered, then breathed out heavily. “I don’t really know what to say,” he continued, so obviously deflated.
“Do you mind me mentioning it?” I asked, as the silence on the other end of the phone started to unnerve me.
“No, gosh, no,” Robin replied, seemingly snapping out of his melancholy. “It is the waiting for news,” he added matter-of-factly. “The fear and dread that they are going to deliver another nail in the coffin. It is exhausting. The stress is something to add to the bucket of pain.”
Whenever I finished my conversations with Robin, I usually returned to whatever I’d been doing—another mind-numbing meeting, an overly complex spreadsheet, a pointless conference call. But after this one, I needed time to reflect. His reaction stayed with me. Robin had always struck me as emotionally consistent: calm, friendly, and honest. Hearing the dissatisfaction in his voice when I suggested the CCRC could be right was unnerving. It must have been a double sucker punch: I was questioning his innocence while defending the institution he blamed for keeping him locked up so long.
What surprised me most was my own reaction. I was genuinely worried I’d upset Robin—not that he might stop talking to me, ending my plans for a book, but that he could be sitting in his cell, sadly pinching the bridge of his nose the way he did when I’d met him, because of me. It was the first moment I realized Robin might be becoming more than the subject of my research. He might be becoming a friend. And I wasn’t only troubled by having upset him. Robin hadn’t actually answered my question; the one that suggested he might be guilty.
The following week, Robin didn’t call. It wasn’t unheard of for him to miss a week: Despite prison life seemingly leaving him to watch time pass, he actually had a job running admissions as lorryloads of young men arrived each week. Phone calls were also expensive, and sometimes he simply couldn’t afford one. But with no way to reach him, a nagging feeling took hold that he was upset with me.
Another week later, an A5 envelope arrived in the post. On the back, in tiny writing: Robin Garbutt and his seven-digit prisoner number. I could feel there was something inside besides the card. With excitement, I tore it open.
Ed,
I’m very conscious that you have very little paperwork on my case, despite everything Jane has sent. Anyhow, when at Frankland, I applied for and was given a laptop solely for my case—on it was tonnes of paperwork, legal letters, CCRC stuff plus a PDF file of all my solicitor’s correspondence. This file will show you the layout of the house and post office, there are no horrific scenes of Di, but some distressing ones of blood—so not nice. When I left Frankland they put all that onto a ‘dongle’ which is enclosed. It is my only one (!!) so we will want it back in your own time—no rush at all.
That’s me Ed. Take great care and speak soon.
Many thanks,
Robin
It took months to wade through what was on the stick. The material was vast: witness statements; unused evidence; legal correspondence; letters Robin had sent to lawyers, forensic experts, and private investigators around the world, begging for help and, in most cases, receiving no reply. Reading them was quietly devastating.
There were also spreadsheets he had meticulously compiled: “Timeline for Moor Road and the Shop 6.30 to 8.30” runs 240 rows deep, cataloguing every witness’s recollection from the morning of the murder, each one cross-referenced to a statement number. I pictured Robin in his cell in the small hours, tapping away on his laptop while over 800 fellow inmates slept around him.
What struck me first was not what was in the files. It was the fact that he had sent them at all. I had just confronted him with the possibility that he was guilty—the most direct challenge I had put to him in months of conversation. His response was not to go quiet, not to cut me off, not to become defensive or combative. He had flooded me with everything he had. His only copy. A man with nothing to hide, or a man who had calculated, very precisely, that transparency was his best remaining move. I genuinely could not tell which.
Among the files were some truly fascinating nuggets, some of which made me question the case in its entirety. Buried in one of the tedious police reports was a reference to the discovery of underwear found at the top of the contents in Robin and Diana’s outside bin, stained with what appeared to be rust, consistent with that found on the murder weapon. Apart from that paragraph, it was not mentioned again. It took considerable searching before I found a witness statement, taken from one of Robin’s neighbors more than six months after the murder. “I have also today been shown some pictures of a pair of grey Calvin Klein boxer shorts, which were labelled as exhibit KC8. I can say that I have boxer shorts like this. I think that I had two pairs and when I checked today, I only have one pair left.” This piece of evidence was never explored further, and the underwear was never tested to establish whether the brown substance was rust from the murder weapon.
Then there was a Crimestoppers report stating that a man who lived nearby had been seen with a firearm and a large amount of cash the day after the murder, boasting that he had “bashed her around the head.” What was most interesting was the timing. I have not been able to establish exactly when the tip was submitted, but several days passed after the murder before police released details of how Diana had been killed. Had this tip come in before that information was made public, it could be very significant. I have since tracked down the person named in the report. His address, age, and name match a man currently serving a lengthy sentence for trying to rob a safe in a shop in Manchester, 100 miles from Melsonby, with an imitation firearm. He has not responded to my attempt to contact him.
These were the first credible alternatives I had come across. I was now not just considering whether Robin might not have murdered Diana—I was looking at other suspects. But the nature of Diana’s murder gave me pause. It seemed personal. The ruthlessness of the beating she sustained while she slept pointed to someone who knew her. Someone who resented her. Not a stranger.
I had been sitting with that thought for some time when a name began to crop up in witness statements from Diana’s family and school friends: her stepfather. The statements referred to her troubled relationship with him and alleged that she had sustained sexual abuse at his hands throughout her childhood, which had never been reported. In the months before her murder, however, she had apparently told members of her family that she had finally built up the courage to go to the police. Her stepfather has since died, so the full truth may never be known.
Each of these threads complicated the picture further without resolving it. I had begun with one question—Did Robin kill Diana?—and ended up with several more, each pointing in a different direction.
Around this time, I started working with a production company on a documentary that would become “Murder at the Post Office,” a three-part television series for Sky. The question of how to frame Robin on screen was one I avoided as long as possible. In print, ambiguity is easier to sustain; you can hold two possibilities open simultaneously and let the reader sit with the tension. Television is less forgiving. Producers want a direction. I found myself in conversations about whether Robin should be presented as likely innocent, contested, or unknown—and I realized I genuinely did not know which category I believed he belonged in. I settled on contested. It felt the most honest. Robin watched the documentary when it aired. He called me the following week. He was grateful, he said. He thought it was fair. I was relieved, then immediately suspicious of my own relief. Why did his approval matter to me? I was supposed to be a journalist, not his advocate.
I still regularly make the eight-hour round trip from my home in the South of England up to Yorkshire to see Robin. I spend more time with him than many of my other friends. Each visit reminds me of the power of face-to-face conversation in a world that is moving increasingly online. Being able to look Robin in the eye as he answers a question gives me a perspective no phone call can replicate. Since the awkwardness of suggesting he could actually be guilty, I have felt freer to challenge him when we are together, to ask the questions that have been nagging at me. Was his marriage to Diana as happy as he makes out? From speaking to some people who still live in Melsonby, I had heard rumors of Diana seeking comfort elsewhere. Robin was quick to dismiss this. “Every marriage goes through difficulties, Ed,” he said calmly. “We had our tough patches, but we were happier than ever by the time she was taken from us.”
One of the unexpected consequences of spending five years on this case has been getting to know Diana. Not literally, of course; I never met her. But through her letters, her photographs, the testimonies of her family and friends, a person has gradually come into focus. A woman who, like all of us, was imperfect, but also deeply loyal, loving, and by all accounts great fun. The more I have learned about her, the more I have felt a responsibility toward her. Whatever the truth turns out to be—whether it was Robin who killed her, or someone else entirely—Diana deserves better than to remain a footnote in someone else’s story. That feeling has kept me going on the days when the case has felt too complicated, too unresolvable, and too consuming to continue with.
It also makes me wary of Robin. The what-ifs constantly circle. The question I find myself asking is no longer simply whether Robin is innocent or guilty, but whether he is the person who killed Diana. It has become personal. When I sit across from Robin in the visiting room, listening to him talk about her with what seems genuine tenderness, I cannot always hold those two things together: the man in front of me and what was done to her. Yet some days the contradiction is easy to set aside, and it is just a husband sitting across from me, eager to talk about his wife. Robin will dig deep into the back of his mind for seemingly mundane moments from their past. The time they could not find the car keys. When she found his hidden stash of biscuits. The dinner party they hosted in fancy dress. Although I have so many questions circling in my mind about their respective lives, one thing I am certain of is how much Robin loved Diana. Whether he killed her in a fit of rage or not, there is no question that he worshipped her.
I have recently allowed myself to lean toward a belief in Robin’s innocence, or at least toward a version of events in which the truth is considerably more complicated than the one a jury was asked to believe. I haven’t concluded, of course; I am not sure I will ever conclude.
Five years ago, I believed I could read people. I prided myself on it. It is, after all, a useful quality in business: the ability to size someone up quickly, to sense when you are being told what you want to hear. I assumed that five years of phone calls and prison visits, of watching Robin answer difficult questions, of learning when he deflects and when his tone changes, would have sharpened that instinct further. Instead, the opposite has happened. All our time together has— unintentionally—created a relationship, and my vision is clouded. I find myself second-guessing judgments I would once have made instinctively at work, with my friends and even my family. There is always a small voice now, asking whether I am simply a bad judge of character who got lucky, or unlucky, with Robin. Because the truth is that he is the only person on the planet who knows what happened in that bedroom to Diana.
My current relationship with Robin is still confusing. Our conversations are not like my conversations with other friends. I am still restrained. We rarely talk about films, or sport, or what we did at the weekend in any sustained way; when we do, those exchanges feel slightly performative on both sides, as though we are both trying to prove to the other, and perhaps to ourselves, that this is a normal relationship. It is not. The case is always underneath everything, even though I am yet to write that book. I have not found the right angle to tell Diana’s story.
But over time, I have, gradually, found myself opening up a little more to Robin. When my second child was born at the start of 2022, among the well wishes that arrived at our home was a card he had sent. According to the British justice system, one of the oldest and most revered on the planet, it was a card from a murderer. And yet here he was, sharing the moment with me, becoming in some small way part of my life alongside my family, my closest friends, my colleagues.
I have become more conscious of this recently. Whenever Robin calls, I still try to answer. Often it will be over the weekend, when I am with my family.
On one crisp, bright morning, I was in the garden speaking to Robin while trying to play hide-and-seek with my two daughters.
“Daddy, who are you speaking to?” my eldest asked.
“Robin,” I replied, apologizing down the phone, embarrassed by our opposing situations.
“Is he your friend?” she asked, with a child’s complete innocence. She looked at me for an answer. On the other end of the phone, Robin waited too, silent.
“Yes, darling,” I replied. What else could I say?
Edward Abel Smith is an author, producer, and investigative journalist. His work has covered some of the UK’s most serious claims of miscarriages of justice, including his multimillion-downloaded podcast about convicted nurse serial killer Lucy Letby, Was There Ever A Crime. His latest book, Murders in the Dark (DK, March 2027), reopens the case of the 1942 London Blackout Ripper and reveals new evidence that the wrong man may have gone to the gallows.
Editor: Carolyn Wells

Copyeditor: Brendan Fitzgerald

Education Shouldn't Be Held for Ransom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:33:46 UTC
03:33:46 KST

An open letter to the tech industry
If you ask any educator what the key to learning is, they won't say it's finding the right answer. They'll say it's what you gain from the struggle of getting there. Learning is found in the time and effort spent trying to understand an idea before it just "clicks."
That's what makes Google's latest announcement so galling to educators. Google announced this week that, starting in early 2027, AI tools will be turned off by default for K-12 Google Workspace for Education accounts.
On the surface it sounds like a win for schools until you read the fine print: Google Search will be switched off along with them. Google's explanation, from Chris Phillips, its vice president for education, speaking to The New York Times, is that "Search and AI are deeply integrated," so one cannot be switched off without the other.
After the backlash, Google walked part of it back, saying schools could switch on Search by itself, without the rest of its Gemini products. But the core problem remains. Search still can't be used without AI features like AI Overviews.
The educators asking for choice aren't anti-technology. They have spent years in the classroom, and they know firsthand that handing kids AI-generated answers doesn't build critical thinking; it weakens it.
Search is how students reach the open web. A search engine that arrives only with AI attached isn't offering a choice. It's holding education for ransom.
Learning to search is learning to think
A search engine is really an engine of discovery. When we search, we reflect, weigh, question, and synthesize, all at once. We’re exposed to rival sources and clashing perspectives, and we need sharp critical-thinking skills to discern the quality and relevance of what we find.
Technology companies are optimizing for speed. They talk about "removing friction," which is fine for unimportant things. There’s no benefit to friction when ordering takeout or getting a ride to the airport. But the same doesn't hold for education, because effort is the education. Friction, struggle, and perseverance is the learning. You simply can't speed-run understanding.
It helps to compare classroom learning with other kinds of training.
Imagine runners on the track team riding golf carts around the oval during "training" because the carts are faster and easier than running. They wouldn’t be preparing themselves to succeed in competition. That’s not how athletic training works. Progress is built out of sweat and discomfort.
Imagine band practice consisting of nothing but listening to Spotify, with no one painstakingly struggling to master their instruments or sheet music.
Science, math, and history are no different from athletics and music.
The best teachers rarely answer questions directly. They answer a question with a question of their own. The point isn't to hand over the answer but to make students wrestle with the question until they work it out on their own.
Likewise, a librarian doesn't hand you answers. A librarian's goal is to help you sharpen your research question and steer you toward better sources. That's the kind of help students need right now, especially in a world where the internet is being flooded by low quality AI slop. What students need more than ever are tools that teach them how to think, not what to think.
Information literacy is a practice, not a lesson
The educators I talk to aren't asking for a “magic wand.” They're asking for common-sense safeguards and controls that protect students at every grade level. This is scaffolding to make learning appropriate for all learners.
There’s nothing inherently wrong with giving students an AI answer occasionally, depending on the situation. But over-reliance can quickly turn into outsourcing the very thinking they’re in school to learn. The result over time is the acceptance without challenge of any information presented by AI. This is especially problematic when AI "hallucinates" or fabricates information.
Educators should get to decide when and how AI shows up for their students. Not a vendor. And certainly not under threat of losing basic access to web search.
Follow the incentives
Google is a successful company because they do a great job serving their customers. Unfortunately for educators and students, Google’s customers are advertisers, not users.
Google is the world's largest advertising company, so it's important to understand that when a search engine is funded by ads, it makes every user the product. Google's own founders saw this coming. In a 1998 Stanford paper they warned that advertising-funded search engines "will be inherently biased towards the advertisers and away from the needs of the consumers."
So when Google tells schools that Search and AI can't be separated, we need to ask who this serves. Is it because it isn’t technically feasible or simply because it isn’t in the best interest of Google advertisers and shareholders?
When educators ask for choice or a slowdown of AI in education, it isn’t because it benefits them directly. It’s because their incentives are aligned with student incentives and they believe in slower, evidence-based approaches over experimenting on kids with brand-new technologies.
At Kagi, we believe in choice
Like Google, Kagi also does a great job serving our customers. The difference is that Kagi’s customers are the users. We build tools that are in the best interest of the people using them. That's why we created Kagi Search with a different user-aligned model. Instead of building at the expense of users, we seek to empower our users with choice.
Our users pay us in order to NOT be the product. And in return we give them the best search with no ads, no tracking and no selling of data. Because when the user is the customer, the user's interests and the company's interests are aligned and in harmony.
For schools, this means:
- AI is optional, not required. Quick Answer only appears when a student asks for it, and schools can turn AI features on or off for the students who are ready.
- Schools stay in control. Block low-quality or distracting sites for everyone, raise trusted sources, and build custom Lenses with teacher-approved resources for class projects
- Fewer dead ends. Students can see when a result is paywalled before they click, instead of hitting a wall mid-research.
- Less noise. Kagi has no ads and no clickbait thumbnails. But it does have filters that hide AI-generated slop images, so students can focus on the information itself.
- Tools that guide, not answer. We're building features that empower students to refine their research questions and search better.
Our ask
To Google and the rest of the industry: Let’s stop putting corporate profits over the civilizational imperative to truly educate students. Let’s give schools choice over coercion and lock-in.
To schools facing this choice: You don't have to accept it. There are alternatives to mandatory AI, and Kagi is one of them.
Kagi for Education
Your students shouldn't have to accept AI to use search. Kagi gives schools clean, ad-free results with AI off by default, and the controls to decide when it comes on.
Contact us for a quote or a free trial for your school or district.
By Kevin Elgan
Kevin Elgan is Head of Marketing at Kagi and has spent over 15 years in education technology working alongside educators. In prior roles he trained thousands of teachers to use technology effectively in the classroom.

- Less noise. Kagi has no ads and no clickbait thumbnails. But it does have filters that hide AI-generated slop images, so students can focus on the information itself.
- Tools that guide, not answer. We're building features that empower students to refine their research questions and search better.

Benchfmt.rs: Bringing Go's benchmarking and benchstat workflow to Rust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:20:06 UTC
03:20:06 KST

benchfmt.rs: Bringing Go's Benchmarking and benchstat Workflow to Rust
TL;DR: I built benchfmt.rs, a zero-dependency Rust benchmark runner and Criterion converter for Go’s benchstat. It adds /key=value projections, heap tracking for allocated bytes (B/op) and objects (allocs/op) per op, and pprof profiling.
In this post, I am benchmarking varint and Prometheus Remote Write 2.0 decoding across Go and Rust to showcase the benefits of benchstat-like flow in Rust. I’m also sharing some fun learnings on the way (e.g., yes Rust is faster).
Recently, I’ve been working on a few Rust projects across Google and open source. I came to Rust after years of writing performance-sensitive Go in Prometheus, Thanos, and teaching Go in the “Efficient Go” book. For me, much of Rust’s performance story is really good, until…. I wanted to run A/B microbenchmarks.
Perhaps I was spoiled by the Go benchmarking ecosystem, with the go tool -bench and benchstat in the center. To me, Rust standard benchmarking tools are lacking:
- Standard format for case comparison projections.
- Standard heap allocation measurements.
- Standard pprof support.
- Simple to understand reliability scoring.
DISCLAIMER: A standard here means something that will be familiar to large number of developers, and I biased on Go experience for sure!
As a result, I asked myself: can we get benchstat-compatible output for Rust microbenchmarks? Wouldn’t that make A/B testing easier and unlock fun Go vs Rust comparisons?
Here we are! I built benchfmt.rs, a zero-dependency Rust benchmark runner with a thread-local heap allocation counter, pprof profiler integration, and the same CLI flags as go test -bench. For those who don’t trust a new benchmarking runtime (you shouldn’t from the start!), it also ships a Criterion and libtest converter that emits Go’s benchfmt format directly.
In this blog post, we will implement the same pieces of code in Go and Rust, benchmark them across different Rust frameworks, and compare the results. We might learn something new along the way (I did when building this!). Enjoy!
All benchmark code and raw outputs live in bwplotka/benchmarks/benchmarks/rust-go-decode.
Benchmarking two workloads
Let’s pick two workloads to implement and benchmark in both Go and Rust. I am particularly curious about protobuf decoding performance, which, funny enough, is often one of the main costs of running distributed systems these days. Thus, let’s decode our Prometheus Remote Write 2.0 protocol. Because protobuf code generators have different maturity and trade-offs across languages, let’s also measure something simpler alongside it, a standalone varint decoder.
Workload details:
- DecodeVarints. A 36-line unsigned LEB128 varint stream decoder. Varints are the integer encoding underneath Protocol Buffers. Our fixture varints_2000.bin is 4,798 bytes and packs 2,000 uint64 values mixing 1-byte symbol indices, 2-byte bucket offsets, 4-byte deltas, and 6-byte millisecond Unix timestamps. The function writes into a preallocated 2,000-element slice with zero heap allocations.
- DecodeRemoteWrite2. A full HTTP request body decoder for Snappy-compressed Remote Write 2.0 (io.prometheus.write.v2.Request) payloads. We test batches of 200 and 2,000 series, where 2,000 matches Prometheus’s default max_samples_per_send. The 2,000-series fixture mixes counters, gauges, classic and native histograms, 1,000 trace exemplars, and metric metadata. Remote Write 2.0 interns all strings into a top-level symbols table and stores packed varint labels_refs per series. That shrinks the 2,000-series batch to 244.9 KiB uncompressed and 57.0 KiB Snappy-compressed.
Implementing and benchmarking in Go
Let’s start with Go. First, DecodeVarints writes straight into a caller-provided slice, with a fast path for single-byte values below 0x80:
func DecodeVarints(src []byte, dst []uint64) (int, error) {
	n := 0
	i := 0
	for i < len(src) {
		if n >= len(dst) {
			return n, ErrDstTooSmall
		}
		b := src[i]
		i++
		if b < 0x80 {
			dst[n] = uint64(b)
			n++
			continue
		}
		x := uint64(b & 0x7f)
		shift := uint(7)
		for {
			if i >= len(src) {
				return n, ErrUnexpectedEOF
			}
			b = src[i]
			i++
			x |= uint64(b&0x7f) << shift
			if b < 0x80 {
				break
			}
			shift += 7
			if shift >= 64 {
				return n, ErrOverflow
			}
		}
		dst[n] = x
		n++
	}
	return n, nil
}
Second, for DecodeRemoteWrite2, we tune the Go implementation the way Prometheus runs in production rather than benchmarking slow reflection-based unmarshaling. We pair github.com/golang/snappy, which uses x86-64 assembly on linux/amd64, with vtprotobuf and its generated, optimized UnmarshalVT decoder:
func DecodeRemoteWrite2(compressed []byte) (*writev2.Request, error) {
	raw, err := snappy.Decode(nil, compressed)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	req := &writev2.Request{}
	if err := req.UnmarshalVT(raw); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return req, nil
}
Now let’s measure the efficiency of our Go code!
Notice Go’s /key=value sub-benchmark names (samples=2000/lang=go), which let Go’s official benchstat tool pivot across /lang or /samples later, along with b.SetBytes, b.ReportAllocs, and for b.Loop():
func BenchmarkDecodeVarints(b *testing.B) {
	manifest := ensureFixtures(b)
	raw, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join("testdata", "varints_2000.bin"))
	if err != nil {
		b.Fatalf("read varints: %v", err)
	}
	dst := make([]uint64, manifest.VarintsCount)
	// Encode dimensions as /key=value so benchstat can pivot across /samples or /lang.
	b.Run("samples=2000/lang=go", func(b *testing.B) {
		b.SetBytes(int64(len(raw)))
		b.ReportAllocs()
		// NOTE: b.Loop() resets the timer on its first call, stops it on exit, and keeps
		// call arguments and results alive without package-level sink variables.
		for b.Loop() {
			n, err := DecodeVarints(raw, dst)
			if err != nil || n != manifest.VarintsCount {
				b.Fatalf("unexpected decode result: n=%d err=%v", n, err)
			}
		}
	})
}
func BenchmarkDecodeRemoteWrite2(b *testing.B) {
	ensureFixtures(b)
	for _, samples := range []int{200, 2000} {
		file := fmt.Sprintf("rw2_%d.snappy", samples)
		compressed, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join("testdata", file))
		if err != nil {
			b.Fatalf("read %s: %v", file, err)
		}
		b.Run(fmt.Sprintf("samples=%d/lang=go", samples), func(b *testing.B) {
			b.SetBytes(int64(len(compressed)))
			b.ReportAllocs()
			for b.Loop() {
				req, err := DecodeRemoteWrite2(compressed)
				if err != nil || len(req.Timeseries) != samples {
					b.Fatalf("unexpected v2 decode: err=%v", err)
				}
			}
		})
	}
}
Finally, let’s run 6 benchmark runs (“epochs”) for 2s each at -cpu 2 on a 24-core Intel Xeon 2.20GHz Linux workstation (Go 1.26.8, Rust 1.99.1):
go test -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkDecode' \
    -benchtime 2s -count 6 -cpu 2 -timeout 999m -benchmem \
| tee results/go.txt
One epoch looks as follows:

Implementing and benchmarking in Rust with Criterion
Now let’s port both decoders and benchmarks to Rust. First, decode_varints mirrors the Go loop line for line:
pub fn decode_varints(src: &[u8], dst: &mut [u64]) -> Result<usize, VarintError> {
    let mut n = 0usize;
    let mut i = 0usize;
    while i < src.len() {
        if n >= dst.len() {
            return Err(VarintError::DstTooSmall);
        }
        let mut b = src[i];
        i += 1;
        if b < 0x80 {
            dst[n] = u64::from(b);
            n += 1;
            continue;
        }
        let mut x = u64::from(b & 0x7f);
        let mut shift = 7u32;
        loop {
            if i >= src.len() {
                return Err(VarintError::UnexpectedEof);
            }
            b = src[i];
            i += 1;
            x |= u64::from(b & 0x7f) << shift;
            if b < 0x80 {
                break;
            }
            shift += 7;
            if shift >= 64 {
                return Err(VarintError::Overflow);
            }
        }
        dst[n] = x;
        n += 1;
    }
    Ok(n)
}
Second, decode_remote_write2 pairs the snap crate with prost compile-time generated Message structs:
pub fn decode_remote_write2(compressed: &[u8]) -> Result<proto::v2::Request, String> {
    let raw = snap::raw::Decoder::new()
        .decompress_vec(compressed)
        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
    proto::v2::Request::decode(raw.as_slice()).map_err(|e| e.to_string())
}
Now, let’s write both Rust benchmarks using Criterion, the default choice for stable-Rust microbenchmarking. We keep the same /key=value benchmark IDs and configure Throughput::BytesDecimal to match Go’s decimal MB/s:
fn bench_varints(c: &mut Criterion) {
    // Resolve testdata/ from the crate directory baked in at compile time.
    let root = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("testdata");
    let raw = fs::read(root.join("varints_2000.bin")).unwrap();
    // Preallocate the output buffer outside the timed loop so each op does 0 heap allocs.
    let mut dst = vec![0u64; 2000];
    // Group + function ID join into "DecodeVarints/samples=2000/lang=rust" to match Go's b.Run.
    let mut group = c.benchmark_group("DecodeVarints");
    // Report decimal MB/s (1e6 B/s) to match Go's b.SetBytes; Throughput::Bytes prints MiB/s.
    group.throughput(Throughput::BytesDecimal(raw.len() as u64));
    group.bench_function("samples=2000/lang=rust", |b| {
        // b.iter runs the closure across Criterion's warmup and 100 linear-ramp samples.
        b.iter(|| {
            // std::hint::black_box is an LLVM optimization barrier: Unlike Go's b.Loop(), Rust
            // would constant-fold known inputs or delete unused work without black_box hints.
            let n = decode_varints(black_box(&raw), black_box(&mut dst)).unwrap();
            assert_eq!(n, 2000);
            // Observe the written buffer so LLVM cannot optimize away stores into dst.
            black_box(dst[n - 1]);
        });
    });
    group.finish();
}
fn bench_remote_write2(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let root = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("testdata");
    let mut group = c.benchmark_group("DecodeRemoteWrite2");
    for samples in [200usize, 2000usize] {
        let file = format!("rw2_{samples}.snappy");
        let compressed = fs::read(root.join(file)).unwrap();
        group.throughput(Throughput::BytesDecimal(compressed.len() as u64));
        let id = format!("samples={samples}/lang=rust");
        group.bench_function(&id, |b| {
            b.iter(|| {
                let req = decode_remote_write2(black_box(&compressed)).unwrap();
                assert_eq!(req.timeseries.len(), samples);
                // Force req to materialize before dropping at the end of the iteration.
                black_box(req);
            });
        });
    }
    group.finish();
}
// Generate the benchmark group runner and custom main() required by harness = false in Cargo.toml.
criterion_group!(benches, bench_varints, bench_remote_write2);
criterion_main!(benches);
Finally, let’s run the Criterion benchmark suite:

Criterion downsides
Criterion is convenient when you want confidence intervals and HTML plots from a single cargo bench command without external tools. However, compared to go test and benchstat, four design choices get in the way:
- Compile weight. Pulling in criterion with default-features = false still compiles clap, regex-automata, ciborium, oorandom, itertools, tinytemplate, and anes. That adds 42 transitive crates and ~19s to a cold cargo bench build.
- Linear-ramp sampling vs steady-state epochs. 
  - Go’s testing.B calibrates a fixed iteration count N for -benchtime 2s and runs -count 6 equal steady-state epochs, which benchstat summarizes using the outlier-resistant median and Mann-Whitney U test.
  - Criterion defaults to Linear sampling: after a 3-second warmup, it collects 100 batches of [1d, 2d, ..., 100d] iterations and fits a least-squares line y = m * x through the origin. Because the line is forced through zero, it does not subtract a fixed timer-overhead intercept. Instead, it computes a k^2-weighted average where batch 100 carries 10,000x the weight of batch 1 and late OS spikes pull the slope up.
Comparing those two models directly introduces two measurable distortions: 
  - First, grouping Criterion’s 100 ramp samples into 6 benchstat epochs gives epoch 1 11.5x fewer iterations than epoch 6 (24,888 vs 286,212 on DecodeVarints). Mixing short bursts with long runs inflates variance to ± 5%, compared to ± 1-2% in steady-state epochs.
  - Second, timing 100 separate closure batches adds +8.6% overhead on microsecond loops (5.36 µs vs 4.90 µs, p=0.002) and skews early allocating samples with cold allocator caches (+2.3% on DecodeRemoteWrite2).
- No heap allocation tracking. Criterion reports wall-clock time and throughput only. On DecodeVarints at 0 allocs/op, that is fine. On DecodeRemoteWrite2, we cannot tell whether prost made 500 heap allocations or 500,000, or whether a refactor doubled heap churn.
- Pairwise baseline folders vs multi-dimensional tables. Criterion compares target/criterion/<id>/base against new. You cannot feed a single run file into a table that pivots -col /samples or -col /lang across Go and Rust.
Converting Criterion output with the benchfmt CLI
If a Rust codebase already uses Criterion, rewriting benchmarks just to get a benchstat table is not ideal. That is why benchfmt.rs includes a standalone benchfmt CLI binary. It reads benchmark.json and sample.json directly from target/criterion, extracts Throughput::BytesDecimal (or Throughput::Bytes) as decimal MB/s, and groups Criterion’s 100 samples into 6 contiguous epochs via --epochs 6:
cargo install --git https://github.com/bwplotka/benchfmt.rs
benchfmt criterion target/criterion \
    --pkg github.com/bwplotka/benchmarks/benchmarks/rust-go-decode \
    --cpu 2 \
> results/rust_criterion.txt
benchstat -col /lang results/go.txt results/rust_criterion.txt
Without touching the benchmark implementation, benchstat gives us a side-by-side Go vs Rust table:

Now, with this view we finally have a readable, standard benchstat output Go developers love. It clearly shows the Go vs Rust efficiency for our example functions. Rust is 37.16% faster on DecodeVarints (5.36 µs vs 8.54 µs) and 13.37% to 15.72% faster on DecodeRemoteWrite2.
Unfortunately, there are some gaps:
- The B/op and allocs/op tables only have a go column because Criterion never recorded allocations
- Criterion’s linear-ramp epochs still leave ± 5% variance on DecodeVarints.
Native benchfmt runs with benchfmt::Suite and CountingAlloc
For new Rust benchmarks, we can skip Criterion and use benchfmt::Suite with harness = false in Cargo.toml. Registering CountingAlloc as #[global_allocator] tracks every alloc, alloc_zeroed, and realloc in a thread_local! Cell<(u64, u64)> with zero atomic contention and zero external dependencies:
// Wrap Rust's System allocator globally so every heap alloc/realloc on the benchmark thread
// increments thread-local (allocs, bytes) counters for B/op and allocs/op.
#[global_allocator]
static ALLOC: CountingAlloc = CountingAlloc::new();
fn main() {
    let root = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("testdata");
    let raw_varints = fs::read(root.join("varints_2000.bin")).unwrap();
    let rw2_200 = fs::read(root.join("rw2_200.snappy")).unwrap();
    let rw2_2000 = fs::read(root.join("rw2_2000.snappy")).unwrap();
    let mut dst = vec![0u64; 2000];
    // Parse go-test-compatible CLI flags (-bench, -benchtime, -count, -cpu, -benchmem,
    // -cpuprofile, -memprofile) from std::env::args() and set the default "pkg:" header.
    // Using the same pkg path as Go's go.mod lets `benchstat -col /lang` join Go and Rust rows.
    Suite::from_env("github.com/bwplotka/benchmarks/benchmarks/rust-go-decode")
        // Attach ALLOC so each benchmark snapshots thread-local allocation deltas per epoch.
        .with_alloc(&ALLOC)
        // Suite prepends "Benchmark" in benchfmt output, matching Go's BenchmarkDecodeVarints.
        .bench("DecodeVarints/samples=2000/lang=rust", |b| {
            b.set_bytes(raw_varints.len() as u64);
            b.report_allocs();
            // Go b.Loop() equivalent: starts timing, alloc snapshots, and any pprof capture on the
            // first call, runs the calibrated N steady-state iterations, then stops all three.
            while b.keep_running() {
                let n = decode_varints(black_box(&raw_varints), black_box(&mut dst)).unwrap();
                assert_eq!(n, 2000);
                black_box(dst[n - 1]);
            }
        })
        .bench("DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=200/lang=rust", |b| {
            b.set_bytes(rw2_200.len() as u64);
            b.report_allocs();
            while b.keep_running() {
                let req = decode_remote_write2(black_box(&rw2_200)).unwrap();
                assert_eq!(req.timeseries.len(), 200);
                black_box(req);
            }
        })
        .bench("DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=2000/lang=rust", |b| {
            b.set_bytes(rw2_2000.len() as u64);
            b.report_allocs();
            while b.keep_running() {
                let req = decode_remote_write2(black_box(&rw2_2000)).unwrap();
                assert_eq!(req.timeseries.len(), 2000);
                black_box(req);
            }
        })
        .run();
}
Does CountingAlloc work with Tokio and custom allocators? Mostly yes. You can wrap custom allocators like jemalloc or mimalloc via CountingAlloc::with_allocator(Jemalloc). Because CountingAlloc uses thread-local counters on the benchmark thread, single-threaded Tokio current_thread works out of the box, while multi-threaded pools like tokio::spawn or rayon need a process-wide atomic AllocTracker passed to Suite::with_alloc.
Suite::from_env reads std::env::args(), auto-detects goos, goarch, and cpu, and writes the passed string as the pkg: metadata line (matching Go’s module path so benchstat joins Go and Rust rows into one table). Passing flags after -- mirrors go test:
cargo bench --bench suite_decode -- \
    -bench '^BenchmarkDecode' -benchtime 2s -count 6 -cpu 2 -benchmem \
| tee results/rust_suite.txt
First, let’s verify that benchfmt::Suite agrees with Criterion on timing, even with CountingAlloc active on every allocation:
benchstat criterion=results/rust_criterion.txt suite=results/rust_suite.txt
                                            │  criterion  │               suite               │
                                            │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base              │
DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=2000/lang=rust-2   2.082m ± 1%   2.033m ± 2%  -2.33% (p=0.015 n=6)
DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=200/lang=rust-2    235.1µ ± 4%   231.5µ ± 1%  -1.55% (p=0.004 n=6)
DecodeVarints/samples=2000/lang=rust-2        5.364µ ± 5%   4.902µ ± 2%  -8.60% (p=0.002 n=6)
geomean                                       138.0µ        132.1µ       -4.21%
On DecodeRemoteWrite2, Criterion and benchfmt::Suite agree within 1.6% to 2.3%, while Suite’s steady-state 2s epochs tighten worst-case variance from ± 4-5% down to ± 1-2%. On DecodeVarints, while b.keep_running() runs 490,000 back-to-back iterations in one tight loop instead of 100 short ramp batches, clocking 4.90 µs vs 5.36 µs.
Comparing Go vs Rust
Now let’s run the full Go vs Rust comparison with results/rust_suite.txt:
benchstat -col /lang results/go.txt results/rust_suite.txt
