The Unexpected Ingredient I Reach For Every Time I Cook Chicken
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

I Never Use Oil to Marinate Chicken Breast — This Beloved Southern Ingredient Works Magic
I don’t recommend betting on whether there’s a partial container of buttermilk in my fridge at any given time; I’ll always win! Because buttermilk is typically sold by the quart, and my favorite buttermilk biscuit recipe only uses 1 cup, I always have some left over. I could freeze extra buttermilk, but I don’t want to lose it in the icy dark hole that is my freezer. Instead, I’ve been looking for new, simple ways to use buttermilk that make the most of the thick, tangy, creamy liquid.
I was recently making chicken for dinner, and buttermilk became an unexpected kitchen hero. I usually toss my boneless, skinless chicken breasts with spices and oil before cooking to create an even, flavorful coating. Somehow I was nearly out of oil (!), and needed the dregs for the hot skillet. I grabbed some buttermilk and added just enough to disperse the spices and coat the chicken before searing it. I figured if buttermilk works as a marinade, why not try it in a quicker application? Not only did it work, but it also created the most beautifully browned, juicy chicken. I’ve found my new go-to method.
What Makes Buttermilk-Coated Chicken So Great
Buttermilk is a popular choice for marinades, like in this buttermilk-brined grilled chicken, because its acidity tenderizes proteins as it sits, and its thick viscosity clings to meat, carrying flavor. Here, buttermilk brings something different to the table. Buttermilk isn’t as rich as oil, but it does contain fat and natural sugars (lactose). Coating chicken lightly before searing creates a barrier between the meat and the hot pan, preventing the exterior from becoming tough while allowing the sugars to caramelize and brown the surface. Because it doesn’t sit as long as a marinade, you can’t really taste the buttermilk, but it deepens the flavor through the Maillard reaction and makes the chicken look oh-so-beautiful.
How to Cook Buttermilk-Coated Chicken
- Dry and season the chicken. Pat 1 1/2 pounds boneless, skinless chicken breasts dry (3 medium or 2 large). Season both sides with kosher salt, freshly ground pepper, and your favorite dry spices. I like garlic powder, paprika, and dried oregano, but buttermilk is neutral enough to pair well with whatever you like.
- Add buttermilk and toss to coat. Drizzle 2 tablespoons shaken buttermilk over the chicken and turn the pieces a few times to fully coat both sides.
- Cook the chicken. Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large, oven-proof skillet over medium heat until hot, but not smoking. Add the chicken breasts, leaving a bit of space between them, and cook until golden on both sides, flipping halfway, 8 to 10 minutes. Transfer the skillet to a 400°F oven and roast until the chicken reaches 165°F in the thickest part, 10 to 15 minutes more.
Tips for Making Chicken with Buttermilk
- More is not better. This isn’t a marinating technique where you want the chicken fully submerged. There should be virtually no buttermilk pooling in the bottom of your bowl because any drippy excess will just splatter in the hot oil. If you accidentally added too much, lift the chicken up and give it a gentle shake over the bowl so the extra drips away.
- Whole-milk and low-fat buttermilk are both fine. Low-fat cultured buttermilk is often the only buttermilk on the shelf at my store, but when I spot whole-milk buttermilk, with its thicker consistency and richer taste, I always grab it. Either one will work great, although you might need a little more whole-milk buttermilk to get the same even coating.
- Don’t skip seasoning. Buttermilk has a lovely, milky, mild tang, but you don’t taste it after it’s cooked, so don’t equate a slick of buttermilk with seasoning your chicken. You can stay simple with salt and pepper, or get inspired and use spice mixes from around the world.

I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
16:51:35 UTC
01:51:35 KST

On Tuesday, Apple rolled out a potentially controversial set of Audio Intelligence features into testing with the first developer beta versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The betas bring four new AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
After just a day with Apple’s Siri Recaps feature on my Apple Watch, I can already see how its value may ultimately outweigh any creepiness factor that comes from the AI-powered audio recording and summarization it provides. However, I also see areas where AI-assisted note-taking can go too far, capturing things that aren’t worth remembering, and where there’s room for improvement.
The first two, sound and song detection, don’t represent potential privacy concerns; they are designed to detect either important sounds — like an alarm or doorbell — or identify a song using Shazam’s technology. The former helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users navigate the world, and the latter is something we’ve already done with our iPhone for nearly two decades now.
It’s the two other features, Live Rewind and Siri Recaps, that have raised concerns. The features record and then transcribe or summarize the conversations happening with and around the Apple Watch’s owner. Live Rewind lets you go back to see what was said in the past 15 seconds, while Siri Recaps summarize audio throughout your day, saving notes of the important things that were said.
Apple has taken care to ensure the privacy of these AI features by processing the audio and running AI models on-device, when possible, and by not identifying speakers, storing raw audio files, and redacting private information, like government ID numbers or personal account information.
Still, some are put off by the idea that we’re now normalizing the idea that technology is always listening.
I find myself sympathizing with both camps. I often lament that we’ve allowed technology to become so pervasive in our daily lives, but I still see the value in what Apple has built.
I haven’t yet had an appropriate time to test Live Rewind, nor do I think this will be a feature I use as often. I’m more likely to say “sorry, what?” or “can you repeat that?” if I missed something that was said, before turning to my Apple Watch for help.
But with Siri Recaps, I immediately saw how this could become a feature I rely on regularly to save important notes for later.
I was able to test the feature in a real-world scenario yesterday, when we were dropping off my teen’s car for repairs and picking up a rental. At both places, employees shared a lot of information about time frames, prices, and policies that were delivered verbally. The information came too fast to stop and write anything down. Yet when I returned to Siri Recaps later in the day, it had captured key details that I may need to refer back to.
For instance, it noted the deductible, the repair time frame, the amount of gas we had in the rental at the start, and other things I wanted to remember.
One complaint is that Siri Recaps had mixed this information with other topics that were later discussed in the home, like an errand we needed to run and what time babysitting was this week, something we were discussing in order to create an appointment on the family calendar with an appropriate alert time frame.
I think these items should have been saved in a separate note titled “family schedule and errands,” rather than in the same note with the car repairs, but under a separate heading.
Because I configured Siri Recaps to run at all times, it also captured non-essential things, like our “plan” to watch the midterms coverage on TV, which is not the kind of thing you’d normally jot down a note about. It also was a stark reminder that the feature was listening in on our everyday conversations. That’s something that could feel invasive in different scenarios, if the subject being discussed was more personal in nature.
This had me considering turning off the Recap feature while at home in the evening, so family dinner table chatter doesn’t become note fodder.
While I appreciated that the Recap picked up a reminder about an errand I needed to run from one of the family conversations, other tidbits it saved — like what we were watching on TV — would only be valuable if you were exporting a Siri Recap note to Apple’s Journal app, because it was something you wanted to record for personal reasons.
I’d like to see these sorts of extraneous details saved as separate notes — or at least as dedicated sections that could be exported or deleted on their own at the end of the day.
I’d also love to be able to swipe left on an individual bullet point to remove it from the Siri Recap entirely, rather than having to enter edit mode, place the cursor, and then start deleting the text I don’t need.
Another option I’d like to have would be a setting that would allow you to automatically export any saved Siri Recap (the ones you click the bookmark icon to save) to Apple’s Notes app, instead of that being an extra step.
These Recaps could go into their own folder in the Notes app for easy reference. I can understand why this option is not the default, given how many different ways people use a general-purpose app like Notes. However, it would be useful for those of us who want to keep Notes as the central starting point for all our jotted-down reminders and to-dos.
Though I wasn’t immediately warmed up to the idea that my Watch was always listening, so to speak, I see the value of this sort of automated note-taking in daily life.

It installs right against a window using an including mounting sticker to reduce glare and reflections, but the camera doesn’t require any weatherproofing since it’s not enduring the elements outdoors.
Anker’s new window-mounted camera monitors the outside of your home from within it
The Eufy Window Cam E10 sticks directly to the inside of a window so installation takes less than a minute.
The Eufy Window Camera E10 is available now for $79.99 through Anker’s online store and Amazon, making it more than twice as expensive as the $34.98 Wyze Window Cam. The E10 also offers a slightly wider and taller field of view than Wyze’s camera at 105 degrees horizontal and 57 degrees vertical. But to accommodate a wider range of installations such as an upstairs window the angle of the E10’s camera can be manually adjusted up and down by 25 degrees using a wheel on the back to ensure the areas you want monitored are properly in frame.
Other features of the E10 include color night vision, AI-powered motion detection and alerts that can differentiate between humans, animals, and vehicles, and a microphone that’s limited to louder noises given the camera’s location. Footage can be recorded locally to a microSD card up to 256GB in size, or pushed to the cloud with an optional subscription. And while Anker claims installation can take less than a minute, you will have to deal with potentially routing and hiding a power cord since the E10 lacks a rechargeable battery.

Google faces backlash for plan that would turn off Search for schools that restrict AI

2026-11-04

01:17:22 KST

Google was met with swift backlash on Tuesday after it announced that schools using Google’s K-12 software will not be able to use Search unless they opt in to using AI tools.
Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” so if a student’s school doesn’t opt in to using AI tools like Gemini, then students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”
Even as Google made this announcement on a busy Election Day, several left-leaning politicians took time to speak up about their concerns.
Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) accused Google in an X post of “extortion,” writing that “Google is threatening schools: if you stop your students from using AI, we will cut off your access to Google Search.” Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said on X that Google is “more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed.”
Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair and staunch advocate against monopolies, also condemned Google’s decision as anticompetitive.
“This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” she wrote. “Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened.”
New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of being a monopoly, commenting, “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”
While Search is a necessary tool for information gathering, educators worry that its built-in AI overviews could dissuade students from finding answers themselves. For millions of students required to use Chromebooks and Google education tools, using a different search engine isn’t a simple fix.
Google says that it’s working on a “Guided Learning” tool for student accounts in Search, which is supposed to walk students through the process of solving a problem or finding information, rather than just handing them the answer. If a student is struggling with a math problem, for example, the feature may prompt them to refresh their memory about the rules for dividing exponents, instead of spitting out a number.
In response to the backlash, Google pointed out in a post on X that it had listened to educators by turning off access to AI products by default and noted that schools could turn on Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually.
“We know there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control,” Google wrote in its statement. “That’s exactly why we are making these changes today to address the feedback we’ve heard from educators in recent months. And we’ll continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.”

'It's just vape, nail, charity shops': Can anything save UK high street?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
16:11:33 UTC
01:11:33 KST

On 22 May 1987, retail history was made in Rotherham. Parkgate Retail World, thought at the time to be the UK’s largest open-air shopping centre, welcomed shoppers for some one-stop retail therapy. The official opening was marked in swanky fashion with a “breathtaking” display from Marlboro’s red-and-white branded biplanes, followed by a “spectacular” laser show, the first in South Yorkshire. Helen Worth – Coronation Street’s Gail Platt – cut the ribbon before jovial local people jostled to fill their car boots with goods from Comet, Jolly Giant and Poundstretcher.
Almost 40 years on, the razzle is a bit less dazzling. Parkgate, as the retail park is called now, looks like any large big-box outdoor shopping centre you might find on urban fringes. There’s a Primark, a Sports Direct and a Matalan, plus (of course) a Frankie & Benny’s. Shoppers still seem to love it. “I think it’s ideal. It’s got everything here,” says Robert Gordon. The 66-year-old retired factory production manager had popped to Pets at Home to get a cupcake and toy for his dog Bruno’s fourth birthday.
Gordon has lived in Rotherham for 24 years. “A lot of people come to outlets like this. It’s very rare we go into the town centre and, if we did, we’d go to Sheffield,” he says. He is hardly an outlier. Almost half of Britons don’t visit their high street weekly. Instead, shoppers are opting for retail parks. Business is so strong, retailers are scrambling for spots, even paying extra to secure their place. By the end of 2025, only 4.8% of retail park lots in Britain were vacant, according to real estate consultancy Knight Frank – the lowest level on record. Vacancy rates for UK high streets, on the other hand, sit at 13%, reports Savills.
Gordon remembers a time two decades ago when you “couldn’t move” in Rotherham town centre, especially at the weekend. “It was packed and all the local shops were busy. Now these big outlets have taken over.” He admits his shopping habits come at a cost to the local community. “We are part of the problem,” he says. “It’s not progress. You used to meet people, but now you’re lucky to see anyone you know. Most people will come here and shop, get what they need and go back home.”
Jo Hill, 59, and her husband Richard, 65, are also Rotherham locals. Until recently, they hadn’t set foot in the town centre in nearly two decades. “What you see is either vape shops, nail shops or charity shops,” says Jo, who is semi-retired. Rotherham town centre is bookended by Parkgate at one end, and Meadowhall – one of the UK’s largest indoor shopping centres – at the other. The couple were visiting Parkgate to buy a printer from Currys. “For the big stuff, it’s either here or Meadowhall,” says Richard.
A short journey away, in Rotherham town centre, the picture is different. About 70 retail units, 24% overall, are vacant, far higher than the national average, and it is immediately apparent. One of the first things you see when leaving the train station is a derelict branch of BrightHouse, a rent-to-own retailer selling large appliances and furniture, which shut down in 2020. Further up is an anonymous-looking shopfront with smashed windows, graffiti and empty panelling where a shop sign should be – another shuttered chain, Fultons Foods, which closed in 2022. The only identifying mark is a window sticker: “There’s always change at Fultons.” Vape shops, discount chains and charity shops dominate the street.
The arrival of Parkgate Retail World nearly four decades ago wasn’t without friction. Even then, market traders expressed fears about the impact on business and, in Westminster, parliamentarians warned that these mini shopping metropolises would drain jobs from the high street, “disembowel towns and villages” and disadvantage those unable to drive.
Donna, who owns a furniture shop, and Saj, who runs a sandwich deli, are on their lunch break when I stop them. “It’s declined totally. I really wish it hasn’t, but it has,” says Donna. Nowadays she usually serves about four or five customers, and her daily takings have declined to “virtually nothing”, she says. Saj agrees that footfall is nonexistent.
The pair say safety is one reason that locals, especially elderly people, are staying home. “People have had their bags stolen, or been followed into banks; you’re watched when using the cash machines,” says Donna. “People will only come if they feel safe. It was always the older generation that came into the shop buying beds. Now their families won’t let them come out.” In 2023, a government analysis found that the number of crimes carried out per 1,000 people in Rotherham town was 160, 72% higher than the national average at the time. Recent police data shows there were 1,105 crimes, including 356 violent and sexual offences and 188 instances of shoplifting recorded in central Rotherham in August of this year alone. Nearby Sheffield city centre recorded 836 crimes in the same period. Donna says drug users also hang around her shopfront. “They sleep in my doorway sometimes. There’s needles and all sorts left. We’re not getting anybody into the shop because it looks bad.”
For Saj, the lack of affordable parking is another problem killing the high street. Car ownership has soared since the advent of the retail park. In 1971, 52% of households in Britain owned a car. A decade later, this had jumped to 60%, and by 2022 nearly three-quarters of households had a car. On its website, Parkgate touts its “over 2,000 free parking spaces”, all in one concentrated area.
Within Rotherham town centre, there are 1,610 spaces, which, until fairly recently, were all paid – though the council has recognised parking as a challenge. In 2016 it cut long-stay charges from £6.50 to £3.50 a day, and last year, it introduced free parking for one hour on weekdays. At the weekend, some spaces are free all day, but many, while acknowledging the council’s efforts, say it is not enough.
Sitting on a bench and lapping up the sun on Rotherham High Street are Leo Lopez and Claire Mercer. “I’ve seen a massive change,” says 50-year-old Lopez, a support worker. Mercer, also 50, a road safety campaigner, agrees. “You don’t come here to do general shopping after 3.30pm. It’s aggro caused by drugs mainly. People are more out of their head by that time. It’s an unfortunate truth, but it’s everywhere.”
The state of the town centre “deteriorates the morale”, says Lopez. And it may be contributing to the rise of rightwing populism: research by the thinktank Power to Change published last year found higher support for Reform UK in areas with run-down high streets that have high vacancy rates. Mercer says a part of town filled with ethnic minority shops and restaurants has been disparaged by some as “a foreign bazaar”. “Would they prefer the shops were empty? It’s much better to have busy shops, but people don’t like change.”
The town centre isn’t totally devoid of good news. Days before I came to town, Yella Brick Road – a quirky clothing and homewares shop – was preparing to close its doors, a decision it reversed after loyal shoppers flocked to keep the business afloat. Owner Dannii Paston has been trading in the town centre for 17 years. “Recently, people are just careful with money. We’re a shop where you don’t need anything in here – it’s all treat spends,” she says.
Surprisingly, it was the relocation of Primark, the supposed big, bad clothing behemoth, that Paston believes cost her the most business. “I didn’t think they were our customers, but actually, people would go to Primark for certain things like pants, tights or a cheap dress for the 10-year-old, then come to us for themselves,” she says. Even when the chains were in the town centre, their limited stock couldn’t compete with their warehouse-sized counterparts in Parkgate, says Paston. “It’s a societal shift on how people want to shop. Why would you go into a tiny high-street shop that’s got a quarter of the selection?
She believes supermarkets were the first to pull customers from town. In many large Morrisons branches, for example, you can take your passport photo, wash your clothes in an on-site launderette and even have keys cut while doing the weekly shop. Sainsbury’s has closed 420 Argos high-street shops since 2020, after acquiring its parent company, and shifted them inside its larger stores. “It’s like a little high street,” says Paston.
The out-of-town shopping destination – whether it’s a retail park, mall or outlet – hasn’t always been part of British life. The UK’s first such complex, Gem Superstore, opened in West Bridgford, Nottingham in 1964. Operated by an American company, Government Employees Mart, it brought US-style shopping to Britain – and demand was through the roof. The Goldfinger star Shirley Eaton was brought in for the official opening day, when 30,000 people rushed down its aisles. At 110,000 sq ft, fairly paltry compared with the sprawling shopping complexes that followed, it was more akin to a modern-day large supermarket. Two years later, Asda, then still a fledgling chain of small grocers, bought the site for its first superstore.
London’s Brent Cross Shopping Centre, which opened in 1976, took things to the next level. Traders feared that the 800,000 sq ft behemoth – boasting air conditioning (unheard of at the time) and the triple threat of Fenwick, John Lewis and Marks & Spencer under the same roof – would hammer local trade, and the Labour government tried to thwart the development. But Barnet council, in a Tory stronghold where Margaret Thatcher held her parliamentary seat, gave it the enthusiastic thumbs up. The indoor shopping centre opened the year after Thatcher’s ascendancy to leader of the opposition in 1975. Already there was consensus among local authorities that out-of-town shopping centres would destroy high streets but, after the Tories entered Downing Street in 1979, planning rules were eased. “There is a change of attitude in the 1980s which begins to allow these out-of-town locations,” says Alistair Kefford, the chair of urban studies at Leiden University in the Netherlands. In 1981, there was one out-of-town retail park in the UK. By 1988, there were 90 and at the end of 1996, there were 385.
In the end, the critics were right. “There’s only a certain level of consumer demand within a regional economy,” says Kefford. “If you build a wonderful, shiny, exciting new shopping mall or retail park, it doesn’t create a lot of new shoppers. They just stop going somewhere else.”
The bruising figures bear this out. In 2024, 13,479 shops across the UK closed their doors. While retail accounts for 5% of the UK economy and less than a tenth of employment, an area’s former glory is often starkly highlighted by its decrepit high street. “Dying high streets make people feel ashamed of their place, that their life is falling apart,” says Eddie Blake, a director at the architecture practice Studio Weave.
How to save the high street has become fertile political territory. Parkgate lies within John Healey’s constituency. In 2019, the now-chancellor scolded M&S for shutting its branch in the shopping complex, about a decade after relocating from Rotherham town centre, meaning the retailer would “disappear from the town for the first time in 125 years”. Since entering No 11, Healey has said “blighted” high streets will soon be “on the up”. Last month, Andy Burnham announced £210m in funding to regenerate down-on-their-luck high streets. But Kefford is sceptical. “Retail is a barometer – it’s not an engine. Where you see retail doing well, it’s a sign that the regional economy itself is doing well, but retail by itself won’t make a place wealthy. It’s not an engine of growth because it relies on people spending their disposable income,” he says.
Efforts to turn the ship can often be futile. “Once a location has set off down a particular path, it’s very hard to get out of it. In fact, everything leads further and further down that path. The narrowing range of shops, the growth of empty properties – these are things that snowball and get worse and worse,” says Kefford.
So, are UK high streets doomed? Shops “are probably not going to come back”, says Kefford, but there’s still hope. “In the 1950s and 1960s, town centres sustained loads of uses. There were many more houses and social activities: churches, working men’s clubs, community associations, charities, theatres. We need to think more fundamentally and creatively about what is the point of a town centre,” he says.
This may be good for society, too. Blake says the retail parks and shopping centres, and the cars we use to get to them, contribute to an “atomised culture that makes people feel alone”. A multifunction high street can better facilitate social interaction: “The small-grain interactions of social life are better, higher quality, and more frequent.”
Until then, many of us will be drawn to these bland, uninspiring shopping pens on the fringes of town. On my way to the train station, the No 8 bus pulls up on the high street, having just stopped at Parkgate. Sure enough, the passengers who alight are carrying bags from Primark, TK Maxx and Sports Direct.

Rian Johnson explains why he had to build his own iPhone camera app
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
16:10:05 UTC
01:10:05 KST

Rian Johnson is an analog photography devotee. The director of Knives Out and The Last Jedi can often be spotted on set with a Leica M6 at his side, documenting production on film. But sometimes, it’s still easier to reach for a phone. So Johnson started wondering if the photos from his iPhone could be made to look more like the grade he applies to his movies.
Rian Johnson explains why he had to build his own iPhone camera app
Johnson wanted to bring the look of his films to the look of his iPhone photos — and let everyone else give it a try, too.
Rian Johnson explains why he had to build his own iPhone camera app
Johnson wanted to bring the look of his films to the look of his iPhone photos — and let everyone else give it a try, too.
The result is Chromagraph Camera, a $13 iOS app that bypasses elements of Apple’s image processing pipeline and applies the same look used on Johnson’s movies. The app, made by Johnson and his longtime cinematographer, Steve Yedlin, is shockingly simple, with just a few primary settings, but it gives anyone who buys it access to image processing decisions good enough for a Hollywood production.
“The reality is, as much as I love my Leica, as much as I love my other gear, it’s a pain in the butt having a camera on your shoulder, or a massive backpack with four cameras in it,” Johnson says. “And I always have my phone with me.”
Watch | Listen | Get ad-free
Johnson has been tinkering with phone photography for a long time. Back before the smartphone days, he bought a Nokia phone with a proper camera — at least, proper for the time. “It was like the first one where they advertised the camera on it as the main feature of it,” he says. “And it was garbage, the camera was awful, but it took these photos that were grainy and contrasty and funky and beautiful.”
Smartphone photography has progressed substantially since then, but that progression has also come with a loss of character. The default photos coming out of modern phones tend to look sharper, brighter, and more clinical than in the days before computational photography took hold. You can work around this, but it generally means shooting RAW and editing the images yourself.
Initially, Johnson tried shooting with the iPhone’s default camera and editing in Snapseed to get his desired look. He then graduated to third-party RAW camera apps, only to get bogged down shuffling files back and forth and tweaking endless sliders. “I would do a lot of messing with every photo,” he says, “and then it was a little like I’d wandered through the woods and I wasn’t sure how I’d gotten there.”
Smartphone makers have started including tools to add more character to their images. Apple added a texture panel with film, grain, and halation settings to the iPhone 18 Pro, and Google put a new “Camera Looks” panel in the Pixel 11. But these still don’t afford the level of control you get from starting with a RAW image. And if you really want to dial in a look that feels unique to you, that’s what you need to start with.
Yedlin is convinced that given the right set of algorithms and settings, there is no perceivable difference between an image shot on film and one shot on digital. A few years back, he set out to make a series of color grading scripts to give Johnson’s movies the organic look of celluloid. Eventually, those tools allowed Johnson to apply their movie color pipeline to his still RAW files and film scans. That gave Johnson the confidence to bring the same ideas to mobile.
“I knew he could do it,” Johnson says. “I called Steve up and bullied him ... I kept saying, ‘Can we do it for iPhone photos?’”
Chromagraph Camera is a camera, of course, with settings for maximum exposure time, burst mode, and color tuning, but maybe one of the most fun things to do is to import RAW images you’ve already shot and process them in the app. It’s a camera and editor in one, but I’ve found myself importing old RAWs and seeing what Yedlin’s film-like processing does to my existing library. It doesn’t work for every photo right out of the gate, but after import you’ll have tons of options for tuning, like tone, color, saturation, and texture.
Johnson’s app is clearly still in its early stages, with settings and UI elements laid out in sometimes unexpected places. But the core of the app, the processing, is what is drawing people toward it. Over the weekend, Chromagraph went viral on social media, with many early users marveling at the app’s results compared to Apple’s defaults.
Even though this app gives Johnson what he’s been craving with smartphone photography, he remains entranced by much earlier photographic techniques. While chatting with me over coffee, I saw his eyes light up when he started talking about the 8 x 10 wet plate photography he’s been experimenting with at home. He even recently set up his own darkroom and continues to experiment with the chaotic, exciting art of analog photography.
“It’s like nerd fishing,” he says. “It’s about the actual process of doing it for me.”

Data centers lost the midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
16:05:39 UTC
01:05:39 KST

Data center developers are poised to face a more restrictive building environment after voters across the country voted in candidates who favor moratoriums and ballot measures that put more obstacles on their expansion, delivering a stinging blow to a central pillar of the AI industry.
Data centers lost the midterms
In ballot measures and exit polls, voters across the country rejected unrestrained development.
Data centers lost the midterms
In ballot measures and exit polls, voters across the country rejected unrestrained development.
Of voters polled by NBC News on Election Day, 76 percent said they opposed data centers in their communities. Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development through ballot measures. And upset winners like Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Michigan’s Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed support moratoriums on development.
It’s hard to draw a direct line from data center backlash to the election of any of these candidates, and there were still some races where candidates who favored more limited restrictions on data centers prevailed. Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who previously lauded development in Florida, was elected as governor, and Iowa’s Democratic Governor-elect Rob Sand opposed a moratorium that his challenger favored. But even these candidates were forced to engage on data center issues during their campaigns, and will be likely to face continued pressure to put at least some guardrails in place.
Ballot measures
Voters were faced with questions about data centers directly in 45 local ballot measures nationwide. As of Wednesday morning, according to a site compiled by Redbud Consulting, the results of 33 of those will restrict data center development. The Town of Wells, Maine, favored a 180-day moratorium on large data centers, backdated to mid-June 2026. Several cities in Ohio voted to ban data centers over 25MW. The City of El Dorado, Kansas, voted to ban data centers with peak electrical load over 10MW for 10 years.
Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development
Texas
Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa will take over the governor’s seat from Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, marking a major Democratic flip in a state with the second-highest number of planned data centers. Hinojosa supports a statewide moratorium on data center development, while Abbott took a more measured approach. He announced a new audit this summer on data centers that could slow new developments from connecting to the state energy grid, but has previously praised data center expansion in the state.
In another major upset, Democratic State Rep. James Talarico flipped Texas blue in a landmark Senate victory against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Talarico and Paxton wanted to remove some tax exemptions for data centers, and to make them responsible for their own energy infrastructure-related costs. But Talarico also put an emphasis on the facilities’ environmental impact and ensuring they shared their profits with the public, while Paxton’s message focused on keeping Chinese tech out of data centers.
Florida
Republican congressman Byron Donalds won the governor’s seat over Democratic former congressman David Jolly. Donalds opposed an outright ban of data centers, while Jolly said he’d bar hyperscalers for a year beginning on day one in office. In Congress, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would make developers pay for their own energy and water needs. Donalds’ win was still closer than expected in a state that’s been a Republican stronghold in the Trump era. As of Wednesday morning, NBC News reported that Donalds had exactly 50 percent of the vote, with 99 percent of expected votes already counted, while Jolly had 48.7 percent, and the rest went to an Independent candidate.
Pennsylvania
Democratic incumbent Governor Josh Shapiro held onto his seat against Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Both Shapiro and Garrity toughened their stances against data centers as the race went on, despite previously touting their potential benefits to the state. Shapiro signed an executive order that barred nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and took proposals for AI data centers off the fast track. Garrity has said she supports a development pause of up to three years.
Ohio
Democrat Sherrod Brown won back his former Senate seat from Republican incumbent Jon Husted, whom Brown had labeled “the face of data centers.” The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned this summer in a leaked memo that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates. Husted earlier helped install data center tax breaks as lieutenant governor, though he more recently introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act in Congress to force large data centers to cover their infrastructure upgrade and energy costs. Brown hammered Husted on the issue throughout the campaign, and while he hasn’t gone as far as to call for a moratorium, he’s said that developers shouldn’t get tax breaks or get a go-ahead without local input.
Republicans warned that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates
Michigan
Democrat and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate race over Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers. El-Sayed was one of the earliest politicians to stake his position on data centers, and has called for a pause on new developments “until we can do it safely and with federal protections.” Rogers called for a one-year state moratorium this summer, but not a federal ban.
As of Wednesday morning, NBC News had not yet called a House race between Democratic organizer William Lawrence and Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, but Lawrence held a lead with 92 percent of the vote in. Similar to El-Sayed, Lawrence stated his position on data centers early on, calling for a one-year federal moratorium on new developments during his primary campaign. Barrett introduced legislation this summer to bar nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and give locals more control.
Maine
Democrat and former Maine State Senator Troy Jackson ousted Republican Sen. Susan Collins from her Senate seat. The state legislature passed what would have been the country’s first moratorium on data centers, had the governor not vetoed it. But polls show that opposition to data centers among Maine residents remained strong. Jackson supported a state moratorium on data centers, while Collins opposed such a measure but called for more local control and protection for energy ratepayers.
Wisconsin
Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley won the governor’s race over Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany. Neither Crowley nor Tiffany favored a moratorium on data centers, and have distanced themselves from previous support. Crowley won his primary over progressive primary opponent Francesca Hong, who supported a moratorium. Both Crowley and Tiffany said they wanted to end state tax subsidies for data centers though they’ve accused one another of flip-flopping their stances.
Nevada
Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford successfully flipped the governor’s seat from incumbent Republican Joe Lombardo, whom he’d branded “data center Joe.” Lombardo has previously made supportive comments about data centers, but more recently introduced an executive order making tax incentives contingent on data centers covering power costs and meeting certain environmental standards. Ford previously championed a 2015 data center tax-break bill, but said today’s data centers are different from those years ago, and now supports a pause on all tax breaks for new data centers.
Georgia
Democrat and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the Georgia governor’s seat over Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson. Bottoms favored a moratorium on data centers to review environmental and cost effects, while Jackson preferred to leave decisions up to locals.
Arizona
Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs fought off a challenge from Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. Both opposed a moratorium on data centers in favor of power and water use standards.
Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes held onto her seat over a challenge from Republican state legislator Warren Petersen. Mayes took a more hardline view than her Democratic peer, Hobbs, by endorsing a state moratorium on data center development. Petersen opposed a moratorium, and said data centers are necessary for technology residents use every day.
Iowa
Democratic state auditor Rob Sand won the governor’s seat over Republican businessman Zach Lahn. Sand did not support a data center moratorium, which Lahn did. But both agreed on ending tax breaks for the developments.
South Carolina
Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews flipped South Carolina’s Senate seat blue in a race against Republican incumbent Darline Graham, who had taken over the seat after her brother Lindsey Graham died. Andrews supported a two-year data center moratorium, while Graham opposed a pause and got significant support from a super PAC allied with the data center industry.

AI agents won’t be stealing Uber’s lunch any time soon.
Uber only fulfilled 4 rides from AI agents last quarter
Despite growing concerns over AI disintermediation, Uber executives revealed that third-party bots accounted for just four rides and 500 food deliveries out of 320 million transactions.
Only four rides were arranged by third-party AI agents during the third quarter of 2026, Uber executives disclosed during an earnings call this morning. The volume of Uber Eats orders fulfilled by AI agents was a little higher, with the company recording “around 500” during the week of Halloween, out of a total 320 million Uber rides and Uber Eats deliveries.
This is the first time that Uber has disclosed the number of third-party AI agents that have arranged deliveries or rides on its platform. With the rise of AI agents like Meta’s Muse or OpenAI’s Dots, some experts are predicting that platforms like Uber and DoorDash are at risk of disintermediation, in which customers use AI agents to order food or book a ride, rather than visiting the app itself.
But in these early days, it seems like the risk is still very small. During the call, Uber’s executives expressed an openness to working with third-party AI companies to make things easier for agents to use their platform — while also expressing confidence that their customers will continue to prefer the experience of using the Uber app directly.
“We hope that there will be more traction,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the call. “We do think that we want to make services that are available to consumers in a delightful, easy way. We think our direct services are going to be the most delightful and easy, but we will work with these third parties.”
He continued, “It is just very, very early, and we want to make sure we are not dependent on any one player, and I think we are very well positioned in this environment going forward.”
As we’ve noted before, this first wave of AI agents still have a long way to go before people begin seeing them as a viable way to order food or book a ride somewhere. There still is a lot of friction points. And platform operators like Uber or DoorDash have little incentive to allow these agents to barge in and replace their own customers.
Which is not to say the AI companies won’t inevitably figure it out! These companies know this is one of their primary use cases, and their best path to a more profitable future. But getting Uber to agree to more disintermediation will be a tough ask.
Uber is developing its own AI tools that are designed to keep customers using its own platform. Earlier this year, the company rolled out a new Cart Assistant for Uber Eats, in which an AI bot will build a grocery list based on an image of a recipe or a text prompt.

Kemi Badenoch says Africans should apologise for slavery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:40:02 UTC
00:40:02 KST

Despite reports that the UK attempted to keep reparations off the formal agenda for the Commonwealth summit attended by King Charles and the UK prime minister, they are in the air. British Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch is among those detractors who have argued that it is African nations who should apologise for the transatlantic slave trade. It may seem like a spectacular case of whataboutery (it is) but it also touches on an enduring tension in some Black communities surrounding African involvement in capturing and enslaving people. This week, I speak to two historians to sort fact from fiction.
When discussing slavery, we should be “honest about the whole history”, Kemi Badenoch wrote in a recent post on X. Her statement comes after months of mounting pressure on Britain’s monarchy and politicians to formally apologise for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, and offer reparations to affected Caribbean nations. Badenoch continued: “If Caribbean countries are asking Britain for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, will they also be asking the same of the descendants of African kingdoms, rulers and merchants who captured, sold and profited from the trade?”
While the question was asked in bad faith, many within Black communities are unable to confidently answer it. In conversations with African and Caribbean colleagues at the Guardian, plenty of us experience division within our communities around the subject of African people’s participation in enslavement. The topic can be incredibly sensitive and difficult to tackle without a firm grounding in the history and political economy of the transatlantic slave trade. Yet, the experts I spoke to made it clear why African nations should not be held to the same standard as European countries and the US when atoning for their historical crimes.
Slavery was a system created by Europe and the US
Writer and historian Panashe Chigumadzi says that in understanding enslavement and who should be held to account, it is crucial that we see it as a system. Chigumadzi – who was the architect of the continental African Union’s landmark reparations framework – tells me that the trade was a structure that legally positioned all Black people as enslaveable property. No one was safe from this, whether on the continent or in the diaspora, king or commoner. She says: “[Badenoch] assumes Africans are ‘co-defendants’ and not ‘co-plaintiffs’ in prosecuting the case for a crime that fundamentally restructured the world as we know it, and created what we now know as the modern world racial capitalist system.”
Bayo Holsey, an associate professor of African American studies who specialises in west Africa at Emory University, agrees. She emphasises the overarching system that created a slave economy: the colonisation of the Caribbean and the Americas. “Europeans created the demand for enslaved labour,” the academic tells me. “The Atlantic slave trade would not have existed without this demand.”
In the latter part of the 17th century, demand for African captives on plantations had grown so much that capturing enslaved people was only possible through raiding and warfare. Given this, UK reparations would not only help repair the harm that the descendants of enslaved people have inherited, but would redress what Holsey describes as “the ill-gotten wealth of western nations”.
African people were victims of enslavement, too
We must also look at present day wealth – the economic growth of many European nations and the US was facilitated by enslavement. “The slave trade shaped the economic advantages that these countries enjoy today,” Holsey tells me. The case is fundamentally not the same in Africa. “Much of the wealth that select African individuals gained from the slave trade evaporated with the onset of colonial rule,” she says.
Africa was victimised by the slave trade too. Holsey tells me that while a small number of African people engaged in slave trading and accrued wealth, many more were victims of the trade. “They experienced fear, social instability, and the loss of loved ones as a result,” she says. Estimates based on the Slave Voyages database suggest that approximately 12.5 million enslaved Africans were forced aboard ships bound for the Americas, of whom 10.7 million survived the crossing. These figures exclude those who died before embarkation.
This depopulation destabilised the west and west-central coasts of the continent, devastating entire societies. Chigumadzi argues that the “scramble for Africa” in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the continent was invaded, divided and colonised, was a “structural continuation of the original crime of racialised chattel enslavement”.
Holsey tells me: “Today, most African nations face economic precarity as a result of historical and present-day inequities within the global economic order”. “So, unlike European nations and the US, African nations do not enjoy ongoing benefits from past participation in the slave trade. Therefore, they should not be targeted to repair the harm done by this vile system.”
Many African nations have made efforts towards repair
“Britain has already paid reparations for racialised chattel enslavement,” Chigumadzi says. “It paid them to the enslavers.” After the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, the British government agreed to pay 40% of the national budget in compensation to 46,000 enslavers, a sum that wasn’t paid off until 2015.
Passing the buck to African nations ignores the fact that many have attempted to meaningfully address their role in slavery and its ongoing legacy. In recent decades, leaders from Libya, Nigeria, Benin, Ghana, Cameroon and Uganda have apologised for enslavement – and a number of countries offer citizenship to diasporans. But these gestures are still either symbolic or individual, and fail to make a dent in the ongoing economic impacts of enslavement. “Addressing this issue is a much more difficult task,” Holsey tells me.
It also requires genuine unity across the diaspora. This shouldn’t revolve around a story of winners and losers, but rather an understanding of the slave trade’s devastating impact on African and Caribbean nations. March’s historic UN resolution, which declared the trade as the “gravest crime against humanity” and called for reparations, was tabled by Ghana and coordinated by the African Union – representing this kind of cross-diaspora solidarity.
“The question we should ask is not, ‘What do African nations owe to the African diaspora?’” Holsey says. “Instead, we should ask: ‘How can African nations and the African diaspora work together toward the creation of a more just world?’”

AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:38:34 UTC
00:38:34 KST

AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history — $17B guidance would exceed Intel's projections
AI boom drives record quarterly revenue, but client and gaming business faces double-digit declines going into 2027
AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds.
As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history.
AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year.
Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue
AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%.
The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems.
AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025.
"We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Client revenue up, gaming revenue drops
AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter.
Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago.
Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%.
"In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."
AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027.
Embedded business strong, set to accelerate
As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers.
AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years.
"Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year."
Beating Intel
For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint.
In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints.
If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead.
The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages.

Not even $200 million could help Elon Musk buy Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:33:59 UTC
00:33:59 KST

James Talarico, the Democratic Texas senator-elect, not only managed to flip the state in yesterday’s midterms but prevailed in the most expensive Senate election to date. More than $573 million was spent on advertisements between Talarico, his Republican opponent Ken Paxton, and their aligned PACs. And a big chunk of that money came from just one man: Elon Musk.
Not even $200 million could help Elon Musk buy Texas
Elon Musk’s wall of money fell to the blue tsunami.
Musk reportedly spent more than $445 million supporting Republicans in the midterms, making him not only by far the biggest donor in the 2026 election cycle but also in American history. And most of his money was spent in Texas, his home state and the headquarters of both Tesla and SpaceX. Musk funneled more than $168 million to super PACs that supported Paxton; Musk’s own America PAC, to which he funneled $216 million, also spent $34.7 million of those funds in Texas. All told, that’s more than $200 million spent on a single state.
But Musk’s millions couldn’t buy him an election. Talarico beat Paxton by more than 12 points, becoming Texas’ first Democratic senator since 1988. And the governor’s seat flipped, too: Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousted Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, another beneficiary of Musk’s largesse. The Democratic fantasy of a blue Texas finally became reality — and it happened despite the efforts of the world’s first trillionaire.
More than a blue wave, the midterms were a bloodbath for Republicans, who underperformed nationally even in the states they won. Democrats’ victories across the country often came down to money. But in Texas, it didn’t happen in the way Musk hoped. Talarico framed the race as a “top versus bottom” struggle between the ultrarich and everyone else. Musk’s donations to Abbott and Paxton may have emphasized America’s wealth inequality at a time when many Americans are struggling to make ends meet under an economic crisis caused by inflation, tariffs, and the ongoing war against Iran — all the results of policy choices made by the current administration.
It’s hard to imagine just how poorly Paxton would have performed without Musk’s money. Paxton’s campaign received just $22.3 million in direct donations, a paltry sum compared with the $146 million Talarico raised from voters. Paxton got a much-needed boost from Musk, who ensured that Texans were flooded with anti-Talarico ads. Those ads, however, didn’t focus on the issues that mattered most to voters. In Texas, anti-Talarico ads largely focused on culture war issues like transgender people, a fixation of Musk’s. (Musk is estranged from his oldest daughter, who is transgender, and he has described her as having been “killed” by the “woke mind virus.”) One Facebook ad that cost between $15,000 and $20,000 urged voters to “defeat Talarico and his radical trans agenda.” According to an analysis of America PAC’s spending by 19th News, the ad was one of dozens of anti-trans ads paid for by Musk.
But Musk’s money was also a liability for Paxton, which is perhaps why the now-near-trillionaire chose to operate from behind the scenes this time around. Musk endorsed Paxton on X — claiming the “fate of Texas and America is at stake” in the election — but against all Musk’s instincts for public spectacle, he didn’t take on a surrogate role in the midterms, in Texas or elsewhere. There was no Musk-led rally, no onstage jumping, no chainsaw in sight. Instead, Talarico repeatedly emphasized the relationship between Paxton and Musk, suggesting that to vote for one man was to benefit the other. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat,” he said at a rally in El Paso in late October. “In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your TV screen, that was Elon. If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you’ve received a text message saying scary things about me with scary black-and-white photos, that was Elon too.”
Talarico’s comments may have drawn even more attention to Musk’s cozy relationship with Paxton, which appears to be mutually beneficial. Paxton, who’s served as Texas attorney general since 2015 — aside from a brief stint in 2023 when he was impeached — has launched several investigations into organizations that criticize or antagonize Musk, according to a recent Wired report. Paxton has repeatedly followed Musk’s lead. After Musk sued the progressive media site Media Matters, Paxton investigated the publication; when Musk filed an antitrust lawsuit against an advertising federation, a Paxton probe followed.
“Elon Musk wants our land,” Talarico said at his El Paso rally. “He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator.”
Beyond trying to buy a senator, Musk also tried to chip in for a governor. Though most of the money Musk spent in Texas went to Paxton, he also threw a few million to Abbott, with whom he also has a close relationship — so much so that Hinojosa sued to view all 1,400 pages of correspondence between the two. And Musk wasn’t the only tech executive to support Abbott. The Republican, who promised to make Texas the “epicenter” of AI development, also received $300,000 from Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown, as well as funds from several data center developers.
Musk seems to sense that the political winds have shifted. Usually a prolific poster, Musk deleted a “Vote red early!” post from Election Day and barely had anything to say on X that night aside from a quip about putting data centers in space. The other states he threw money at hardly fared better. Democrats won in Ohio, where Musk’s America PAC spent $10.4 million, and Michigan, where he spent $9.8 million. The Republican party’s only real victory was in Florida, and they barely managed to eke out a victory there.
The amount of money Musk spent on this election cycle is both staggering and unprecedented — and it’s also meaningless to him. Musk lost half a billion dollars in his failed bid to buy the midterms, an amount that adds up to less than half a percent of his net worth. It’s possible that his loss will signal that even the world’s richest man can’t bend the electorate to his will. But it’s just as likely that he’ll spend even more money next time.

Letting users trust their own MCP clients, without opening a phishing hole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:30:57 UTC
00:30:57 KST

Letting users trust their own MCP clients, without opening a phishing hole
The problem
You run your own agent: a Slack bot, a service on a VPS, an MCP client you wrote over a weekend. You want it on your files, which on Stream Vessel means your own S3 bucket, where an agent can read, write and delete through the MCP server. The agent speaks MCP’s standard OAuth sign-in: it registers itself, opens a browser, you click Approve, it gets a token.
It fails at step one. At registration the agent named its redirect URI, the address your browser returns to after you approve, carrying a one-time authorization code the agent swaps for a token. Yours is https://agent.yourhost.example/callback; the answer is invalid_redirect_uri. The server only accepts addresses on its operator’s allowlist: Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code and a few others. Getting yours added means asking the operator to change a config file.
The server cannot simply accept any address. That list is the addresses the post office will deliver your house keys to. Without it, a stranger registers a fake “Claude” that has the keys sent to their place, and phishes your storage with one link. So the server is either closed to you or unsafe for everyone.
Both failures are common. On the closed side, this is what people run into:
“The redirect URI is not allowed, the URL is not part of Atlassian whitelisted domains for registered MCP Clients.” — an error users, Cursor’s among them, reported in the Atlassian developer community
“…each host application must have a registered GitHub App (or OAuth App) to authenticate on behalf of the user.” — GitHub MCP server, policies and governance; otherwise you fall back to a personal access token
On the open side, a May 2026 study that tested 119 OAuth-enabled MCP servers found registration endpoints on 114 of them, 95.8%, that
“accept arbitrary redirect_uri values from anonymous requesters.”
The attack: one link, one click, someone else’s bucket
Say your server accepts any registration and any redirect address. An attacker with no account on it can take over a user’s access in four steps:
- Register a client named “Claude” whose redirect URI is https://evil.example/cb. Open registration is anonymous, by design.
- Send a signed-in user a normal-looking /oauth/authorize link: “Reconnect your storage to Claude”.
- The user sees your real consent screen, on your real domain, in their real session, and clicks Approve.
- The code lands at evil.example. The attacker trades it for a token and is now the user.
PKCE does not help: it lets only the client that started a flow finish it, and the attacker started this one. The client name is self-declared and proves nothing. The consent screen shows the redirect host, but claude-connect.app passes a glance. It is the same trick as the fake-app approval prompts sent to Microsoft 365 users: a real page and a real Approve; there the attacker uses an app the platform registered, here an address the server should never have accepted.
The user does approve, but on false information. A redirect allowlist is what makes an approval mean what the user thinks it means: whatever the name says, the keys can only go where the list says.
This is not hypothetical. In January 2026 Obsidian Security reported this chain against Square’s MCP server: self-registration accepted any redirect address, and one click exposed a merchant’s profile, transactions and bank details. In the researchers’ words, “any user who had previously authorized the Square MCP server was vulnerable.” Square’s fix, they note, only applied to newly registered clients.
Others found the same chain on an MCP proxy in front of a company’s single sign-on, worth a 24-hour access token and a 14-day refresh token per click, and across bug-bounty programs, where it was sometimes waved off as social engineering. SickSec’s answer: the victim never leaves the trusted domain.
A quieter problem rides along. When a request fails a check after its redirect address was accepted, the error is sent to that address. So a server that accepts any address is an open redirector on its own domain: a crafted authorize link with a bad scope bounces visitors to any site, under your hostname. RFC 9700 describes exactly this case.
What the spec says, and what servers actually do
The MCP spec names the risk and leaves the policy to each server. Its security considerations say authorization servers MUST validate exact redirect URIs, SHOULD only redirect automatically to a URI they trust, and MAY instead inform the user and let them decide. The last two are RFC 9700’s sentences, word for word. What “trust” means is left open.
Registration is shifting too. The 2026-07-28 client registration page deprecates Dynamic Client Registration (a client registering itself over an API, no human involved) for Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD), where the client id is an HTTPS URL to a document listing its redirect URIs. CIMD says who publishes a client, not whether this user meant to connect it.
The OAuth working group has been here. In a December 2025 thread on the IETF OAuth list, Warren Parad argued that unauthenticated registration turns an MCP authorization server into an open redirector. Aaron Parecki’s quoted reply points to RFC 9700 §4.11.2, which starts from exactly that setup.
In practice, servers sit at one of two poles:
Loopback means localhost or 127.0.0.1: an app on the user’s own machine, waiting for the browser to come back.
The first pole costs real users, and clients will not fix it for you. A Claude Code issue from June 2026 reports that organizations with exact-match redirect allowlists cannot sign in from Claude Code, because its http://localhost:<port>/callback host and path are fixed. It was closed as not planned in July 2026. The server has to move.
This is not a new idea
Letting users vouch for their own app’s callback is old. GitHub has developers create an OAuth app and type in its callback URL. The MCP spec’s pre-registration option describes a server page where users register a client by hand. And an organization can add trusted redirect domains to Atlassian’s MCP server. None of these fit a client that registers itself anonymously: the first two need a client id made somewhere else, and Atlassian decides for a whole organization. So we kept self-registration and let each user decide at sign-in, for their own account, beside the server-wide list.
Our design: trust is per user, decided at sign-in
We keep the operator’s allowlist and loopback for local clients, unchanged and open to every account. On top of it, each user can trust a handful of exact https redirect addresses for their own account; ours caps at 10. On Stream Vessel that is “Trusted app addresses” on the MCP page of the web app.
The key move is when the check runs. Registration happens before anyone signs in, so it cannot know whose list to consult. So registration accepts any https URI, and the decision waits for the authorize page, where the user is known:
One rule sits under every branch: no code and no error is ever redirected to an address unless every account or this user trusts it. Before sign-in no user’s list applies, so even the OAuth library’s own validation errors (a bad PKCE challenge, an unknown scope) wait for sign-in, and a refusal is a page on our host. That closes the open-redirect hole along with the phishing one, and it covers the Deny button too: n8n’s CVE-2026-42230 (April 2026) sent users who denied consent straight to an attacker’s registered address.
Seven ways around it, each closed
Most of these rules came from trying to break the first version.
- Only the user’s own browser session changes the list, never an app or API token, so a stolen token cannot widen where the user’s codes may go.
- Adding from the refusal page means typing the host. The page shows the host, the full address as plain text (never a link), the account it would join, and a warning: if someone sent you this link, close the page. “Trust and continue” stays disabled until the host is typed, so one click from a phishing email is not enough.
- The consent screen names this sign-in’s redirect, and why it is allowed. A client can register several addresses at once, so it could list claude.ai beside its own. The screen shows only the one this sign-in returns to, and its basis: on the allowlist, loopback, or “you trusted this address yourself on 3 Nov 2026”. The spec requires showing the host for metadata-document clients, though the May 2026 study found 60.5% of tested servers don’t; the basis is what makes it mean something.
- Every addition is emailed, and audited while the activity log is on. The email leads with the host, says when and to which account, and keeps the full address from turning into a link. It is the signal a phished user would otherwise never get.
- Removing an address cuts the app off, even mid-sign-in. It revokes every grant (an approval the user gave) through that address and drops codes approved but not yet exchanged. A code lives about a minute; without this, a code in flight becomes a grant after the removal.
- Hosts the browser and the server read differently are refused. A URI parser may keep good.example%2eevil.example as one literal host while the browser goes to good.example.evil.example. A page that names one host and sends the user to another defeats the typed-host check, so such hosts are refused at registration and on the list.
- Exact match only. No wildcards, no prefix match, no loopback-style port flexibility.
What it does not stop, and what we turned down
It does not stop a determined social engineer: a user talked into typing an attacker’s host and approving is phished, whichever tier they pick. We bound it rather than prevent it: the typed host, the warnings, the email, instant disconnection on removal, and a consent screen that starts at read-only and says the user trusted the address.
We first capped user-trusted addresses at write access, so a phished grant could change data but not delete it. We dropped the cap: users connecting their own agents wanted full access, and the cap was a backstop, not the defense.
Beyond the two poles above, we weighed:
A checklist for your own MCP server
- Decide where codes may go at authorize, with the signed-in user known, not at registration.
- Check every answer, errors included, against that rule before redirecting, and refuse to a page on your own host. Do it at authorize, not only at token exchange: Cloudflare’s workers-oauth-provider shipped CVE-2025-4143 in May 2025 for checking only the latter.
- Show the redirect host of this request on the consent screen, and say why it is allowed.
- Make widening the list a deliberate act outside the sign-in flow, or behind a typed confirmation.
- Email the user every time an address is added.
- Make removal revoke grants and in-flight codes.
- Refuse URIs whose host the browser and your parser read differently.
Want to try it? In your own agent, add Stream Vessel’s MCP server, https://mcp.streamvessel.com, and sign in. If your agent isn’t on our list, you’ll land on the refusal page shown above, where you can trust its address and carry on.
