📰 Tech Blog | 🚀 API Quickstart
1. Model Introduction
Kimi K3.1 Pro is an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model, and our most capable 3T-class model to date. Post-trained from Kimi K3 with large-scale joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains, it is the first model in the K3.1 series. With a 1-million-token context window, Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers substantial improvements in coding, 3D creation, financial research, factual accuracy, and other agentic capabilities.
2. Model Summary
* Compared with Kimi K3, we replace the full-attention Gated MLA layers with Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention (Gated DSA) layers for more efficient long-context modeling.
3. Evaluation Results
Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results use reasoning effort max, temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95. A dash (—) means that the source table does not report a score. Higher scores are better except where the benchmark name explicitly states lower is better; Elo scores and other benchmark-specific metrics are not directly comparable with accuracy or pass-rate scores.
Evaluation Footnotes
Coding benchmarks
- Terminal-Bench 4.0. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude Code harness. The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 score is taken from its release blog. All remaining scores are the maximum values reported in model blog posts or on the official Terminal-Bench leaderboard.
- Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Claude Code. Internal evaluation of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 yields 9.3; the table instead reports 15.7 for the older DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash from the official leaderboard. All remaining scores are from the Terminal-Bench-Science leaderboard.
- SWE-Marathon v1.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 are evaluated with Claude Code. Other scores are from the official leaderboard.
- ProgramBench. The table reports binary scores: a task receives 1 if its ProgramBench score is at least 95%, and 0 otherwise. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Claude Code. DeepSeek and GLM scores are taken from the DeepSeek release blog; remaining scores are from Vals AI.
- DeepSWE v1.1. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Claude Code. Other scores come from the respective technical reports for GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, and GLM-5.3.
- PostTrainBench. K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 are evaluated internally on v1.2 with Claude Code and H20 GPUs rather than H100 GPUs. For stable evaluation, all judge models use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 at maximum effort, which best matched the official GPT-5.6-Terra (xhigh) judge in testing. Other scores are from the official leaderboard.
- Kimi Code Bench 2.0 and Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon. These are internal benchmarks. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Claude Code; all other models use their maximum-effort setting. Proprietary-model testing may involve fallback behavior.
- BenchCAD. Open models are evaluated on 1,000-case subsets randomly sampled from the 17,900-case Vision2Code dataset at maximum reasoning effort. With-tools results use Claude Code; without-tools results use single-shot generation with official prompts and scoring. Claude scores are from the Opus 5.5 System Card, and GPT-6 Astra's with-tools score is from its official report. GPT-6 Astra has no reported without-tools score.
Agentic benchmarks
- BioMysteryBench. Uses the official v11 release, with Kimi K3 as judge. K3.1 Pro uses Kimi Code; GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 use Claude Code; GPT-6 Astra uses Codex. Claude scores are from official system cards.
- Agents' Last Exam. Uses the official v1.1 release, comprising 122 tasks, including 86 CLI tasks. Runs that bypass stated requirements receive zero. DeepSeek and Kimi are evaluated with Claude Code and Kimi Code, respectively; other results are from the official benchmark website.
- OfficeQA Pro and OfficeQA Pro v2. GPT-6 Astra uses Codex; other models use Claude Code. Each task provides the complete PDF corpus as page images without machine-readable text. External-model trajectories that retrieve reference answers online receive zero for those tasks.
- Frontier Finance. Evaluated with the official Finance Agent v2 harness.
- HANDBOOK.md. Evaluated with the official OpenHands-based harness, using tasks from the benchmark's early open-source v1 release.
- Harvey Legal Agent. Evaluated on 1,251 public tasks with Artificial Analysis's Stirrup harness. The reported score is the all-pass rate: the percentage of tasks passing every rubric criterion.
- OSWorld V2.1. Kimi models use the Kimi Agent harness in the official OSWorld v2 repository. GPT-6 Astra's score is taken from Muse Wonder's technical report.
- DECK-Arena and Design Bench. DECK-Arena evaluates presentation generation on real-world queries; Design Bench covers graphic design through direct and reference-image few-shot prompting. Both evaluate python-pptx, pptxjs, and Kimi's in-house DSL in a harness with integrated search and image generation. The automated grader is calibrated on more than 10,000 human judgments.
- BrowseComp. Uses context compaction triggered at 200K tokens and a 500-step maximum. If the limit is reached, the agent is forced to answer before judging. All runs use temperature = 1.0 and top-p = 1.0.
- GDPval-AA v2.1, AA-Briefcase v1.1, and AutomationBench-AA. Scores are cited from Artificial Analysis. APEX-Agents. Scores are cited from the official leaderboard.
- Tool-augmented multimodal evaluations. GDP.pdf w/ python, ZeroBench w/ python, and ChartoGraphy w/ python are averaged over five runs; other multimodal benchmarks with Python are averaged over four. For GDP.pdf w/ python, each original PDF is sent to a sandbox for IPython processing. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash at medium reasoning effort and the official judging prompt. The reported score is the task-macro mean rubric pass rate.
Reasoning, knowledge, and multimodal benchmarks
- GDP.pdf. Each PDF is provided as page images resized to a longest edge of 1,152 pixels, interleaved with Docling-extracted text in page order. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash Medium and the official judging prompt. The table reports the strict pass rate among fully scored responses. GLM-5.3 Max and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Max scores are cited from Artificial Analysis.
- HLE-Full and HLE-Diamond. The full evaluation sets contain 2,500 and 1,000 questions, respectively. For scores marked *, accuracy is reported on the text-only subset.
- Run counts. GDP.pdf, ZeroBench, and ChartoGraphy are averaged over five runs; other multimodal benchmarks are averaged over four.
- MMMU-Pro. Evaluated using the official protocol, preserving the original input order and prepending images to the text input.
- PerceptionBench. An in-house benchmark focused on atomic visual perception capabilities.
- Kimi Hallucination Benchmark. Evaluates factual accuracy on an internal set of challenging, de-identified prompts drawn from practical work tasks. The table reports claim-level hallucination rates assessed by fact-checking agents.
Cybersecurity benchmarks
- ExploitBench. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the official harness under a 300-turn budget. The table reports the pass@5 maximum-capability score: for each environment, the best of five seeds is scored by capability flags reached out of 16; arbitrary code execution counts as all 16 capabilities. Comparison scores are from OpenAI, Anthropic, and GLM-5.3.
- ExploitGym. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Kimi Code under a six-hour wall-clock budget per task. GPT-6 Astra, Claude, and GLM comparison scores are taken from their respective official reports, with Claude results using the same six-hour budget.
- xdev-bench-hard. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Kimi Code; GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 use Claude Code. The internal benchmark contains expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks. The final model is evaluated at pass@3 over a random subset of runs, without hard timeouts or output-token limits.

5. Model Usage
The thinking effort of Kimi K3.1 Pro is configured with the top-level reasoning_effort request field, which supports "low", "high", and "max" (default "max").
For multi-turn conversations and tool calls, Kimi K3.1 Pro requires the complete assistant message returned by the API to be passed back to messages as-is — including reasoning_content and tool_calls, not just content:
import openai
def chat_with_preserved_thinking(client: openai.OpenAI, model_name: str):
    messages = [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Tell me three random numbers."
        },
        {
            "role": "assistant",
            "reasoning_content": "I'll start by listing five numbers: 473, 921, 235, 215, 222, and I'll tell you the first three.",
            "content": "473, 921, 235"
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "What are the other two numbers you have in mind?"
        }
    ]
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model_name,
        messages=messages,
        stream=False,
        max_tokens=4096,
        reasoning_effort="max",
    )
    # the assistant should mention 215 and 222 that appear in the prior reasoning content
    print(f"response: {response.choices[0].message.reasoning}")
    return response.choices[0].message.content
For full guides and examples (vision input, structured output, partial mode, tool choice, dynamic tool loading, context caching), see the Kimi K3.1 Pro Quickstart and Thinking Effort.

						"text": "Describe this image in one sentence."
					},

1. Model Introduction
Kimi K3.1 Pro is an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model, and our most capable 3T-class model to date. Post-trained from Kimi K3 with large-scale joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains, it is the first model in the K3.1 series. With a 1-million-token context window, Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers substantial improvements in coding, 3D creation, financial research, factual accuracy, and other agentic capabilities.
2. Model Summary
* Compared with Kimi K3, we replace the full-attention Gated MLA layers with Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention (Gated DSA) layers for more efficient long-context modeling.
3. Evaluation Results
Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results use reasoning effort max, temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95. A dash (—) means that the source table does not report a score. Higher scores are better except where the benchmark name explicitly states lower is better; Elo scores and other benchmark-specific metrics are not directly comparable with accuracy or pass-rate scores.

5. Model Usage
The thinking effort of Kimi K3.1 Pro is configured with the top-level reasoning_effort request field, which supports "low", "high", and "max" (default "max").
For multi-turn conversations and tool calls, Kimi K3.1 Pro requires the complete assistant message returned by the API to be passed back to messages as-is — including reasoning_content and tool_calls, not just content:
import openai
def chat_with_preserved_thinking(client: openai.OpenAI, model_name: str):
    messages = [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Tell me three random numbers."
        },
        {
            "role": "assistant",
            "reasoning_content": "I'll start by listing five numbers: 473, 921, 235, 215, 222, and I'll tell you the first three.",
            "content": "473, 921, 235"
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "What are the other two numbers you have in mind?"
        }
    ]
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model_name,
        messages=messages,
        stream=False,
        max_tokens=4096,
        reasoning_effort="max",
    )
    # the assistant should mention 215 and 222 that appear in the prior reasoning content
    print(f"response: {response.choices[0].message.reasoning}")
    return response.choices[0].message.content
For full guides and examples (vision input, structured output, partial mode, tool choice, dynamic tool loading, context caching), see the Kimi K3.1 Pro Quickstart and Thinking Effort.

Rosalind Franklin figured out DNA's helical structure before Watson and Crick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:29:08 UTC
00:29:08 KST

'She knew she had something really important on her hands': Rosalind Franklin figured out DNA's helical structure before Watson and Crick, study suggests
Rosalind Franklin knew about DNA's helical structure ahead of Watson and Crick, a new study of her photos and notes reveals.
Rosalind Franklin, whose photographs of the molecular structure of DNA led to a 1962 Nobel Prize for three other scientists, knew that her famous images held the secret of the double helix, new research suggests.
An examination of archival material reveals that Franklin's Photograph 51, which was taken in May 1952 and later published to show the double-helix structure, was specifically taken for the purpose of publication — not, as some narratives have held, an experimental shot that Franklin believed was insignificant. The new research revealed that Photograph 51 was a new exposure of a sample Franklin had already photographed. She started Photograph 51 the same day she saw that photograph, Photograph 49.
"She took it because she wanted to get a really refined version," said study co-author Alistair Sponsel, a historian of science at the Science History Institute in Philadelphia. Making the effort to take a better photograph of the same sample is "a sign she knew she had something really important on her hands," Sponsel told Live Science.
Francis Crick, James Watson and Maurice Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine for the discovery of the double-helix structure of DNA in 1962. As Watson told it in his 1968 autobiography, "The Double Helix: A Personal Account of the Discovery of the Structure of DNA," Franklin's photographs were his "aha" moment: "The black cross of reflections which dominated the picture could only arise from a helical structure," he wrote.
Watson further implied that Franklin was a laboratory automaton, good at the X-ray crystallography techniques used to capture the images of the DNA molecule but bad at interpreting her own data. The new archival work, published Monday (Oct. 5) in the Journal of the History of Biology, suggests otherwise.
Franklin's dearth of published notes about Photograph 51 has been used to suggest she missed a major discovery. But Sponsel said her journals show she noted the possible helical shape and rich structural data in her notes for her first picture of the sample, Photograph 49, which she followed up with the more refined image in Photograph 51.
"In Franklin's mind, they were two different types of scientific image," Sponsel said. Photograph 49 was the experimental image revealing exciting new data. Photograph 51 was the showpiece to convey these findings with the most clarity and sharpness possible.
This new understanding of the relationship between the two images, and how Franklin perceived them, is the most important feature of the new work, Sponsel said, which he conducted with molecular biophysicist Brian Sutton of King's College London. The project began when the Science History Institute acquired a new collection of archival material from Rosalind Franklin and her graduate student Raymond Gosling. The two researchers also combed through the archives at King’s College London, where Franklin was working when she took the famous photos.
Sponsel and Sutton think that Franklin's notes and actions reveal why she didn't rush to publish Photograph 51 right away. Her scientific goals, laid out in a report she wrote in February 1952, were to understand the two separate structures of DNA, then known as A and B. Structure B, illustrated in Photographs 49 and 51, turned out to be the double helix that occurs in nature. Structure A is a form DNA takes when it's dehydrated in the lab.
Structure A, when photographed, appeared more data-rich, so Franklin decided to characterize that structure first before studying structure B. But while she did this painstaking work, Wilkins showed Watson her photographs of structure B. The two scientists, together with Crick, then built a detailed model of DNA's double helix and scooped the discovery from under her nose.
Those three men shared the Nobel Prize for the work less than a decade later. Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958, making her ineligible for the prize — and leaving her insights to come to light only much later.
Editor's note: This article was updated at 3:23 p.m. ET to fix the caption and subhead, noting that Rosalind Franklin had likely discovered DNA's helical, but not double-helix structure. Also, the top photo is not Photograph 51, but another photo taken by Franklin.
Sponsel, A., & Sutton, B. (2026). Photograph 49 is the Key to Understanding the History of Rosalind Franklin’s DNA Photograph 51. Journal of the History of Biology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10739-026-09866-7
Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

YC's Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:28:31 UTC
00:28:31 KST

Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.
“I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.
On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.
“It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said.
He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.”
As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said.
For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.”
Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.
“It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.”
But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.”

Evergreen: A Provably Safe Systems Language
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:25:04 UTC
00:25:04 KST

01 /
Invariants live in your code.
Put preconditions, postconditions, and data invariants beside the code they describe. They become obligations the compiler checks.
fn increment(n: usize) -> usize
    where n < usize::MAX
    ensures result > n
{
    n + 1
}

Adding Window Functions to a Spreadsheet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:21:12 UTC
00:21:12 KST

Running totals, cumulative balances, and nearest matches: formulas between rows that stay correct.
Here is a formula many of us wrote early on. Put transactions in a traditional spreadsheet, like Excel or Google Sheets, one per row, and keep a running balance:
Copy the formula down, and it works. Each balance is the balance above it plus the amount on its own row.
Now you find a receipt from January 11 and insert a row for it, between rows 3 and 4. The new row has no formula, so you type one in, or copy it from above. But the balance below it now says =C3+B5. When the rows shifted, the reference was adjusted to keep pointing at the same cell, and that cell is no longer the row above. The new transaction is skipped without showing an error of any kind. The balance is just wrong from that row on.
Delete a row instead, and the formula below it becomes #REF!, and so does every balance after it.
None of this is a bug. To a traditional spreadsheet, “the previous transaction” means “the cell above”. The two agree only as long as nobody rearranges anything.
Surely there’s a better way?
There is, if you know the tricks. Vertex42 suggests OFFSET(), or a relative named range, to point at “the cell above” in a way that survives edits. Exceljet suggests a single SCAN() formula for the whole column in Excel 365.
What about the spreadsheet-like tools with database foundations? In Airtable and Baserow, a formula can only see the record it’s in, and the same goes for NocoDB and Notion databases. People asking on their forums how to do a running total in Airtable or Baserow get pointed to scripts, or to linking each record to the previous one by hand.
So these tools avoid the problem by not having a “row above” at all. But the need is there: a running balance, the days since a patient’s last visit, the stock left after each shipment.
SQL has an answer: window functions. There’s LAG and LEAD for the previous and next row, or SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY date) for a running total. They also work, but they’re an advanced tool for developers writing queries, not for people working in a table.
The actual better way: PREVIOUS()
What we really mean by “the previous row” is “the previous transaction, by date”. So let’s say exactly that. In Grist, a running balance, or any cumulative total, looks like this:
prev_balance = PREVIOUS(rec, order_by="Date").Running_Balance or 0
prev_balance + $Amount
PREVIOUS(rec, order_by="Date") sorts the table by ‘Date’, finds the current record (rec), and returns the previous record. It’s a whole record (not just a cell), so .Running_Balance gets that record’s balance. The very first transaction has no previous one, so its balance comes out empty, and or 0 takes care of that.
The ordering is in the formula, not in the view. Insert a transaction anywhere, and it falls into place by its date. Delete one, and the balances close up around it. Sort the table by ‘Amount’ or filter it, and each record still holds its balance by date, because that’s what we asked for.
Now, a credit card account may have several cardholders, and each might want their own balance. You might be tempted to split the data into a table per person. Please don’t do that. Keep one table, and be specific:
prev_balance = PREVIOUS(rec, group_by="Card_Member", order_by="Date").Balance or 0
prev_balance + $Amount
PREVIOUS() now finds the previous transaction by date among those of the same card member.
And since the order lives in the formula (order_by), nothing stops you from having several running totals side by side: one for the whole account, one per card member, one that starts over each month. Each column keeps its own count. Add a view linked to card members and sorted by date, and you can pick a card member and see their transactions, with their balance adding up row by row.
PREVIOUS() has two siblings. NEXT() looks the other way, and RANK() gives each record its position in the order, so RANK(rec, order_by="-Amount") <= 10 marks the ten largest transactions. The help article covers all three in more detail.
Nearest match, latest record, and effective rate
Once a lookup knows about order, “previous” is just one thing you can ask of it.
Say people’s pay rates change over time, and you keep the history: Bertha earns $110 an hour starting August 30, 2019, and $125 starting March 24, 2020. A payroll entry from February 2020 needs the rate in effect on its date, which is the latest rate that started on or before that date:
rates = Rates.lookupRecords(Person=$Person, order_by="Rate_Start")
rates.find.le($Date).Hourly_Rate
lookupRecords() gets Bertha’s rates, sorted by start date. find.le() finds the last one that’s less than or equal to (that’s the le) the payroll date.
Nothing about this is specific to dates. Commission tiers work the same way: sell $5,000 and earn 7%, sell $10,000 and earn 10%, and so on.
rates = Commission_Rates.lookupRecords(order_by="Sales_Target")
rates.find.le($Sales_Amount).Commission_Rate
Excel and Google Sheets users know this as an approximate match: VLOOKUP() with TRUE as the last argument. Microsoft’s own docs say the first column then needs to be sorted, and if it isn’t, “the return value might be something you don’t expect.” No error, just a different answer. In Grist, the order is part of the formula: it sorts the tiers itself, no matter how you choose to present them on the screen.
The same two lines answer a whole family of everyday nearest-match (sometimes called “approximate match”) questions:
- the pay rate in effect on a given date
- the commission tier a sales total falls into
- the shipping rate for a package’s weight
- the tax bracket for an income
- the exchange rate on the day of a purchase
- the volume discount for an order size
And for the simplest question of all (the first or last record in a group) you don’t even need find(). Here’s a customer’s most recent order:
Orders.lookupOne(Customer=$id, order_by="-Date")
The minus sign means descending, so the first match is the latest.
The need for speed
Grist formulas are Python, so you could always write all of this by hand: get the records, loop over them, pick the right one. We should check what that costs.
A running total done by scanning, SUM(r.Amount for r in Transactions.all if r.Date <= $Date), looks at the whole table for every record. With 1,000 transactions, that’s a million steps. With 20,000, it’s 400 million.
On a test table of 20,000 transactions, PREVIOUS() computed the whole column of running balances in seconds. The scanning version was still running after five minutes.
The ordered lookups don’t scan. They keep the records sorted, and find what you ask for with a binary search, which is the fast way to do it.
All caught up
Remember when we added the receipt from January 11 and it broke the running total? In Grist, you can add it anywhere. It takes its place by date, and every balance after it recalculates. The new row’s balance is right, and so is each card member’s. Nobody has to copy a formula down, check an adjacent row, or fix an error.
That’s what you get from formulas that say what they mean: they update on their own, and they’re right every time.
For more details, see the help article Running totals, PREVIOUS, and ordered lookups. For a walkthrough of these examples, watch the webinar Advanced formulas with ordered lookups.
Dmitry Sagalovskiy, Co-founder and Head of Product

Coffee's new status symbol is a machine without plastic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:20:49 UTC
00:20:49 KST

For decades, it was all the bells and whistles that was the selling point for a fancy coffee machine. Now, consumers are looking for what it lacks.
Growing concern over microplastics and sustainability is sparking a wave of plastic-free coffee pods and machines.
Coffee companies and appliance makers have released new machines and redesigned capsules in recent months. Keurig and Lavazza’s new pods ditch the traditional plastic cups for compostable coffee tablets. Caraway’s new machine uses traditional coffee grounds, but unlike a conventional drip machine, the stainless steel and glass machine doesn’t have plastic in its brew path.
More research is needed to determine the actual harm microplastics cause. But nine in 10 Americans are concerned about the effect of the minuscule plastic pieces on the planet and their bodies, according to a 2025 poll conducted by environmental group 5 Gyres; and studies have shown that pods shed microplastics.
The growth in pricey equipment and plastic-free pods fits a broader pattern of consumers trading up on home coffee equipment since the pandemic, said Peter Giuliano, senior adviser for research at Specialty Coffee Association.
The appeal and growth combine three things: health worries about microplastics, concern about plastic in the environment and the “feeling that metal and glass are more ‘luxury’ than plastic,” he told CNN.
New pods
In June, Lavazza introduced Tablì in the US, a $129 machine that uses only single-serve espresso tablets made with compressed ground coffee — a shift from its capsules made from plastic and aluminum.
The tablets are made by a custom technology that “compresses precisely dosed, ground, and tamped coffee into a solid, ready-to-use tab,” Lavazza said in a press release.
The Italian company says the new machine is its “largest investment yet” in the United States as it looks to double revenue to $1 billion by 2029, unlocking the stranglehold Keurig Dr. Pepper has on the coffee market.
Tablì is aimed at customers who want a sustainable alternative to the traditional pod, according to Daniele Foti, vice president of marketing for Lavazza North America.
“Consumers want to enjoy their coffee without the waste that usually comes with single-serve,” he told CNN.
Keurig, which ushered in the boom of plastics with their K-Cups back in the 1990s, launched in October a new line of compostable pods with a specially designed machine called the Alta. (The new pods don’t fit in the old machines.)
Called AltaRounds, the pods have been in development since 2020 in response to consumers’ shifting sustainability and health preferences.
The new pods represent a “significant reduction in plastic compared to our K-Cup pods,” said Phil Drapeau, senior vice president for Keurig’s Future Coffee Systems unit.
“We’ve heard clearly from customers that they want more sustainable products and specifically less plastic and plastic waste,” Drapeau told CNN. “Our data shows that drink variety, quality, and less plastic waste are high priorities across almost every group.”
Keurig has come under fire in the past over its pods, agreeing in 2022 to pay $10 million to settle a class-action lawsuit alleging it misled consumers by marketing its plastic K-Cups as recyclable, though it denied any wrongdoing.
But while the pods and the machine contain less plastic, they are considerably more expensive than a traditional Keurig machine. The Alta bundle that includes glassware and pods costs $499.
Melissa Valliant, director of communications for 5 Gyres, said that both the Lavazza and Keurig products still use plastic packaging, which “ends up in a landfill, incinerator, or our environment after use, contributing to the planet’s growing plastic pollution crisis.”
New machine
Caraway has focused on developing a $495 coffee machine, released last month, that’s created entirely of stainless steel and glass, ensuring that no plastic touches the ground coffee. (Lavazza’s and Keurig’s machines contain some amounts of plastic.)
Developing a coffee machine with plastic-free brew path was challenging, according to Caraway CEO Jordan Nathan. That’s because the pricey glass and steel parts all need to be custom-made.
“We had to make the best coffee possible with no plastic on the interior with a full metal body, but also in a small (counter) footprint that had a single dial,” he told CNN.
Concern over plastic in the kitchen and its affects on the endocrine system has been growing for the past few years, Nathan said, referencing a viral article that linked black plastics in the kitchen to alarming levels of toxic flame retardants.
Social media, influencers and various scientific studies have all fueled the conversation, with parents and other health-conscious shoppers avoiding plastic where they can, including in makeup, food and bedding. Caraway’s other plastic-free products, like cutting boards, have soared in sales over the past three years.
Coffee is a natural next step, Nathan added, because “you never want to heat plastic.”
Demand for Caraway’s new 10-cup coffee maker has been so strong that it’s sold out until January, forcing the company to ramp up production. Meanwhile, Keurig and Lavazza reported similar interest with both company’s product selling out quickly after their initial release.
That appetite for these pods and machines signals the industry will move toward more plastic-free alternatives, Nathan said.
“If you’re not doing it, you’re behind where the puck is moving,” he concluded.

Bluetooth is getting a big boost to data transfer speeds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:19:54 UTC
00:19:54 KST

The Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG), which oversees the wireless standard, has formally adopted Bluetooth High Data Throughput (HDT) as an optional feature of the Bluetooth Core 7.0. It’s an upgrade the Bluetooth SIG has been previewing over the past year, and it increases Bluetooth LE’s maximum supported bit rate from 2 Mbps to 7.5 Mbps. It will allow for higher-resolution audio streaming as well as improvements to battery life and reliability.
Bluetooth is getting a big boost to data transfer speeds
The maximum bit rate of Bluetooth LE will increase by nearly four times.
The primary application for Bluetooth HDT once again will be for wireless audio, with the first devices supporting the new feature expected to appear sometime in 2027. The increased bit rate will support high-resolution audio but also new wireless audio experiences, including spatial audio and multichannel surround sound without requiring proprietary wireless formats.
Bluetooth HDT will benefit other wireless devices beyond headphones. Smartwatches could sync more training, health, and fitness data to a phone without a reduction in battery life because HDT can transfer more data in less time, requiring the Bluetooth radio to be on for shorter periods. Spatial computing and extended reality devices could offer more robust experiences without needing a Wi-Fi connection, and HDT will benefit the ever-growing number of personal AI devices, allowing them to more efficiently hand off data to be processed by a smartphone so they can be lighter and smaller.
Even the simple act of updating the firmware on a smartwatch or smart home accessories could feel faster and become a task that doesn’t need to be put off until later when you’re not using your device. “Bluetooth HDT brings a new level of performance to Bluetooth technology, expanding the role it can play across consumer, commercial, and industrial markets and creating a powerful foundation for the next generation of wireless innovation,” says Neville Meijers, CEO of the Bluetooth SIG. “As the world’s most widely used wireless standard, Bluetooth technology has continually evolved to meet the growing demands of an increasingly connected world.”

Show HN: Codemap – one-page interactive map of any Go repository
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:18:24 UTC
00:18:24 KST

One HTML page that maps a Go module: every package, what it builds on within the module, and the functions in each of its files. Search it, click a package to see what it uses and what uses it, and, for a module on GitHub, jump to any function's line. Tests are left out.
Open that example to try it.
In your module's folder, with Go 1.24 or later:
go run github.com/peterretief/codemap@latest -o code-map.html
Then open code-map.html in a browser. It's one file with nothing to serve,
so it can go on any website. -root DIR maps another folder.
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: peterretief/codemap@v0.1.3
  with:
    output: code-map.html
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: code-map
    path: code-map.html
- Each row builds only on the rows below it, so the foundations are at the bottom and your commands at the top.
- Wider boxes have more functions, and colours are top-level folders.
- Lines show direct links; ones already implied by others appear when you pick a package.
- internal/ is left off names. vendor, testdata and folders with their
own go.mod are left out.
- The page loads its fonts from Google Fonts, and falls back to system fonts without them.
MIT

Visible Brushstrokes Push on a Subtle Grid in Stelios Pupet’s Contemplative Scenes

Visible Brushstrokes Push on a Subtle Grid in Stelios Pupet’s Contemplative Scenes
From his studio in Athens, Stelios Pupet renders meditative paintings that place organic elements within a subtle grid. The artist always begins with a structural matrix that he builds upon, sometimes leaving a square angle for a cloud or section of grass and other times manipulating the form into a natural curve.
In recent months, Pupet has begun to experiment with different media like pastel pencils and plans to incorporate oil pastels into his larger works on canvas. The shifts in his practice have been small, and “I think that just things got a little bit more wise,” he tells Colossal. In addition to a trio of works in progress in his studio, Pupet has several murals planned for 2027, which you can keep up with on Instagram.

CVE ID         : CVE-2026-109518
Max Justicz discovered a vulnerability in the APT package manager. APT
can merge two different package downloads after an HTTP redirect gives
them the same URI. Improper file handling when resuming an HTTP download

The fight for tech accountability starts now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:02:25 UTC
00:02:25 KST

When Donald Trump began his second term as president, Silicon Valley gratefully embraced moral nihilism. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and more collectively donated millions to Trump’s inauguration fund to ensure his favor in a new era of gangster tech regulation. Meta overhauled its content policy to allow calling gay people mentally ill and women property. Elon Musk started throwing Nazi salutes — yes, allegedly, but he would soon be posting nonstop about protecting the white race from extinction, so that’s the most fragile of fig leafs.
The fight for tech accountability starts now
Trump is still in office, but the era of gangster tech regulation needs to end.
As of mere months ago, this was working out pretty well for them. The Trump administration took a mostly hands-off regulatory approach, particularly in the burgeoning field of AI. It decided to simply not enforce a divest-or-ban law against TikTok (something that was originally Trump’s own idea!), leading TikTok to thank Trump by name in its app. A Republican-led Congress was too dysfunctional to pass the tech regulations it did want. The Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission still pursued some existing Big Tech lawsuits, but the flood of high-profile investigations we saw under the Biden administration — and the first Trump administration — slowed markedly. Musk functionally ran the US government for a few months.
And beyond simple regulatory favors, Trump, once a vituperative critic of Big Tech, became joined at the hip with it. Tech CEOs prominently attended his inauguration, and their companies showered him with ballroom donations and gold gewgaws. The White House hosted the reveal of the Stargate Project, OpenAI’s massive data center plan. The US Army created a special detachment for executives from Meta, Palantir, OpenAI, and Thinking Machines Lab, and Trump tapped tech leaders as advisers. He ordered an entire technology renamed because he thought it would make the AI industry look better, and the industry duly fell in line.
Now, these companies’ all-in support is looking awfully risky.
Yesterday’s midterm elections were a historic disaster for Republicans. Democrats not only won the House and Senate, they flipped seats that were considered long shots or downright impossible six months ago: Texas has a Democratic senator and a Democratic governor. Trump is still president, but in Congress, Democrats will be empowered to launch investigations and haul tech execs into hearings, and they’ll have leverage to negotiate over budget and defense bills. And the electoral backlash, of course, bodes ill for Republicans’ prospects of holding the presidency in 2028.
Americans are angry. Trump and his administration’s actions invited much of that anger: his pointless trade wars, a senseless actual war, adviser Stephen Miller’s brutal and lawless immigration crackdowns, and much more. But the tech industry is an easy target, too. Its hyperscale data centers became a flashpoint in numerous midterm races, and public trepidation about AI — a technology whose defenders argue it will destroy countless jobs and possibly kill everyone — is high.
There’s a lot of dirt for newly empowered Democratic lawmakers to investigate. Google may strenuously deny a specious $24.5 million legal settlement was a bribe, for instance, but even as the minority party, Democrats rightly raised questions about it. Trump has enriched himself through connections with the cryptocurrency industry and in the process backed off investigating crypto fraud. Musk may have benefited financially in countless ways from his ties to Trump, and that’s on top of his reckless, destructive, and allegedly illegal actions with DOGE, which devastated parts of the federal government and likely led to hundreds of thousands of deaths.
But tech is so overdue for a reckoning that the very term “reckoning” has started to feel like a joke. AI companies have been making vague “please regulate us” overtures for years, and it’s time to take their incessant doom-bragging seriously — by, for instance, using subpoena powers to push them on their responsibility for “rogue” AI agent hacks. Actual legislation likely won’t happen with Trump in office, but if there’s private information that suggests companies should bear legal liability, congressional investigations can help dig it up.
The fight over data centers so far has mostly taken place at a local level, and newly elected Democrats at the state level will likely keep the pushback high. Given how many Republicans hate hyperscale centers too, a Democratic majority could also make a serious bid for federal action — at the very least, they could put a bill on Trump’s desk and force him to own his unpopular pro-data-center stance by vetoing it. And far more easily, they can stymie Trump’s push to override local regulations. Trump’s long-favored state AI law moratorium, which Republicans have tried to sneak through Congress multiple times, seems gone for good.
The fight over data centers will probably only escalate from here
Democrats shouldn’t replicate Republicans’ bad-faith attacks on the tech industry during the Biden administration, which saw Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) weaponize congressional committee powers to accuse social media platforms of censorship. But they shouldn’t be afraid to crack open the alliance between a lawless, grift-friendly administration and a powerful industry that paid him handsomely and was rewarded with regulatory favor. They’re also poised to figure out just how much Trump and his administration — where figures like FCC chair Brendan Carr display contempt for basic constitutional rights, to a point even some Republicans can’t support — have threatened that industry with punishment if it didn’t support him.
Unfortunately, even with an undeniable mandate for change, there’s a huge risk that lawmakers will deliver exactly what they have for the past decade in tech reform: almost nothing. Despite the best efforts of some reformers in Congress, the US has perennially failed to pass even laws with bipartisan support, like antitrust overhauls and a data privacy framework. Hauling tech execs into court creates good sound bites, but without any real action, it only cements the idea that the government is useless.
Democrats probably will soon have tech execs courting them as well. Meta, the fairest-weather friend in Silicon Valley, appeared to be already hedging its bets before the election. They’ll be tempted to retreat into the friendly relationship they had with tech companies during the Obama and early Trump years. But it’s too late to go back. Even at its best, the tech industry needs a check on its power — and the past two years have shown it at its worst.

Guerrilla Bike Lanes: San Francisco Makes Illicit Infrastructure Permanent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:01:44 UTC
00:01:44 KST

When two cyclists were tragically killed in hit-and-run collisions this past summer, a group of anonymous urban activists known as the San Francisco Transformation Agency erected a set of protected bike lanes using traffic cones. Usually such guerrilla interventions are temporary. They raise awareness but ultimately get taken down by municipal authorities. But when the same group recently (and illegally) installed a set of soft-hit posts alongside Golden Gate Park, the city reacted by making the change official.
The SFMTrA, a play on the city’s Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), “is a collective organization of men and women committed to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, and doing it quickly.” According to the organization, their members use tactical urbanism to accomplish a range of objectives, including:
- Provide a real safety increase for cyclists and pedestrians.
- Draw attention to areas of the city that are unsafe for vulnerable pedestrians and cyclists.
- Put pressure on the SFMTA and public officials to make proactive, rapid and substantive improvements in street safety.
Many of their interventions involve orange traffic cones, which do grab visual attention but are also impermanent and easily damaged. Adding more robust traffic delineators (also known as soft or safe hit posts) may have helped persuade the city to retain this particular recent installation along John F. Kennedy Drive.
“Generally, we have no choice but to remove cones and posts that do not go through an official process,” wrote the city agency in a statement, “because it’s a code violation to place objects in the roadway, and they could create conflicts for various types of traffic.” But in this case, they plan to install official safe hit posts and leave the temporary ones in place until their review process is complete.
Guerrilla activists in other cities have tried similar things with mixed results. When the group Reasonably Polite Seattleites installed a similar set of delineators along a stretch of road in Seattle, the city initially took them down. Subsequently, though, officials wrote the activists an exceedingly nice response and eventually agreed to reinstall the posts.
City traffic engineer Dongho Chang of the Seattle Department of Transportation explained that a combination of issues (including the height of the posts and state control of the street) forced the removal at first. At the same time, he acknowledged the “time, money and risk” invested by the group and even offered to give the posts back. He later followed up with a letter indicating the city and Washington State Department of Transportation would put the delineators back in place.
In New York City, a perhaps less-polite group has been known to take things even further by building out entire bike lanes from scratch. After a local community board rejected plans to extend an extant lane, Right of Way took to the streets at night to paint their own. As a catalyst, the group cited an accident that took place after a taxi driver struck a pedestrian (after reportedly arguing with a cyclist sharing the lane).
Guerrilla interventions like these can provoke a variety of responses from critics and cities alike. In some cases, tactical urbanists are celebrated by communities but also jailed or fined by officials for their actions. In other instances, though, such installations can give a city an opportunity to publicly support a direction of change. In San Francisco, which has already built out 27 miles of protected bike lanes over recent years, the city seems to be signalling it is open to progress.

Titan OS raises $46 million to expand its smart TV OS internationally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Barcelona-based smart TV operating system maker Titan OS has raised $46 million in new funding, consisting of both equity and debt, the company announced on Wednesday.
The money comes from debt facilities provided by funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, along with existing investors like Highland Europe and Mangrove Capital Partners. The startup, which secured $58 million last year, has now raised $110 million in total. The company said that it could have chosen not to raise money and grow slowly, but it wants to be more ambitious to create more partnerships and expand into more geographies.
Titan OS’s promise to TV makers is that it offers better value from their unit sales by loading an operating system where they can generate money through partnerships with FAST channels (free ad-supported television) and ads on different screens.
The company now serves 30 million users, up from 18 million last year. This includes being a sales partner for TiVo in some regions, along with Tubi in the U.K.
Compared with last year, the startup has also added Sharp, AOC, Vestel, and Skyworth as partners. Its partnership with Philips has been a success, as the Dutch electronics maker has switched to Titan OS and ditched Google TV for its 2026 models.
The extended coverage means that it has a bigger advertiser footprint and better audience engagement metrics to offer to marketers.
“Our bread and butter is the monetization of our inventory on our own network. But the point is that we’re going beyond that. That’s why our reach has increased significantly, which then triggers the flywheel effect by also attracting more sales partners and more agencies that want to spend on our platform, whether it’s owned and operated or via our extensions,” Hyoung-Ung Kim, the company’s newly appointed CFO, told TechCrunch over a call.
In the last year, the company has increased its headcount to 250 people, and also opened an office in London to concentrate on advertising. It already has offices in Barcelona, Amsterdam, and Taipei.
With the new money coming in, the company wants to focus on a few areas. First is content discovery. It still takes everyone a long time to find something to watch. For that, it is using interface tweaks and AI to boost discovery, alongside partnering with more content providers like FAST channels.
“What differentiates us here from the walled gardens is that we do not have our own content offering. Like Google is trying to channel people to YouTube. We do not have that, and we are impartial in our role in content discovery. We are working and trying to reduce time spent searching,” Tobias Pfalzgraff, SVP of people and marketing at Titan OS, said.
Pfalzgraff also emphasized that the company is using AI to improve its ad recommendation and segmentation. While the company is dominant in Europe, it thinks that there are only a few manufacturers creating their own operating systems; more set makers would like to adopt its operating system, just like Philips did. The company also said that with increasing costs of hardware due to AI, manufacturers are thinking about long-term revenue generation opportunities as gadget sales slow down.
“The TV hardware industry is not a very profitable business. That’s why they are so reliant on partners like Titan OS that share revenue after the sale of the TV. But now, of course, the chip sets, the chip prices are increasing more and more. Right. With the AI boom, they have basically doubled down on our partnership,” Kim said.

Cheeseburger Soup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

I love a hearty soup, and this easy Cheeseburger Soup recipe is one the whole family will enjoy! Inspired by the flavors of a classic cheeseburger, it’s thick, creamy, and packed with savory ground beef, tender potatoes, flavorful veggies, and loads of melty cheddar cheese. I garnish mine with crispy bacon and green onions, but you can get a little crazy and top it with pickles or a drizzle of burger sauce, too! At just $1.65 per serving, that’s a pretty good deal for a big bowl of beefy, cheesy comfort food.
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
All the Cheeseburger Flavor, None of the Bun!
Apparently, I really like turning my favorite dinners into soups! I did it with my stuffed pepper soup, and this time I took inspiration from a cheesy burger. I layer in the flavors to give each spoonful the rich, savory taste you’d expect from a loaded cheeseburger, starting with crispy bacon and browned ground beef. Once cooked, set both aside, but leave those flavorful drippings in the pot. I cook the veggies in those drippings, too, so none of that delicious bacon and beef flavor goes to waste. Plus, the fat comes in handy for thickening the soup!
Instead of making a separate roux with butter, I stir the flour directly into the veggies and drippings already in the pot. The flour thickens the broth as it simmers, and with just a little milk and plenty of real cheddar cheese, it turns into a creamy soup (with no Velveeta, heavy cream, or extra butter!). The potatoes and veggies also help stretch just one pound of ground beef into eight generous servings, so you still get a hearty, stick-to-your-ribs meal without needing loads of meat.
Recipe Success Tips
- Don’t drain that grease! I know it looks like a lot of fat after cooking the bacon and ground beef, but don’t pour it away. You’ll use those flavorful drippings as the base for the roux, which is a mixture of fat and flour that thickens the soup. This also means there’s no need to add extra butter.
- Give the flour a good stir. Once the veggies have cooked for 10 minutes, sprinkle in the flour and stir for another minute, making sure everything is evenly coated. This gives the flour a chance to cook in the fat before the liquid goes in, which helps prevent a raw, floury taste. Stir thoroughly as you add the broth and milk to help prevent lumps.
- Keep those potatoes small! I use red potatoes and cut them into relatively small, evenly sized pieces so they cook through in the time given and still hold their shape in the soup. Big chunks will take longer to soften, so don’t rush the simmer! After about 15 minutes, check a piece with a fork. It should slide through easily without the potato falling apart. If it’s still firm, give it a few more minutes.
- Use freshly shredded cheese. I recommend shredding the cheddar yourself if possible, since pre-shredded cheese contains anti-caking ingredients that can affect how smoothly it melts.
- Load up those toppings! I always set the cooked bacon aside until serving so it stays crispy, then sprinkle it over each bowl with sliced green onions. But this is cheeseburger soup, so have some fun with it! Chopped dill pickles, diced tomatoes, extra shredded cheese, or a drizzle of burger or comeback sauce would all be delicious additions. You can even let everyone build their own bowl. And if you love that combination of crispy bacon, cheddar, and green onions, you should also try our loaded potato soup recipe next.
Cheeseburger Soup
Cost $13.16 recipe / $1.65 serving
Ingredients
- 4 strips of bacon (chopped, $1.21)
- 1 lb. ground beef (I use 73/27 fat beef, $5.74*)
- 1 tsp salt (divided, $0.04)
- 1 tsp black pepper (divided (freshly cracked) $0.16)
- 1 small (165 g) onion (small dice (heaping 1 cup) $0.78)
- 2 ribs (130 g) celery (small dice (1 cup) $0.38)
- 1 medium (130 g) carrot (small dice (1 cup) $0.28)
- 1 lb. (453 g) red potatoes (peeled & medium dice, $1.25**)
- 1 tsp garlic powder ($0.03)
- 1 tsp dried oregano ($0.06)
- ½ cup all-purpose flour ($0.09)
- 4 cups chicken broth ($0.52***)
- ½ cup milk ($0.10****)
- 8 oz. (226 g) cheddar cheese (shredded, $2.24*****)
- 2 green onions (sliced, $0.28)
Instructions
- Gather and prepare all ingredients.
- In a large pot over medium heat, add the bacon. Cook the bacon for 10 minutes, or until it’s crispy. Using a slotted spoon, remove the bacon from the pan, leaving the grease in the pan. Set the bacon aside.
- Add the ground beef, ½ tsp salt, and ½ tsp pepper. Brown the meat for 5 minutes, breaking it up as it cooks. Remove the beef from the pot, leaving as much grease in the pot, and set it aside. (see notes)
- Add the onions, celery, carrot, potatoes, remaining salt, pepper, garlic powder, and dried oregano. Continue cooking for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
- Sprinkle in the flour and cook for 1 minute.
- Add the chicken broth and milk. Bring to a simmer. Once the soup is at a simmer, continue cooking for 15 minutes, until the soup has thickened and the potatoes are tender.
- Add the cheese and beef back in, and stir for 2 minutes until melted.
- Garnish with sliced green onions and cooked bacon.
See how we calculate recipe costs here.
Notes
Nutrition Information
how to make Cheeseburger Soup step-by-step photos
Gather and prepare all of your ingredients: Chop 4 strips of bacon, finely dice 1 small onion, 2 celery ribs, and 1 medium carrot, then peel and dice 1 lb. of red potatoes into small, even pieces. Slice 2 green onions for garnish and have your shredded cheddar cheese ready.
Cook the bacon: Add 4 strips of chopped bacon to a large pot over medium heat. Cook for about 10 minutes, or until the bacon is browned and crispy. Use a slotted spoon to remove the bacon and set it aside, leaving the rendered grease in the pot.
Brown the ground beef: Add 1 lb. ground beef (I use 73/27% fat), ½ tsp salt, and ½ tsp black pepper to the same pot. Cook for about 5 minutes, breaking the beef into small crumbles as it browns, until fully cooked (160°F). Remove the beef from the pot and set it aside, leaving as much of the grease behind as possible. This will form the base for thickening the soup.
Cook the vegetables: Add 1 diced onion, 2 ribs diced celery, 1 diced carrot, and 1 lb. diced potatoes to the pot, along with the remaining ½ tsp salt, ½ tsp pepper, 1 tsp garlic powder, and 1 tsp dried oregano. Cook for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables begin to soften. The potatoes will finish cooking in the broth, so they don’t need to be completely tender just yet.
Add the flour: Sprinkle ½ cup all-purpose flour over the vegetables and cook for 1 minute, stirring to coat everything evenly. The flour combines with the fat left in the pot to create a thickening base for the soup, so make sure there are no dry bits of flour left in the pot.
Add the broth and milk: Pour in 4 cups chicken broth and ½ cup milk, stirring to incorporate the flour. Bring the soup to a simmer (don’t boil to avoid the dairy from splitting), then cook for 15 minutes, or until the broth thickens and the potatoes are fork-tender. A fork should slide easily into a potato without it falling apart. Keep simmering if they’re still a little firm.
Stir in the cheese and beef: Add 8 oz. cheddar cheese and the cooked ground beef back to the pot. Stir for about 2 minutes, until the cheese has melted and the beef is evenly distributed throughout the thick, creamy soup. Again, avoid letting the soup boil as the cheese melts, as too much heat can cause it to separate and become grainy.
Garnish and serve: Ladle the cheeseburger soup into bowls and top with the crispy bacon and sliced green onions. Adding the bacon just before serving keeps it nice and crunchy against the creamy, cheesy soup. Enjoy!
What to Serve with Cheeseburger Soup
I consider 1½ cups of this cheeseburger soup a serving, and with all that beef, cheese, and potatoes, it’s pretty filling on its own! I usually top mine with the crispy bacon and green onions, but I also love adding homemade croutons for some extra crunch. Warm Hawaiian rolls are another delicious option if you want to play into those classic burger-and-bun flavors, though any crusty bread works well for dipping. For a proper burger-and-fries dinner, try serving it with air fryer French fries and a few dashes of your favorite hot sauce. Or, if you’d prefer something fresh alongside all that cheesy goodness, our cucumber tomato salad has a light, tangy vinaigrette that helps balance the richness of the soup.
Storage & Reheating
Store leftover cheeseburger soup in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3-4 days. Refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking to keep everything food-safe. I recommend keeping the bacon and green onion toppings separate so the bacon stays nice and crispy.
Reheating
Reheat the soup in a saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally until heated through to 165°F. The soup will thicken as it cools, so I usually add a splash of chicken broth to loosen it up. You can also reheat individual portions in the microwave. Stir between intervals to help everything heat evenly. Avoid boiling the soup for longer than necessary, as too much heat can cause the cheese to separate and become grainy.
Freezing
You can freeze this soup for up to 1 month, but keep in mind that the texture may change once thawed. The potatoes can become soft or grainy, and the cheesy broth may separate slightly. If you’re making a batch specifically for the freezer, I recommend leaving out the potatoes to help avoid some of those texture issues. Let the soup cool, transfer it to freezer-safe containers, and freeze. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator or use the thaw setting on your microwave before reheating.
Other Cheeseburger-Inspired Recipes
- Our Cheeseburger Meatloaf is packed with melty chunks of cheddar and topped with a sweet and tangy ketchup-mustard glaze. It’s comfort food at its finest!
- For something a little fresher, try this Cheeseburger Salad with juicy mini beef patties, crisp lettuce, cheddar, and a homemade burger-style dressing.
- This Cheeseburger Pasta has all the cheesy, beefy goodness of a homemade Hamburger Helper, with a little relish added for that classic burger flavor (and I love how it’s made all in one pot!).

Where did you shop?
I live in Bed Stuy, Brooklyn, which has an unfortunately long history of being underserved when it comes to access to quality affordable places to buy groceries. The corner stores and small grocery stores that I have near me don’t have amazing selections of fresh produce or the best prices. I make do throughout the week, but will occasionally trek downtown to stores like Trader Joe’s and Whole Foods where the prices are better and the selection is more consistent.
What’s your grocery strategy?
With my hectic schedule of part-time and freelance work and a long commute, my strategy these days is to get in and out as quickly as possible. Grocery stores in NYC are notoriously crowded during peak hours, and from my experience can be a little overwhelming. I’m a no-cart shopper, preferring to load up my arms or use a shopping basket. 
Being mostly a vegetarian, I shop the produce area first just in case a particular quality vegetable catches my eye. If it does, I’ll use that item as an anchor for the rest of my meal. I’ll then head to the center aisles for canned goods and more pantry heroes. I almost always leave with a can of beans and coconut milk. I can make so many things out of these two ingredients alone. 
How do you meal plan?
This is tough! I wish that I devoted more time to this, but my weeks get so busy that I’m often figuring out dinner during my commute home from work. I get home around 7 p.m. and often have another three to four hours of baking to do, so dinner sometimes looks like popcorn, carrots and hummus, chips and dips, or leftovers if I’ve had enough time to cook earlier in the week. 
When I do have time to plan ahead, I try to focus my meals on groups of three: a protein, a carb, and a vegetable. I usually cook things separately and store them in containers that way so I can remix them throughout the week with different pantry sauces and condiments.

US voters roundly reject data centers in ballot measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
14:27:02 UTC
23:27:02 KST

American voters roundly rejected data centers nearly anywhere they were on the ballot Tuesday, a rebuke sure to rattle investors already growing skittish about the AI buildout. Residents in more than 30 localities across nine states voted for moratoriums, outright bans, and other measures, some in direct response to specific projects underway. Edgewater, Fla. overwhelmingly voted to embed a data-center ban in the city’s charter, and voters in Perry, Ohio passed a measure placing financial and operational constraints on hyperscalers seeking tax breaks. Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, one analysis showed. The pressure pushed some Republican candidates including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, an AI booster just a few months ago, into promises of tougher regulation; he lost anyway.
Banks and asset managers financing the buildout have already begun treating local opposition as a credit risk, while hyperscalers are rushing to hire community liaisons. Meanwhile, tech companies bracing for the vibe shift are trying to rebrand the data centers as “compute campuses” with mixed results, Semafor’s Ashley Gold reported.

Thoughts From a Tsunami
Unknown

Thoughts From a Tsunami
Posted on November 4, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 56 Comments
Thank you, America, you understood the assignment.
But also, Jesus, what a faceplant for Trump and all of the Republican party. Do you understand how much you have to have fucked up that Kansas elected a Democratic senator? That literally hasn’t happened since the New Deal. Do you know how much you have to have fucked up to have Mississippi still in play as of the writing of this post? MISSISSIPPI. You don’t get any more Republican territory than Mississippi, goddamn. Except maybe South Carolina, which just elected a Democrat to Lindsey Graham’s old seat. North Carolina elected a Democratic senator and flipped one of their state legislative bodies to Democrat.
And holy shit, Texas! Not just senator Talarico, not just Governor Hinojosa, but as far as I can tell every single statewide office went blue, down to and including the railroad commissioner. The Democrats look like they’re going to flip the Texas house, too. FUCKING TEXAS WENT BLUE Y’ALL. Not just a little, but a lot.
(And Ohio, too, where I live, but I’ll get to that in a second.)
Now, credit is due to the Democrats actually fielding decent candidates this year and doing the work — you don’t get Abdul El-Sayed into the senate (as an example) without Abdul El-Sayed being a generationally sensational candidate. But let’s make no mistake that this blue wave is a response to an administration and political party so corrupt and awful and, yes, actually fucking evil, that a certain number of people who have perennially voted red either voted blue or stayed at home, and a lot of blue-voting people who might have stayed home for a mid-term went out of their way to get to the polls this time around.
This election was a rebuke and a repudiation, and I hope to the sweet and merry God above that the Democrats remember that when they’re seated in January. They were not elected to office to play nice with the fascists in the halls of power. They were elected to punch them in the face, repeatedly, the president most of all, but, be assured, not only him. There is to be a lot of punching going on.
Now, Ohio. When I went to bed last night Amy Acton was elected governor and Sherrod Brown senator, but all the other statewide offices were still showing as red. Well, I just checked this morning, and holy buckets, every state office but auditor, including the Ohio Supreme Court seats, looks to have gone to the Democrats. By extremely small margins, to be sure! But you know what you call a win by an extremely small margin? A win.
And the US House races, with a new map that the state GOP designed to be gerrymandered as fuck to their advantage? Seven seats went to Democrats, which brings them to near parity with the GOP in a state with fifteen congressional districts. Shit, in my district, OH-8, Warren Davidson, who since 2016 has won his seat with between 60%-70% of the vote every election, scraped by this time with just 52% of the vote. The GOP nearly just gerrymandered themselves out of a state congressional majority. The GOP also looks to have lost its supermajority in the Ohio house, so, goodbye ignoring the governor’s veto for them. This is all excellent news.
As I noted the other day, and without taking away from the work of Acton, Brown and all the rest of the Democrats, it’s the fact the GOP voters, in their infinite wisdom, chose Vivek Ramaswamy as their candidate for governor in the primary, largely on the endorsement of Trump, that helped tip Ohio back into purplehood. It’s hard to overstate what a historically bad candidate Ramaswamy was, and ultimately how poor a fit he was for the Ohio GOP (much less any other Ohio voter). And even then he still got 44% of the vote, because tankies gonna tank. But 44% was not enough. So much for the power of a Trump endorsement in 2026.
Speaking of Trump, I have no doubt if the Democratic margins had been smaller this year that Trump would be doing his usual thing of belching about fixed elections and other such nonsense, but at the end of the evening the wave was high enough that even he couldn’t pretend that it was anything other than a wipeout. He rather meekly went on record that he would “respect the results” and then went on Truth Social to bluster that if he had been on the ballot things would have turned out differently. Motherfucker, you were on the ballot. Everything you’ve done in the last two years is why this election went the way it did.
I still expect Trump and his odious cronies to pull hijinks, and never forget that he is actually still president for two more years, unless he dies, resigns, is impeached, or just one day boards a plane for Russia just for fun and never comes back. We’re still stuck with him through January 2029. Adjust expectations accordingly.
But no matter what, last night was the beginning of the end of the Trump era. I’ve said such things before, mind you, and have been wrong. But I feel pretty good about this time. This wasn’t a normal election. Ask Texas about that. It’s not just a wave. It’s a sea change.
— JS

Revolut’s valuation jumps 53% to $115B in new share sale as it prepares to launch US bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
14:10:10 UTC
23:10:10 KST

Revolut’s investors have completed a secondary share sale that values the British fintech at $115 billion, 53% more than the price tag it had gained in another share sale a year ago, as the company prepares to launch a U.S. bank in 2027.
Investors including Glade Brook Capital Partners, Coatue, Durable Capital Partners, T. Rowe Price Associates, and Baillie Gifford led the share sale, which brought no new money into Revolut. The company declined to say how much stock was sold.
Founded in 2015 by Nik Storonsky and Vlad Yatsenko, Revolut has grown from a money-transfer app into a financial services platform with more than 80 million retail customers across over 40 countries. It has established banking operations across Europe, and launched banks in the U.K., Mexico, Australia, and New Zealand this year, as well as secured banking licenses in France, Colombia, and Argentina.
The company also began rolling out financial services in India earlier this year, and has received conditional approval from the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to establish a national bank, which it plans to launch in the first half of 2027, subject to final regulatory approval.
The London-based company has grown increasingly profitable, achieving profit margins of 38% on revenue of $6 billion in 2025.
Even though Revolut has built much of its business around consumers, its business banking division, launched in 2017, has become an increasingly lucrative endeavor. The division accounts for about 20% of Revolut’s gross profit, James Gibson, head of Revolut Business and a partner at the company, told TechCrunch in a recent interview.
Available across Europe, the U.K., Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, and the U.S., Revolut Business processes more than £36 billion (about $48.6 billion) in transactions each month, including over £1 billion (around $1.35 billion) in the U.S. alone. The division generates more than £950 million (about $1.28 billion) in annualized revenue and holds more than £18 billion (roughly $24.3 billion) in customer deposits, the company told TechCrunch.
Nearly half of Revolut Business’ new customers in the U.S. are newly incorporated companies, the company said.
Revolut is looking to bring its business banking services to more markets, including Mexico, Brazil, and India, Gibson said, though he did not specify when the company expects that to happen. The fintech also aims to grow its business customer base from over 800,000 businesses to a million by 2027, he said.
The company’s rising valuation comes as it weighs a public listing. Storonsky has considered a dual listing in New York and London and indicated a preference for a primary listing in the U.S. However, an IPO, which could reportedly value Revolut at $200 billion, would come no earlier than 2028, depending on market conditions.
