The lost malloc()
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
07:37:30 UTC
16:37:30 KST

The lost malloc()
(Sorry, I couldn't resist not putting a catchy title :)
Prompted by another project idea that popped into my mind, I did some Unix archaeology and looked at the original sources. This is the most fun I've ever had reading someone else's code - probably due to the historical significance. But also because of how delightfully approachable it was, compared to modern monstrocities.
This is a short(-ish) post regarding how they handled the mundane and boring task of allocating and managing memory (in C). In the future I'd like to read more about Unix the OS, its design, architecture & implementation.
A long time ago...
In a PDP far, far away, our journey begins with the fourth edition of Unix, released November '73, more than half a century ago. C actually first appeared in the second edition, released the year before, but wasn't extensively used. V4 is special because even the majority of the kernel was written in (let's call it "medieval") C by that point. The system had grown, however, and it was quite capable. You'll find that many Unix things we have today in POSIX-land were already present in V4.
Super fun fact: A tape containing V4 was only found last year! Previously, it was thought to be completely lost to time.
Linear allocation
The first interesting bit is found among the C "compiler" sources. In quotes, because it wasn't a monolithic compiler as we know it today. Rather, it was a set of distinct tools which you chained in order to get an object file from C code.
In /usr/c/c20.c:814, from what I can gather a very primitive optimiser, if you will (referred to as "C object code improver" in V5; there aren't many comments in V4) you see:
alloc(an)
{
    register int n;
    register char *p;
    n = an;
    n++;
    n =& ~01;
    if (lasta+n >= lastr) {
        if (sbrk(2000) == -1) {
            write(2, "Out of space\n", 14);
            exit(1);
        }
        lastr =+ 2000;
    }
    p = lasta;
    lasta =+ n;
    return(p);
}
Isn't that fascinating? This routine is used throughout the program to allocate memory. And if you squint, this is just a linear allocator. It aligns the size, checks if the region is big enough, otherwise tries to extend it. On failure, it just cold-exits. Which means callers don't have to check for NULL every single time, and indeed they do not.
The "region" isn't named, unlike how you'd do it today with arenas. However, the above does have a nice property, in that by using sbrk(), when we extend the heap, no pointer is invalidated.
And they don't bother freeing memory, because why would they? There's no need. Everything exists for the lifetime of the program.
dmr/malloc
This is the most interesting bit in my opinion, and the reason why I chose that title.
In Dennis' directory, you find a file named malloc.c. And you see two functions there:
struct map {
    char *m_size;
    char *m_addr;
};
malloc(mp, size)
struct map *mp;
mfree(mp, size, aa)
struct map *mp;
Seems familiar? Yep, it's mfree() with an m. These functions obviously deal with memory (de)allocation, and are the precursor to the ones we're familiar with today. But, the interfaces are different.
malloc() receives an additional first argument called mp (for "map"), and so does mfree(). What is that? Well, let's see how they're used:
p = malloc(coremap, sizeof foo);
...
mfree(coremap, sizeof foo, p);
q = malloc(swapmap, sizeof bar);
...
mfree(swapmap, sizeof bar, q);
So, they pass in some objects coremap and swapmap. What are those?
From /usr/sys/systm.h:2:
int	coremap[CMAPSIZ];
int	swapmap[SMAPSIZ];
They're just flat memory regions! So these malloc() and mfree() work on explicit memory regions! Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should. Those are just infinitely-times better interfaces than traditional malloc()/free().
Imagine using a library that has such an interface. You could deallocate all its memory resources by just discarding the entire region you delegated to it. Heap corruption bugs would be less severe because you could partition memory. You could trivially limit the amount of memory third party code allocates. The list goes on and on...
(Side note: They slightly messed up here and the regions should've been sized CMAPSIZ/2 and SMAPSIZ/2 respectively. They did fix that later.)
However, I don't think all these benefits were in the minds of Dennis and Ken. So why did they go with that interface and why did they partition memory to "core" and "swap"? The reason is, I believe, just hardware constraints. These interfaces stay like that up to V6 (maybe V7 too?), released the spring of '75, and thankfully there's an infamously good resource about that edition.
From A Commentary on the Sixth Edition UNIX Operating System by John Lions:
These are concerned with the allocation and subsequent release of two kinds of memory resources, namely:
- main memory in units of 32 words (64 bytes);
- disk swap area in units of 256 words (512 bytes).
For each of these two kinds of resource, a list of available areas is maintained within a resource "map" (either "coremap" or "swapmap"). A pointer to the appropriate resource "map" is always passed to "malloc" and "mfree" so that the routines themselves do not have to know the kind of resource with which they are dealing.
And it goes on to explain how the underlying allocation algorithm works. These do not do linear allocation (hence the mfree()). Basically, it's a list of blocks (struct map), ordered by address, where you do first-fit and also coalesce neighbour blocks.
The sixth edition is also the first where the term "arena" appears, in /usr/source/s4/alloc.s:17:
/char *allocs[2] {		/*initial empty arena*/
Rolling back
... to the topic of linear allocation... In V6's /usr/source/s1/diff1.c:88, I think the first ever version of diff(1), you find:
char *area;
char *top;
alloc(n)
{
    register char *p;
    p = area;
    n = (n+1) & ~1;
    area =+ n;
    while(area > top) {
        if(sbrk(1024) == -1) {
            mesg("Out of space\n");
            exit(1);
        }
        top =+ 1024;
    }
    return(p);
}
This is not all that much different from the previous alloc(), but this time it handles any allocation size. It uses a while to continue extending the region and stops when enough space has been reserved. The actual interesting part happens later, at unsort():143:
unsort(f, l, b)
struct line *f;
int *b;
{
    int *a;
    int i;
    a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0]));
    for(i=1;i<=l;i++)
        a[f[i].serial] = f[i].value;
    for(i=1;i<=l;i++)
        b[i] = a[i];
    area = a;
}
I'm not exactly sure what that function does, but it doesn't matter. What matters is that they allocate some memory (a = alloc(...);), then roll back the region (area = a;)! Though they subsequently just copy it to b, so it seems like this was redundant.
Computing sizes
Most of the code directly calls malloc()/alloc() and friends, and inlines the size computation logic. Like the line we saw earlier:
a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0]));
I don't do that anymore, and neither should you! I use a couple macros akin to C++'s new that handle all the sizeof business. But I am a dumb-dumb. Surely these guys must've come across the same pain points, and, if so, what did they do? Let's jump to V7, released January '79, four years after V6. You find this macro:
#define ALLOC(x) (struct x *) ckalloc(sizeof(struct x))
where they use it like:
struct foo { ... };
p = ALLOC(foo);
Nice! It's interesting to note where you find it; In /usr/src/cmd/f77/defines:38 and /usr/src/cmd/make/defs:38. Slightly suspicious. The former is part of the Fortran 77 compiler and latter of make. Stuart Feldman is the person who worked on both of those programs! It's clear that multiple people were working on the system at that time. A macro like that isn't used in any other program, sadly.
V7 is the first edition where you also find the assert() macro, and it was used extensively back then too. Good job! They also significantly expanded the number of man pages. Fun fact: I did $ man V7/usr/man/man3/foo.3 -- on 47 year old pages -- and it worked first try absolutely fine.
Let's go to V8, released in February '85, four years before the first C standard. You find this wild macro in /usr/src/cmd/ideal/memut.c:7:
char *fooalloc;
#define	tryalloc(new,kind)	\
    if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\
    emergency ();\
    if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\
        fprintf (stderr, "ideal: Out of space\n");\
        exit (1);\
        }\
    };\
    for (fooalloc = (char *) new;\
        fooalloc < ((char *) new) + sizeof (kind);\
        fooalloc ++)\
        *fooalloc = '\0';
If someone is too harsh because you used macros, point them at the above. Usage is bit different this time:
struct foo *x;
tryalloc(x, struct foo);
I decided to include it because the macro zero-initialises by default whatever was allocated! You also see a more familiar-looking malloc() being used. It appears this is the edition that they switched to the more traditional malloc()/free() interfaces we know. I'll hypothesize why that is at the very end.
But it gets even more interesting. In V8 you also find these macros:
#define new(type) ((type *) alloc (sizeof (type)))
#define new(t) ((t *) alloc (sizeof (t)))
#define        new(s)  (s *)alloc(sizeof (s))
When I saw these definitions I jumped out of my chair. It's basically how I'd define it too! You'll find them in:
- /usr/src/cmd/finddev.c:245, part of finddev(8).
- /usr/src/cmd/asd/asd.h:13, part of asd(8).
- /usr/include/ic.h:55, part of *checks notes* I have no idea.
respectively.
Unfortunately, I can't find the author(s) of any of these.
Cfront
In V8, you'll also find Cfront, a.k.a. medieval C++. It's then reasonable to assume that Stroustrup was inspired by the above macros and decided to incorporate new as a language-level feature. However, in A History of C++: 1979−1991, he writes:
In Simula, it is not possible to have local or global variables of class types; that is, every object of a class must be allocated on the free store using the new operator.
Huh. So C++'s new was inspired by the programming language "Simula". It's fair to say that the macros above were likely also derived from there. But Simula was quite old even by the 70s, let alone 1985. Perhaps Stroustrup persuaded people, or wrote those macros himself. He later writes:
The new operator that both allocates memory from the free store and invokes a constructor to ensure initialization was borrowed from Simula. The delete operator was a necessary complement because I did not want C with Classes to depend on a garbage collector. The argument for the new operator can be summarized like this. Would you rather write:
X* p = new X(2);
or
struct X * p = (struct X *) malloc(sizeof(struct X));
if (p == 0) error("memory exhausted");
p−>init(2);
and which version are you most likely to make a mistake in? The arguments against -- which were voiced quite a lot at the time -- were "but we don’t really need it," and "but someone will have used new as an identifier." Both observations are correct, of course. Introducing operator new thus made the use of free store more convenient and less error−prone. This increased its use even further so that the C free store allocation routine malloc() used to implement new became the most common performance bottleneck in real systems. [...] Having real programs spend 50% or more of their time in malloc() wasn’t acceptable.
(emphasis mine :P)
He makes a compelling argument, which I agree with, but doesn't mention the new() macros that basically did the same thing. Although you'll find many programs in V8 that do the latter, verbose thing. Now I want to know the author(s) of those macros even more!
Sims
This is a big parentheses because I wanted to know how Simula came up with new. Wikipedia states:
Simula 67 introduced objects, classes, inheritance and subclasses, virtual procedures, coroutines, and discrete event simulation, and featured garbage collection.
And it appeared in 1967. Wow! In the 1964 report of SIMULA I, you'll find:
[...] The symbol "new" only serves to resolve an ambiguity of the identifier A inside the activity blah blah blah [...]. Elsewhere the symbol new is redundant, but can often be used to advantage to improve readability.
So it was only used to resolve grammar ambiguities (I think?). And Stroustrup re-purposed it. Clever!
Further reading
The History of Simula, by Jan Rune Holmevik. Reads like (bad) Sci-Fi. All the politics nonsense aside, what I found most curious is that they completely specified the language before attempting to write a compiler for it. They started writing the first compiler atleast a year after. This would sound insane today, but I guess the cost of writing code was substantially higher back then.
Also: The development of the SIMULA languages, by the authors. I didn't read that one, although I should...
It's honestly amazing how influential Simula was. In "10.5 Operating Instruction" they even use the term "run time system" and give it the same meaning we're accustomed to.
Simula, in turn, was partly inspired by SIMSCRIPT (don't laugh). If you skim its 1962 report, you won't find a mention of new. You'll however find CREATE:
When a new Entity is created by a CREATE statement, space for storing its Attribute values is allocated in the amount specified on the Definition Form. This record is given an identification number, and the Variable specified in the CREATE statement is automatically set equal to this number.
For example, the statement "CREATE DOG CALLED FIDO" allocates the required amount of storage for the Attributes of a DOG, and sets FIDO equal to the identification number of the Attribute record.
Fascinating. The whole SIMSCRIPT report is fascinating actually, and I only briefly skimmed through it. At the beginning, it even describes something like a primitive ECS, by my understanding. At the end though it slaps you back to reality:
and you remember what year it was.
Later editions
In V9's /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:14, part of the Sam editor by Rob Pike, you find a "generalised" version of new():
#define    new(t, n)       ((t *)alloc(((ulong)(n)*sizeof(t))))
Although, by and large, almost every program doesn't do this. Most just directly call malloc() and friends, and do size calculations \w error checking at every call site. I don't know why, considering how much error-prone that is, but maybe due to inertia. It's a similar story in V10, but I didn't check it as thoroughly since it's quite big (it includes medieval GCC!).
So what happened?
They were so close to arenas; with linear allocation and explicit memory regions, rolling back, and even having a nice new() macro. All this is speculation at this point, but maybe some of it is correct. First of all, most programs had trivial object lifetimes. Allocate memory, read some data, process/crunch and spit out some result. You don't need any disciplined memory allocation strategy for that. You can even use malloc() for everything and let the OS reclaim it once the process exits. Given how simple malloc() was at first, it wouldn't be much of a bottleneck either. The philosophy of programs only "doing a single thing well" also fitted this pattern.
Secondly, it's clear some decisions were motivated by the very little memory they had to play with. And there was no virtual memory either (initially, that is). Nowadays, you can "allocate" however big of a memory region you want and all will probably be okay. They couldn't really do that, so they were fighting to reclaim every empty block and gap there was and scale a program's space with how much is actually needed. There's a counterpoint to this, however, because some code is confused. Sometimes you see fixed-size buffers/arrays pop up, seemingly out of nowhere, and the program bail out if they fill. I'm not sure why, but perhaps they didn't deem it worthwhile the complexity to use malloc() in those cases and/or "don't fix it if it ain't broke" kind-of thing.
And clearly, when they could get away with simple linear allocation, they did so.
Thirdly, I suspect they had grown tired of doing any manual memory management at all. Dropping explicit memory regions from the malloc() interface is a change that, on the surface, simplifies stuff even further. You make the implementation-side smarter and you don't have to worry about passing coremap or swapmap or anymap. Remember: the way programs and problems were approached didn't lead to complex object lifetimes. And when you had to deal with tangled lifetimes, malloc()/free() appear deceivably simple in the beginning.
That last point seems more "vibes" than evidence, but there is some evidence actually. In V7 they added galloc(3):
GALLOC(3)                                               GALLOC(3)
NAME
     galloc, gfree, garbage - storage allocation with garbage
     collection
SYNOPSIS
     char *galloc(n)
     unsigned n;
     gfree(p)
     char *p;
     garbage( )
DESCRIPTION
     These functions perform heap storage allocation with garbage
     collection.
     Galloc allocates a block of at least n bytes and returns a
     pointer to it.  Gfree frees a block previously allocated by
     galloc.
     When space gets tight, garbage blocks are freed automati-
     cally.  A block allocated by galloc is deemed to be garbage
     unless it is reachable.  A reachable block is one whose
     first byte is pointed to by a declared C variable or by a
     pointer in a reachable block.
and Rob Pike had this in /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:15:
#define    gcnew(p, n)     ((void)gcalloc((ulong)(n)*sizeof((p)[0]), (long **)&(p)))
Ha, myth busted! The authors and people closest to C wanted garbage collection. Given how fast computers are -- and the pace of that -- this makes sense. It's even clearer if you look at what they did later with Limbo and Go. They wanted a higher level general purpose language to write programs in. They had C, so they tried to bolt GC on top of that.
Lastly, I should note that many of these problems were largely known, even at the time. In The Standard C library (1992), P. J. Plauger writes:
Allocating and freeing data objects on the heap in arbitrary order inevitably leaves unusable holes between some of the allocated data objects. That too lowers the usable size of the heap.
Don't overreact to this knowledge. Gather related data into a structure and allocate it all at once. That minimizes heap overhead, to be sure, but it is also good programming style. Do not gather unrelated data just to save heap overhead. Similarly, allocate data objects with similar lifetimes all at once, then free them at about the same time. That minimizes heap fragmentation, but it too is good style. Do not advance or defer unrelated heap operations just to minimize fragmentation. The storage allocation functions are an important aid to programming flexibility. Use them as they are intended to be used.
Criticism by yours truly: It's much easier to say "just do the right thing™" than show and provide tools for how to actually do it.
Conclusion
I don't know. Pay attention to good ideas, otherwise they might get lost? (literally in the case of V4, lol) Sounds cheesy.
Also, the "C object code improver" shatters the illusion that C was somehow magically fast. In fact, Ritchie later added an expression optimiser, and they kept extending both in each edition. I think C just wasn't slow, and it was made fast only with engineering effort put into the compiler (and even then, they had to add register because the compiler wasn't that smart either). It probably remained fast because Unix spread quickly and it carried C along with it, so hardware manufacturers adapted to C. There's a nice essay by Mike Pall discussing how modern CPUs try very hard to infer invariants from compiled C code (which the compiler tried very hard to optimise) and the costs associated with that.
At one point, I also want to investigate Inferno and Plan 9 more. Maybe the BSDs too. Until then...
Cya!

The lost malloc()
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
07:37:30 UTC
16:37:30 KST

The lost malloc()
(Sorry, I couldn't resist not putting a catchy title :)
Prompted by another project idea that popped into my mind, I did some Unix archaeology and looked at the original sources. This is the most fun I've ever had reading someone else's code - probably due to the historical significance. But also because of how delightfully approachable it was, compared to modern monstrocities.
This is a short(-ish) post regarding how they handled the mundane and boring task of allocating and managing memory (in C). In the future I'd like to read more about Unix the OS, its design, architecture & implementation.
A long time ago...
In a PDP far, far away, our journey begins with the fourth edition of Unix, released November '73, more than half a century ago. C actually first appeared in the second edition, released the year before, but wasn't extensively used. V4 is special because even the majority of the kernel was written in (let's call it "medieval") C by that point. The system had grown, however, and it was quite capable. You'll find that many Unix things we have today in POSIX-land were already present in V4.
Super fun fact: A tape containing V4 was only found last year! Previously, it was thought to be completely lost to time.
Linear allocation
The first interesting bit is found among the C "compiler" sources. In quotes, because it wasn't a monolithic compiler as we know it today. Rather, it was a set of distinct tools which you chained in order to get an object file from C code.
In /usr/c/c20.c:814, from what I can gather a very primitive optimiser, if you will (referred to as "C object code improver" in V5; there aren't many comments in V4) you see:
alloc(an)
{
    register int n;
    register char *p;
    n = an;
    n++;
    n =& ~01;
    if (lasta+n >= lastr) {
        if (sbrk(2000) == -1) {
            write(2, "Out of space\n", 14);
            exit(1);
        }
        lastr =+ 2000;
    }
    p = lasta;
    lasta =+ n;
    return(p);
}
Isn't that fascinating? This routine is used throughout the program to allocate memory. And if you squint, this is just a linear allocator. It aligns the size, checks if the region is big enough, otherwise tries to extend it. On failure, it just cold-exits. Which means callers don't have to check for NULL every single time, and indeed they do not.
The "region" isn't named, unlike how you'd do it today with arenas. However, the above does have a nice property, in that by using sbrk(), when we extend the heap, no pointer is invalidated.
And they don't bother freeing memory, because why would they? There's no need. Everything exists for the lifetime of the program.
dmr/malloc
This is the most interesting bit in my opinion, and the reason why I chose that title.
In Dennis' directory, you find a file named malloc.c. And you see two functions there:
struct map {
    char *m_size;
    char *m_addr;
};
malloc(mp, size)
struct map *mp;
mfree(mp, size, aa)
struct map *mp;
Seems familiar? Yep, it's mfree() with an m. These functions obviously deal with memory (de)allocation, and are the precursor to the ones we're familiar with today. But, the interfaces are different.
malloc() receives an additional first argument called mp (for "map"), and so does mfree(). What is that? Well, let's see how they're used:
p = malloc(coremap, sizeof foo);
...
mfree(coremap, sizeof foo, p);
q = malloc(swapmap, sizeof bar);
...
mfree(swapmap, sizeof bar, q);
So, they pass in some objects coremap and swapmap. What are those?
From /usr/sys/systm.h:2:
int	coremap[CMAPSIZ];
int	swapmap[SMAPSIZ];
They're just flat memory regions! So these malloc() and mfree() work on explicit memory regions! Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should. Those are just infinitely-times better interfaces than traditional malloc()/free().
Imagine using a library that has such an interface. You could deallocate all its memory resources by just discarding the entire region you delegated to it. Heap corruption bugs would be less severe because you could partition memory. You could trivially limit the amount of memory third party code allocates. The list goes on and on...
(Side note: They slightly messed up here and the regions should've been sized CMAPSIZ/2 and SMAPSIZ/2 respectively. They did fix that later.)
However, I don't think all these benefits were in the minds of Dennis and Ken. So why did they go with that interface and why did they partition memory to "core" and "swap"? The reason is, I believe, just hardware constraints. These interfaces stay like that up to V6 (maybe V7 too?), released the spring of '75, and thankfully there's an infamously good resource about that edition.
From A Commentary on the Sixth Edition UNIX Operating System by John Lions:
These are concerned with the allocation and subsequent release of two kinds of memory resources, namely:
- main memory in units of 32 words (64 bytes);
- disk swap area in units of 256 words (512 bytes).
For each of these two kinds of resource, a list of available areas is maintained within a resource "map" (either "coremap" or "swapmap"). A pointer to the appropriate resource "map" is always passed to "malloc" and "mfree" so that the routines themselves do not have to know the kind of resource with which they are dealing.
And it goes on to explain how the underlying allocation algorithm works. These do not do linear allocation (hence the mfree()). Basically, it's a list of blocks (struct map), ordered by address, where you do first-fit and also coalesce neighbour blocks.
The sixth edition is also the first where the term "arena" appears, in /usr/source/s4/alloc.s:17:
/char *allocs[2] {		/*initial empty arena*/
Rolling back
... to the topic of linear allocation... In V6's /usr/source/s1/diff1.c:88, I think the first ever version of diff(1), you find:
char *area;
char *top;
alloc(n)
{
    register char *p;
    p = area;
    n = (n+1) & ~1;
    area =+ n;
    while(area > top) {
        if(sbrk(1024) == -1) {
            mesg("Out of space\n");
            exit(1);
        }
        top =+ 1024;
    }
    return(p);
}
This is not all that much different from the previous alloc(), but this time it handles any allocation size. It uses a while to continue extending the region and stops when enough space has been reserved. The actual interesting part happens later, at unsort():143:
unsort(f, l, b)
struct line *f;
int *b;
{
    int *a;
    int i;
    a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0]));
    for(i=1;i<=l;i++)
        a[f[i].serial] = f[i].value;
    for(i=1;i<=l;i++)
        b[i] = a[i];
    area = a;
}
I'm not exactly sure what that function does, but it doesn't matter. What matters is that they allocate some memory (a = alloc(...);), then roll back the region (area = a;)! Though they subsequently just copy it to b, so it seems like this was redundant.
Computing sizes
Most of the code directly calls malloc()/alloc() and friends, and inlines the size computation logic. Like the line we saw earlier:
a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0]));
I don't do that anymore, and neither should you! I use a couple macros akin to C++'s new that handle all the sizeof business. But I am a dumb-dumb. Surely these guys must've come across the same pain points, and, if so, what did they do? Let's jump to V7, released January '79, four years after V6. You find this macro:
#define ALLOC(x) (struct x *) ckalloc(sizeof(struct x))
where they use it like:
struct foo { ... };
p = ALLOC(foo);
Nice! It's interesting to note where you find it; In /usr/src/cmd/f77/defines:38 and /usr/src/cmd/make/defs:38. Slightly suspicious. The former is part of the Fortran 77 compiler and latter of make. Stuart Feldman is the person who worked on both of those programs! It's clear that multiple people were working on the system at that time. A macro like that isn't used in any other program, sadly.
V7 is the first edition where you also find the assert() macro, and it was used extensively back then too. Good job! They also significantly expanded the number of man pages. Fun fact: I did $ man V7/usr/man/man3/foo.3 -- on 47 year old pages -- and it worked first try absolutely fine.
Let's go to V8, released in February '85, four years before the first C standard. You find this wild macro in /usr/src/cmd/ideal/memut.c:7:
char *fooalloc;
#define	tryalloc(new,kind)	\
    if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\
    emergency ();\
    if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\
        fprintf (stderr, "ideal: Out of space\n");\
        exit (1);\
        }\
    };\
    for (fooalloc = (char *) new;\
        fooalloc < ((char *) new) + sizeof (kind);\
        fooalloc ++)\
        *fooalloc = '\0';
If someone is too harsh because you used macros, point them at the above. Usage is bit different this time:
struct foo *x;
tryalloc(x, struct foo);
I decided to include it because the macro zero-initialises by default whatever was allocated! You also see a more familiar-looking malloc() being used. It appears this is the edition that they switched to the more traditional malloc()/free() interfaces we know. I'll hypothesize why that is at the very end.
But it gets even more interesting. In V8 you also find these macros:
#define new(type) ((type *) alloc (sizeof (type)))
#define new(t) ((t *) alloc (sizeof (t)))
#define        new(s)  (s *)alloc(sizeof (s))
When I saw these definitions I jumped out of my chair. It's basically how I'd define it too! You'll find them in:
- /usr/src/cmd/finddev.c:245, part of finddev(8).
- /usr/src/cmd/asd/asd.h:13, part of asd(8).
- /usr/include/ic.h:55, part of *checks notes* I have no idea.
respectively.
Unfortunately, I can't find the author(s) of any of these.
Cfront
In V8, you'll also find Cfront, a.k.a. medieval C++. It's then reasonable to assume that Stroustrup was inspired by the above macros and decided to incorporate new as a language-level feature. However, in A History of C++: 1979−1991, he writes:
In Simula, it is not possible to have local or global variables of class types; that is, every object of a class must be allocated on the free store using the new operator.
Huh. So C++'s new was inspired by the programming language "Simula". It's fair to say that the macros above were likely also derived from there. But Simula was quite old even by the 70s, let alone 1985. Perhaps Stroustrup persuaded people, or wrote those macros himself. He later writes:
The new operator that both allocates memory from the free store and invokes a constructor to ensure initialization was borrowed from Simula. The delete operator was a necessary complement because I did not want C with Classes to depend on a garbage collector. The argument for the new operator can be summarized like this. Would you rather write:
X* p = new X(2);
or
struct X * p = (struct X *) malloc(sizeof(struct X));
if (p == 0) error("memory exhausted");
p−>init(2);
and which version are you most likely to make a mistake in? The arguments against -- which were voiced quite a lot at the time -- were "but we don’t really need it," and "but someone will have used new as an identifier." Both observations are correct, of course. Introducing operator new thus made the use of free store more convenient and less error−prone. This increased its use even further so that the C free store allocation routine malloc() used to implement new became the most common performance bottleneck in real systems. [...] Having real programs spend 50% or more of their time in malloc() wasn’t acceptable.
(emphasis mine :P)
He makes a compelling argument, which I agree with, but doesn't mention the new() macros that basically did the same thing. Although you'll find many programs in V8 that do the latter, verbose thing. Now I want to know the author(s) of those macros even more!
Sims
This is a big parentheses because I wanted to know how Simula came up with new. Wikipedia states:
Simula 67 introduced objects, classes, inheritance and subclasses, virtual procedures, coroutines, and discrete event simulation, and featured garbage collection.
And it appeared in 1967. Wow! In the 1964 report of SIMULA I, you'll find:
[...] The symbol "new" only serves to resolve an ambiguity of the identifier A inside the activity blah blah blah [...]. Elsewhere the symbol new is redundant, but can often be used to advantage to improve readability.
So it was only used to resolve grammar ambiguities (I think?). And Stroustrup re-purposed it. Clever!
Further reading
The History of Simula, by Jan Rune Holmevik. Reads like (bad) Sci-Fi. All the politics nonsense aside, what I found most curious is that they completely specified the language before attempting to write a compiler for it. They started writing the first compiler atleast a year after. This would sound insane today, but I guess the cost of writing code was substantially higher back then.
Also: The development of the SIMULA languages, by the authors. I didn't read that one, although I should...
It's honestly amazing how influential Simula was. In "10.5 Operating Instruction" they even use the term "run time system" and give it the same meaning we're accustomed to.
Simula, in turn, was partly inspired by SIMSCRIPT (don't laugh). If you skim its 1962 report, you won't find a mention of new. You'll however find CREATE:
When a new Entity is created by a CREATE statement, space for storing its Attribute values is allocated in the amount specified on the Definition Form. This record is given an identification number, and the Variable specified in the CREATE statement is automatically set equal to this number.
For example, the statement "CREATE DOG CALLED FIDO" allocates the required amount of storage for the Attributes of a DOG, and sets FIDO equal to the identification number of the Attribute record.
Fascinating. The whole SIMSCRIPT report is fascinating actually, and I only briefly skimmed through it. At the beginning, it even describes something like a primitive ECS, by my understanding. At the end though it slaps you back to reality:
and you remember what year it was.
Later editions
In V9's /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:14, part of the Sam editor by Rob Pike, you find a "generalised" version of new():
#define    new(t, n)       ((t *)alloc(((ulong)(n)*sizeof(t))))
Although, by and large, almost every program doesn't do this. Most just directly call malloc() and friends, and do size calculations \w error checking at every call site. I don't know why, considering how much error-prone that is, but maybe due to inertia. It's a similar story in V10, but I didn't check it as thoroughly since it's quite big (it includes medieval GCC!).
So what happened?
They were so close to arenas; with linear allocation and explicit memory regions, rolling back, and even having a nice new() macro. All this is speculation at this point, but maybe some of it is correct. First of all, most programs had trivial object lifetimes. Allocate memory, read some data, process/crunch and spit out some result. You don't need any disciplined memory allocation strategy for that. You can even use malloc() for everything and let the OS reclaim it once the process exits. Given how simple malloc() was at first, it wouldn't be much of a bottleneck either. The philosophy of programs only "doing a single thing well" also fitted this pattern.
Secondly, it's clear some decisions were motivated by the very little memory they had to play with. And there was no virtual memory either (initially, that is). Nowadays, you can "allocate" however big of a memory region you want and all will probably be okay. They couldn't really do that, so they were fighting to reclaim every empty block and gap there was and scale a program's space with how much is actually needed. There's a counterpoint to this, however, because some code is confused. Sometimes you see fixed-size buffers/arrays pop up, seemingly out of nowhere, and the program bail out if they fill. I'm not sure why, but perhaps they didn't deem it worthwhile the complexity to use malloc() in those cases and/or "don't fix it if it ain't broke" kind-of thing.
And clearly, when they could get away with simple linear allocation, they did so.
Thirdly, I suspect they had grown tired of doing any manual memory management at all. Dropping explicit memory regions from the malloc() interface is a change that, on the surface, simplifies stuff even further. You make the implementation-side smarter and you don't have to worry about passing coremap or swapmap or anymap. Remember: the way programs and problems were approached didn't lead to complex object lifetimes. And when you had to deal with tangled lifetimes, malloc()/free() appear deceivably simple in the beginning.
That last point seems more "vibes" than evidence, but there is some evidence actually. In V7 they added galloc(3):
GALLOC(3)                                               GALLOC(3)
NAME
     galloc, gfree, garbage - storage allocation with garbage
     collection
SYNOPSIS
     char *galloc(n)
     unsigned n;
     gfree(p)
     char *p;
     garbage( )
DESCRIPTION
     These functions perform heap storage allocation with garbage
     collection.
     Galloc allocates a block of at least n bytes and returns a
     pointer to it.  Gfree frees a block previously allocated by
     galloc.
     When space gets tight, garbage blocks are freed automati-
     cally.  A block allocated by galloc is deemed to be garbage
     unless it is reachable.  A reachable block is one whose
     first byte is pointed to by a declared C variable or by a
     pointer in a reachable block.
and Rob Pike had this in /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:15:
#define    gcnew(p, n)     ((void)gcalloc((ulong)(n)*sizeof((p)[0]), (long **)&(p)))
Ha, myth busted! The authors and people closest to C wanted garbage collection. Given how fast computers are -- and the pace of that -- this makes sense. It's even clearer if you look at what they did later with Limbo and Go. They wanted a higher level general purpose language to write programs in. They had C, so they tried to bolt GC on top of that.
Lastly, I should note that many of these problems were largely known, even at the time. In The Standard C library (1992), P. J. Plauger writes:

Do not gather unrelated data just to save heap overhead. Similarly, allocate data objects with similar lifetimes all at once, then free them at about the same time. That minimizes heap fragmentation, but it too is good style. Do not advance or defer unrelated heap operations just to minimize fragmentation. I don't know. Pay attention to good ideas, otherwise they might get lost? (literally in the case of V4, lol) Sounds cheesy.
Also, the "C object code improver" shatters the illusion that C was somehow magically fast. In fact, Ritchie later added an expression optimiser, and they kept extending both in each edition. I think C just wasn't slow, and it was made fast only with engineering effort put into the compiler (and even then, they had to add register because the compiler wasn't that smart either). It probably remained fast because Unix spread quickly and it carried C along with it, so hardware manufacturers adapted to C. Democrats Rout GOP

Midterm Elections Live Updates: Democrats Vow to Use Majority to Check Trump
Representative Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the next House speaker, said his party would focus on affordability after a remarkable power shift in Congress. President Trump, speaking at the White House, focused on his renovation projects, not the midterms.
Latest
Democrats on Wednesday afternoon were on track to secure at least a 50-seat majority in the House and had captured solid control of the Senate after notching seismic victories across the country that left Republicans searching for a path forward in a drastically reordered Washington.
Triumphant as the scale of their wins came into sharper focus, Democrats vowed to take quick action to challenge President Trump and to aggressively investigate him and his administration. “The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over,” promised Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader.
The party flipped Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and even Texas, according to The Associated Press. Ballots were still being counted in Alaska’s contentious Senate race and in the unlikely battleground of Mississippi, where fewer than 50 votes separated the two candidates.
Mr. Jeffries, who is expected to become the next House speaker, celebrated the blue wave as an “American tsunami” and predicted Democrats would win at least 255 seats in the 435-seat chamber.
Vice President JD Vance placed the blame for the Republicans’ wipeout in the midterm elections squarely on the war with Iran, a remarkable break from Mr. Trump’s defense of his decision to attack. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Mr. Vance wrote on social media. “Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost.”
Mr. Trump used his first public appearance on Wednesday to speak about his ballroom from inside the construction site. He said he thought Mr. Vance’s assertion was “largely true,” but he said if he could go back, he would not have done it differently.
In a triumphant election night, Democrats surged in crucial House battlegrounds and beyond, picking off Republicans who had not expected competitive races in conservative-leaning seats from Indiana to Missouri to Alabama. They were on track to secure the largest majority in the chamber since 2008, when they won 257 seats.
Taken together, the results promised a freshly assertive Congress when it begins in January after two years in which Republicans generally ceded power to Mr. Trump and reduced the legislative branch’s role to that of a mere bystander.
The shock waves from the election quickly reverberated among Republicans, who had feared widespread losses but had not anticipated such a sweeping repudiation of their party.
Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana told aides that he would not seek to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, setting off a scramble among ambitious Republicans to succeed him. Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio announced he would seek the role, arguing that Republicans needed to take a combative approach toward the Democratic majority next year.
“In these next two years, our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democrat party is,” he said. “Offense, not defense, wins elections.”
Mr. Trump told The New York Times in an interview that he was “absolutely willing to accept” the midterm results and was prepared to work with Democrats — despite his repeated efforts to sow doubts about voter fraud and to have the Justice Department intervene in elections.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
- Democratic landslide: The Democrats’ landslide, flipping seats that had spent decades in Republican hands, did not just reach the federal races but also state and local governments. The party notched firsts in governors’ races and won down-ballot races like those for state treasurer, secretary of state and state legislature.
- G.O.P. bright spots: Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida, with Senator Ashley Moody defeating Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat. Byron Donalds, a staunch Trump supporter, was elected Florida’s first Black governor, keeping the Republicans’ hold on that office.
- Ballot measures: Voters across the country also weighed in on a range of statewide issues, including abortion, how future elections would be run and how their own votes would be counted. Read more ›
Voters across every major demographic group — race, age, gender and education — made a drastic swing left in Tuesday’s election, reversing the broad shift in support that Republicans saw in 2024.
The reversal was most notable among young voters and voters of color, particularly Hispanic voters, who swung toward the Democratic Party by nearly 30 percentage points. Democrats also made sizable gains among groups typically seen as stalwarts of the Republican base — white voters without a college degree and older voters — both of which swung left.
An unusual situation is brewing in Mississippi, the only state in the country with no legal provision that allows for a recount of votes in a statewide election.
The Democratic candidate for Senate, Scott Colom, leads the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 65 votes as of Wednesday afternoon — an incredibly tight race that would trigger an automatic recount in dozens of other states.
In fact, 47 states have a provision for an automatic recount if a contest is close or if a candidate requests a recount. Two more states, Illinois and Tennessee, allow recounts if a candidate mounts a formal legal challenge.
Most state recount provisions were instituted during the last century as a result of legal challenges that made their way to state supreme courts. But Mississippi has no recount law on the books, leaving it unprepared to handle a particularly close election.
There are still small batches of ballots to be counted in the state, and the margin between the candidates may widen. Mississippi, unlike many states, accepts mail-in ballots that arrive five days after Election Day, drawing out the counting process.
Ultimately, however, there is no legal path to a recount in the state. Derek Muller, a professor and expert on election law at the University of Notre Dame, said that a losing candidate could instead pursue a legal challenge over the inclusion of specific ballots or sets of ballots, which could result in a change in vote totals.
- By Peter Baker, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Nikolay Nikolov, Thomas Vollkommer, Rafaela Balster, James Surdam, Edward Vega and Rachel Buigas-Lopez
- By Nate Cohn, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega
- By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Thomas Vollkommer and James Surdam
- By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh, Edward Vega and Stephanie Swart
- By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Jon Miller, Edward Vega and James Surdam
- By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh, Stephanie Swart and Edward Vega
- By Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega
- By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Thomas Vollkommer, James Surdam and Edward Vega
- By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh and Stephanie Swart
- By Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega
Representative Richard Hudson, the North Carolina Republican who is the chairman of House Republicans’ campaign arm, conceded his election in a statement on Wednesday. Though The Associated Press has not called his race, Hudson currently trails by about 2 percentage points.
Hudson, who oversaw his party’s efforts to help House Republicans keep their majority, said in a statement that “the voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice, and I respect it.” His loss reflected the extent of Republicans’ troubles on Election Day: Trump carried his district by about 16 points in the 2024 presidential election.
President Trump spent much of the past two years promising to bring down energy prices.
Instead, his war with Iran, as well as other policies, drove up the cost of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time his administration worked to thwart efforts to fight climate change, blocking renewable energy investments that could have reduced the country’s reliance on fossil fuels or brought down costs.
On Tuesday, voters’ frustration with soaring energy prices helped propel Democrats to a blowout, with Republicans losing control of the House and the Senate, as well as the governorships of many historically conservative states.
“It’s quite clear that energy and energy affordability in particular played a big role in the electorate’s decision-making last night,” said Hasan Nazar, head of policy at Crux, a clean energy finance company.
Many Americans said concerns about the cost of gas and electricity informed their voting choices, according to polling from The Associated Press. Gasoline prices across the country were at a record high for an Election Day, according to AAA.
No single action had a bigger effect on energy costs than Mr. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. With the Strait of Hormuz closed and global flows of oil disrupted, gasoline prices in the United States have jumped more than 40 percent since the war began. Diesel prices are up nearly 70 percent.
Catherine Wolfram, a professor of energy economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management, said that launching the war was among the worst decisions Mr. Trump could have made if he was trying to bring down energy costs. “It’s Econ 101 that invading Iran when they control the Strait of Hormuz is going to impact gas prices,” she said.
Daniel Raimi, a fellow at Resources for the Future, a nonprofit research institute, noted that “usually presidents have very little sway over global oil prices, but that was not the case this time.” The Iran war, he said, not only increased fuel prices but also costs for fertilizer “and a whole host of commodities.”
Beyond the war in Iran, the Trump administration has taken a sweeping approach to reshaping the nation’s energy policy, including actions that may have increased costs for consumers.
At a time when electricity demand and prices are soaring because of the data center boom, the administration has blocked the construction of offshore wind farms, despite pleas from governors to allow the projects to get built. It also mandated that coal-burning power plans stay online, even though utilities said that doing so would raise prices for their customers.
Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said on Wednesday that higher energy costs were a factor with voters. “Some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous, but much of the time he implemented things that raised their costs: on electricity, on health care, on goods,” he said, referring to Mr. Trump.
If there was one energy-related issue beyond Iran that broke through, Mr. Raimi said, it was likely higher electricity prices, which many Americans blame on the proliferation of data centers. “Voters are certainly unhappy about higher electricity bills, but the larger driver for those higher prices is increased demand,” he said.
While data centers have become deeply unpopular with voters, Mr. Trump and his administration have offered stalwart support for the industry and dismissed voters’ concerns about them.
Other issues, like keeping coal plants open or blocking wind farms, he said, were less important in the voting booth because their effect on prices would be marginal.
Some of the Democrats who won seized on energy affordability as part of their campaigns. Roy Cooper, who flipped a Republican Senate seat in North Carolina, said at a campaign stop that the war in Iran was “driving the cost of gas through the roof.”
James Talarico, who became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas in decades, has called for suspending the federal gas tax and diesel tax.
And Abdul El-Sayed, who won a Senate seat in Michigan, touted the need to adopt clean energy. “We have all the technology we need to drop the price of electricity via renewable energy,” he said at a recent event. “And all of those renewable energy investments, guess what? They create really great jobs.”
While Democrats will soon be in control of Congress, bringing down energy prices is unlikely to be swift or easy.
Mr. Trump has two years left in office. In recent weeks, he has indicated that he might intensify attacks in Iran following the midterm election, which could lead to further spikes in oil prices.
But with voters signaling their frustration with the high cost of gas, diesel and electricity, some clean-energy supporters said they believed even Mr. Trump might be open to revising his stance on some issues that have driven up prices.
“The election was a compete repudiation of his energy agenda,” said Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power, an environmental group. “The question is what comes next, and one thing he could do is stop blocking clean power that could help meet demand and lower costs.”
Democrats will hold at least 54 seats in the Senate in the next Congress, the party’s largest majority since at least 2012, and at least 237 seats in the House, with the potential for that number to grow significantly once more races are called. If Democrats end up with more than 257 seats, it would be the largest majority for either party in that chamber since 1992.
Black voters remained the backbone of the Democratic coalition across the South in this year’s election. House Democratic candidates won Black voters by a margin of roughly 80 percentage points nationwide, according to Times Voter Trends. That was an increase from 2024, when the Democrat’s presidential candidate, Kamala Harris, won Black voters by about 70 points.
The Democrats expanded their overwhelming margins among Black voters in several Southern states, among them Mississippi, South Carolina, Georgia, North Carolina, Louisiana and Alabama.
But some of the more striking movement came among white voters, who shifted toward Democrats by 12 points in Mississippi, 15 points in Alabama and 19 points in North Carolina.
Starting last summer, President Trump pushed Republicans to engage in an extraordinary mid-decade redistricting project to overhaul congressional maps in favor of the G.O.P. The goal was to protect a House majority during his final two years in office.
It did not work.
Instead, Democrats on Tuesday gained at least eight seats in Republican-run states that had redistricted over the past 16 months. It was a stiff rebuff for a plan to sort just enough Republicans into just enough districts to give the party a 20-seat House firewall.
Months of political warfare, including more than $200 million in spending on referendums in California and Virginia, simply did not anticipate an electorate that backed House Democratic candidates by 13 percentage points.
No map could have produced a Republican advantage strong enough to withstand such a Democratic wave.
“Donald Trump and Republicans poked the bear, and they got mauled,” said John Bisognano, president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee. “There’s no way to look at this cycle and not see that the scheme to gerrymander the country was a complete and utter catastrophe.”
The plan’s demise illustrated once again the perpetual elasticity of the American electorate. Just as the coalitions that elected Barack Obama president in 2008 had evaporated by 2010, groups that backed Mr. Trump in 2024 abandoned him for 2026.
On Wednesday, House Democratic leaders crowed about defeating the Republican redistricting. They stood in front of a poster featuring a May social media post from James Blair, who ran Mr. Trump’s political operation, in which he boasted that redistricting would net the G.O.P. 16 seats.
“The American people hate it when politicians try to pick their voters,” said Representative Suzan DelBene of Washington State, who leads the House Democrats’ campaign arm.
It will take weeks and precinct-level analysis of election results to determine whether Republicans would have won more seats had they not redistricted at all. But perhaps nowhere demonstrated the futility of their plans than Texas and North Carolina.
Texas Republicans anticipated that the Hispanic swing toward Mr. Trump in 2024 would be durable. Instead, five districts in Hispanic-heavy South Texas moved to Democrats.
North Carolina legislators redrew congressional lines ahead of both the 2024 and 2026 elections, producing a map intended to deliver 11 of the state’s 14 districts to Republicans. Though not all of Tuesday’s races have been called, Democrats appear on pace to win 10 out of the 14 seats.
In Florida, Republicans gained zero seats in a map they believed would give them four held by Democrats. An Ohio map designed to shift two seats to Republicans may have handed two more to Democrats. And new maps drawn to squeeze out Democrats in Alabama and Tennessee also failed.
At the same time, Democrats are poised to gain several seats from new California congressional districts they drew in response to the Republican effort. There also will be a new Democratic congressman in Utah, where judges ordered new maps. And White House attempts to force new districts were foiled by legislators in Indiana and Nebraska and the courts in Missouri.
It could have been worse for Republicans. The Virginia Supreme Court invalidated a voter-approved plan that likely would have handed 10 of the state’s 11 congressional seats to Democrats. Under the existing map, Democrats are likely to win eight.
The redistricting fight is likely not over. Democrats on Tuesday won control of state governments in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, which could redraw maps to secure seats for their party.
Maryland voters approved a referendum to allow legislators to draw the state’s one Republican House district out of existence. And Republicans may still attempt new maps in South Carolina and Mississippi.
Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas, who lost his bid for a fourth term, could call a special session before the year’s end and ask legislators for yet another new map that could help Republicans recoup their losses.
In Georgia, however, Gov. Brian Kemp said Wednesday morning that he would not call a special session to redistrict before he hands over control to Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms.
Annie Karni contributed reporting.
William Lawrence, a Democrat and climate activist, scored a marquee victory for the ascendant progressive movement, ousting Representative Tom Barrett, a first-term Republican, to flip a battleground seat in central Michigan, according to The Associated Press. Lawrence campaigned on expanding access to government-funded health care and opposing data centers, issues that progressives have argued could energize working-class voters, not just in Democratic primaries but also in general elections.
Laura Gillen, a one-term Democratic incumbent, fended off a challenge from the Republican Jeanine Driscoll, the receiver of taxes for the town of Hempstead, according to The Associated Press. Gillen will continue to represent New York’s Fourth Congressional District, which includes portions of Nassau County on Long Island.
Formerly the town supervisor in Hempstead, Gillen narrowly defeated a Republican incumbent, Anthony D’Esposito, to flip the seat in 2024.
Tom Suozzi, a Democratic incumbent, won re-election in New York’s Third Congressional District, defeating the Republican Mike LiPetri, according to The Associated Press. In 2024, Suozzi narrowly won a tough battle for the Long Island district, which includes a small portion of Queens.
Suozzi was first elected to the district in 2016, vacated his seat to run for governor in 2022 and reclaimed it two years ago. Both candidates emphasized bipartisanship on the campaign trail this year.
Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, the two-term Democrat from a conservative-leaning rural district in Washington State, won her re-election bid, according to The Associated Press. She holds on to one of the most competitive seats in the country, defeating a Republican who had tried to distance himself from President Trump in a bid to appeal to independent voters.
Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the No. 2 House Republican, announced that he would run to be the minority leader in the next Congress. Scalise, who has been in House Republican leadership since 2014, emphasized his experience in a letter to his colleagues. He called for “substantive changes to the way our conference operates,” arguing that the G.O.P. needed to be more unified in its approach.
Scalise’s announcement will pit him once again against Representative Jim Jordan, the firebrand, hard-line conservative from Ohio. Both men ran for speaker in 2023, but neither of them was able to secure the necessary support to win.
Senator Marsha Blackburn, the governor-elect of Tennessee, declined to say on Wednesday whom she will name to fill her vacant seat in the Senate, calling it a conversation for another day. Rumors have circulated in recent days about who might get the nod. One possibility is Pete Hegseth, the current Pentagon chief who is a Tennessee resident.
Trump ended his public appearance at the White House after about half an hour, during which he focused on renovation projects and appeared to have little interest in discussing the midterms. He did not mention the Republican defeat last night in his remarks until asked by reporters afterward, then defended his campaign strategy. He supported Vice President JD Vance’s social media post that said the Iran War was responsible for Republicans’ electoral loss, but the president also repeatedly suggested he had no regrets on the war, and would do it all again.
“As far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” he said.
Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia shut down speculation on Wednesday that he would call a special legislative session to rush through new congressional maps favorable to Republicans or weaken the powers of his office before his Democratic successor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, could assume it.
“The voters of our state have spoken,” Mr. Kemp, a two-term Republican incumbent leaving office because of term limits, said in a statement on Wednesday morning. “As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state.”
A Supreme Court decision that weakened the Voting Rights Act has prompted Republican lawmakers across the South to redraw federal and state legislative boundaries to benefit their party, eliminating districts that had been created to promote minority representation.
Georgia’s legislature had resisted doing that, despite calls from President Trump and some Republicans in the state to take action. Mr. Kemp declined to redraw maps before the midterm elections, noting that early voting in the primaries had, by that point, already started.
He then called a special session in June to draw up new maps for the 2028 election. But less than an hour after the session began, Republican legislative leaders came out and said they would not present new maps after all.
They cited a desire for a methodical process that would include greater input from voters, rather than rushing legislation through, but the decision was also a recognition of mounting protests against redistricting and fears that moving forward could undermine their party’s already enfeebled fortunes in the midterm elections.
There was also an implicit expectation among many political observers that the matter had been shelved only temporarily, and that a narrow window between the election and when a new governor takes power would provide an opportunity not only to enact new maps but also to strip away some of the authority of the governor’s office. The chatter intensified as polls indicated a greater possibility of victory for Ms. Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta and the first Democrat to be elected governor of Georgia in more than 25 years.
Mr. Kemp moved immediately to cut off that possibility, but he said there were “budgetary issues that may need to be addressed before the convening of the regular session in January.”
After several minutes of watching a beam being lifted to the ceiling, Trump went back to taking questions. He was asked if he knew Vice President JD Vance was going to make the lengthy, critical post he made this morning. “I know how he feels about it, I think it was fine,” he said, calling the post “good.” He said he had spoken to Vance but did not elaborate much.
Trump said he couldn’t predict who would run for president in 2028. “Maybe he won’t run, I don’t know who’s going to run,” he said.
Trump spoke ambiguously of his future relationship with the Democrat-controlled Congress that was just elected. “I’ll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive,” he said, noting he had “the power to veto.” Trump said much the same thing last night, saying in an interview with The Times that he was looking forward to working with Democrats, but also posting an image with the word “VETO” shortly after.
Trump is taking questions from reporters now. He was asked about Vice President JD Vance’s social media post that said the reason Republicans lost so badly was because of the war in Iran. “Well I think it’s largely true,” Trump said. But he said if he could go back, he wouldn’t have done it differently.
Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday placed the blame for Republicans’ wipeout in the midterm elections squarely on the war with Iran, in a remarkable break from President Trump’s defense of his decision to attack.
In a more than 600-word post on social media, Mr. Vance also offered a broader critique of the Trump administration’s agenda and messaging in what appeared to be an effort to separate himself from the president.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Mr. Vance wrote. “The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”
In fact, Mr. Trump told The New York Times on Tuesday night that he had no regrets about the war, though he acknowledged voters “weren’t happy with the oil price.”
“That’s a decision that was a very wise decision for the future of the country and the world,” he said.
Since he became Mr. Trump’s running mate, Mr. Vance had been widely seen as the front-runner to succeed the president and inherit the mantle of the Make America Great Again movement Mr. Trump started. But after Tuesday’s disastrous results, Republicans are already rethinking what the future of the party looks like, and Mr. Vance’s post suggests he is willing to separate himself from Mr. Trump as he considers his own political future.
And yet, the post was not a complete break from Mr. Trump. Before Mr. Vance posted the message, he shared it with the president and received positive feedback, one person briefed on the matter said.
Mr. Trump also told reporters Wednesday afternoon that Mr. Vance’s assessment was “largely true.”
“If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” he said, saying he had “no choice” but to attack Iran.
And Mr. Trump speculated about whether Mr. Vance would go ahead with a presidential bid.
“Maybe he won’t run,” he said. “I don’t know who’s going to run.”
Before Tuesday, Mr. Vance’s allies said that the vice president was in no rush to make a decision about running for president, and that he was unlikely to do so until next year.
In his post on social media, Mr. Vance said that many of the voters who supported him and Mr. Trump showed up in the elections, but that they chose to elect Democrats. He said a Republican pollster he called “one of the smartest people I know in politics” identified the four main reasons voters abandoned Republicans: They wanted to end the war, focus on inflation, put America first and change the country’s relationship with Israel.
That implicitly put Mr. Vance at odds with Mr. Trump, who has steadfastly defended the war with Iran, dismissed affordability concerns as a “hoax” and has closely aligned himself with Israel and its leader, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“Everyone knows why we lost,” Mr. Vance wrote. “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
