Title:The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students.

Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
21:39:05 UTC
06:39:05 KST

Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode
We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark.
In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright. Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web.
You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’.
For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark.
How does Adaptive Dark Mode work?
At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged.
While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio. Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark.
Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear.
It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos.
Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict.
It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy.
Making your site work even better
In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices.
If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.
Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.
Building your own dark mode
For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier.
All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including:
Newer CSS functions like color-mix() and contrast-color(), plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility.
Be sure to declare dark mode support using the color-scheme meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the color-scheme property on :root or body in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this information later via JavaScript. This best practice helps ensure your site is rendered correctly as fast as possible.
Using the “light only” color scheme
If you would like your web app or website to not be transformed by Adaptive Dark Mode, you can communicate this using color-scheme. The HTML <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> tag lets browsers know that 1) this page supports light mode and 2) should only be displayed in light mode. The color-scheme: light only rule does the same thing, but with the flexibility of CSS, allowing you to just target specific elements on the page — or of course, you can target the whole page with :root { }. (Note: the ‘only’ keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Check back as Adaptive Dark Mode evolves through the beta process.)
Protecting user privacy
Apple firmly believes user privacy is a fundamental human right. If websites could detect when a user has enabled Adaptive Dark Mode, that would increase the amount of fingerprintable information and weaken privacy protections against trackers.
As a result, Safari prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied. JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones. Any images drawn into canvas render in their original form.
Feedback
If you manage a website or web app, and would like to discuss how Adaptive Dark Mode is adapting your project, feel free to reach out at web-evangelist@apple.com.
If you try out Adaptive Dark Mode as a user, and find a site that does not work well, we’d love for you to file a report with Feedback Assistant. (Learn more about filing Feedback).

====================================================================================================

Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.
Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.
Building your own dark mode
For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier.
All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including:
Newer CSS functions like color-mix() and contrast-color(), plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility.
Be sure to declare dark mode support using the color-scheme meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the color-scheme property on :root or body in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this information later via JavaScript. This best practice helps ensure your site is rendered correctly as fast as possible.
Using the “light only” color scheme
If you would like your web app or website to not be transformed by Adaptive Dark Mode, you can communicate this using color-scheme. The HTML <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> tag lets browsers know that 1) this page supports light mode and 2) should only be displayed in light mode. The color-scheme: light only rule does the same thing, but with the flexibility of CSS, allowing you to just target specific elements on the page — or of course, you can target the whole page with :root { }. (Note: the ‘only’ keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Check back as Adaptive Dark Mode evolves through the beta process.)
Protecting user privacy
Apple firmly believes user privacy is a fundamental human right. If websites could detect when a user has enabled Adaptive Dark Mode, that would increase the amount of fingerprintable information and weaken privacy protections against trackers.
As a result, Safari prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied. JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones. Any images drawn into canvas render in their original form.
Feedback
If you manage a website or web app, and would like to discuss how Adaptive Dark Mode is adapting your project, feel free to reach out at web-evangelist@apple.com.
If you try out Adaptive Dark Mode as a user, and find a site that does not work well, we’d love for you to file a report with Feedback Assistant. (Learn more about filing Feedback).

Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
21:25:24 UTC
06:25:24 KST

It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge. That said, here are some initial impressions.
Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
The watchOS 27.3 beta adds Live Rewind and Siri Recap to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review.) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public.
The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone.
Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap on only at the office during weekdays from 1PM to 4PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.)
Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two.
I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had many organic, lengthy spoken conversations yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a sense for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims.
My first Siri Recap was for an editorial planning meeting for a story I’m working on. It was decent at identifying different topics discussed, and I was impressed that it stripped out some sensitive information. Any outsider looking at these notes would be terribly confused. Ironically, it meant that this summary wasn’t the most useful for my job.
What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Apple’s said publicly that Siri Recap is meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. That rings true based on my first one. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations.
In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.

Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
21:16:48 UTC
06:16:48 KST

Kairos decides every sign-up, login, order, payment and payout as it happens, and keeps each decision with the signals behind it. It is an open-source alternative to Sardine, Sift, Riskified and SEON, with two things they don't have: your coding agent tunes it, and decision models catch fraud before you have the labels to train on.
- Real-time decisions: one call returns approve, step up, review or block, with a risk score and the reasons, from the subject's history, the devices, cards and addresses it shares with others, and the session.
- Workflows: ask a decision model, score with a model, branch, call webhooks, open cases, and decide again later.
- Queues and cases: review work for people, whose resolutions become labels.
- MCP server: Claude Code, Cursor or Codex read your decisions and build workflows, with every action recorded under its key.
- Experiments: your agent proposes model variants, Kairos trains and tests them on your data, and the agent ships the winner.
- Grayson: Finic's decision model answers questions about each request in plain language. It works with few labels and reads unstructured data.
- Models: logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost-compatible) on your numbers and Grayson's answers, trained in Kairos or uploaded.
- SDKs for TypeScript (@finic-ai/kairos) and Python (finic-kairos), a CLI, an HTTP API, and self-hosting with Docker.
You send Kairos what happens in your product: sign-ups, logins, orders, payouts, chargebacks. It decides each request (approve, step up, review or block) and keeps every decision with the signals behind it.
What makes Kairos different is who tunes it. Connect Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any agent over MCP, and the agent can do the work of a fraud ML engineer:
- Build the workflow. It defines what to decide, which questions to ask a decision model, and which fields to score.
- Design experiments. It proposes variants: a decision model alone, logistic regression on your numbers, gradient-boosted trees, a stack of them, or the decision model's answers combined with your numbers in one model.
- Let Kairos run them. The server trains each variant on your oldest labeled data, chooses on the next, and tests on the newest, then reports ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, the gain over a baseline with its 95% interval, and precision and recall at your thresholds.
- Pick the winner and ship it. The agent explains its choice, applies the variant as the workflow's next version, and comes back when new labels arrive.
You:     "Our chargebacks went up. Find a better model for shopify_order and publish it if it wins."
Agent:   designs six variants → create_workflow_experiment → reads the results →
         "Logistic regression on the order's numbers plus Grayson's answers wins: ROC-AUC 0.949 on validation,
          0.930 on test. Publishing it as v6."
Kairos is built around Grayson, Finic's decision model. You ask it questions in plain language ("Does the shipping address look like a reshipper?", "Is this email throwaway?") and it answers with calibrated probabilities. Decision models are strong where traditional ML is weak:
- Few labels. Grayson works on day one, before you have the thousands of chargebacks a model needs to learn from.
- Unstructured data. It reads descriptions, emails, names, addresses, notes and item titles, which a gradient-boosted tree can't.
- Explanations. Every answer is a question you wrote, so every decision says why.
Traditional models are strong where decision models are weak: they learn your own outcomes precisely, from your own numbers, and they cost nothing per decision. Kairos lets you combine both: Grayson's answers become features next to your fields in a logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost-compatible, trained in Kairos itself), and experiments tell you which combination wins on your data.
Sign up at kairos.finic.ai. Create a sandbox environment, a secret key, and you're ready to send events.
In the console, open Settings › MCP, turn on the tool groups your agent needs, and create a key. Then, in Claude Code:
claude mcp add --transport http kairos https://kairos.finic.ai/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer ksk_…"
Cursor, Codex and VS Code work the same way: see MCP for agents. Then ask your agent to look at your decisions, build a workflow, or run an experiment.
npm install @finic-ai/kairos      # or: pip install finic-kairosimport { Kairos } from "@finic-ai/kairos";
const kairos = new Kairos({ apiKey: process.env.KAIROS_API_KEY!, baseUrl: "https://kairos.finic.ai" });
await kairos.defineAction("withdrawal", {
  subject: "user",
  hold: "Should this withdrawal be held because the account shows signs of fraud or takeover?",
});
kairos.track("login", { userId: "user_42", deviceId: "dev_9", ipCountry: "GB" });
const decision = await kairos.decide({ type: "withdrawal", userId: "user_42", usd: 900 });
// { decision: "approve" | "step_up" | "review" | "block", riskScore, reasons, … }
You need Node.js 22, pnpm 10 and a Grayson API key from portal.finic.ai. No database to set up: the server starts its own Postgres.
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env     # set GRAYSON_API_KEY
pnpm kairos dev          # the API on http://localhost:8787 and the console on http://localhost:5273
For your team, docker compose up --build. See Self-hosting and Local setup.
The CLI
pnpm kairos signup                                                     # the local server, a new account
pnpm kairos login --profile prod --url https://kairos.finic.ai --email you@example.com
pnpm kairos keys create "My server"                                    # a secret key for your code
pnpm kairos actions define withdrawal --data @withdrawal.json
pnpm kairos import events transactions.csv --type transaction --ts created_at --entity user=customer
pnpm kairos decide withdrawal -e user=user_42 -p usd=900
pnpm kairos workflows run review_payout -i user=user_42 --wait
pnpm kairos --help                                                     # every command
To have kairos on your path, run pnpm link --global in apps/cli.
- Shopify: decide every order, hold risky ones for review, and learn from chargebacks. To get the Kairos app for your store, reach the Finic team on Discord or at support@finic.ai.
- Inbound webhooks: take events from providers such as Stripe. See Inbound webhooks.
The docs are at kairos.finic.ai/docs, and in docs/.
pnpm test         # all tests; no network
pnpm test:python  # the tests of the Python SDK
pnpm typecheck
- Discord: questions, ideas and show-and-tell, at discord.gg/4zRwRCK6Mx
- Email: support@finic.ai
- Contributing: issues and pull requests are welcome. Read Working on Kairos first.
Kairos is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

Firefox's New Mini Window Is Every Multitasker's Dream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03

Firefox's New Mini Window Is Every Multitasker's Dream (zdnet.com) 46
			
		 	
				Mozilla is testing a new Firefox Nightly feature called Mini Window that lets users pop an entire webpage into a small, always-on-top window stripped of most browser controls. "The idea behind the Firefox Mini Window feature is simple: allow users to move a currently open tab (or a section of a tab) into a separate mini window," writes ZDNet's Jack Wallen. "Think of it as moving a tab from one window to what appears like a web app." From the report:  At first blush, there's no address bar, controls, scroll bar, or anything else that would normally be associated with Firefox. The Mini Window appears to be a web app, without having to actually create it. However, when I hover my cursor inside the Mini Window, I do see the address bar, the back/forward/reload buttons, and the window close button -- and that's it. The browser gets out of your way, so the only thing I see is the content.
On top of that (pun intended), the Mini Window stays on top of other Firefox windows, so I can have that popped-out content always in focus while I work on other things. This feature comes in handy when I'm working with limited display space (say, on a laptop) and need to reference a page while working on another. For multitasking, it comes in very handy. [...] Let's say I'm writing a paper on Linux and need to read a particular article for background information. I could have my document open in the main window, and then open the article in question in a Mini Window. I could then reference the article without having to click back and forth between them -- even when working on a smaller display.
Here's another use case I've found: When using MacOS's Stage Manager feature, I only have one window available at a time. The Mini Window bypasses that limitation, so I can have my main browser window focused as well as the page open in the Mini Window. Another handy way I like to use Mini Window is to open a favorite search engine, move it to a Mini Window, and then I have an always-ready search tool at my fingertips. I could also open my favorite AI service and use it in the same way.

Don’t be fooled by the fake hair on these famous baldies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
21:01:07 UTC
06:01:07 KST

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and actor Jason Statham have a distinctive feature in common: They’re both famously bald, and that definitely hasn’t changed in the last few days. However, there are some images of the two men circulating around X, Threads, and Bluesky in which they both have substantially more hair than their usual shaved look, which in Bezos’ case appears to be very freshly transplanted. It’s all just photo editing fakery, AI or otherwise.
Those Jeff Bezos hair transplant photos are very fake
In the era of easy AI fakery, edited paparazzi photos are a reminder that not everything is what it seems.
It’s unclear how viral these posts are, but they’re prevalent enough that a few members of the Verge team have encountered them in their social media feeds. Some people who shared them claimed (or were seemingly fooled into believing) that Bezos and Statham had undergone hair transplant surgery. Generative AI tools have made this kind of photo manipulation or outright creation more accessible and convincing, and because AI labeling solutions on social media broadly suck at flagging this fakery, it’s easy to be misled unless you’re wary of everything you see online. In a world where social media shitposters can turn engagement into a revenue stream, they’re not going to stop churning out attention-grabbing fabricated nonsense anytime soon.
We don’t know if AI tools were used to make the follicled Bezos and Statham edits — none of the images I tested flagged for Content Credentials or SynthID markers. We also can’t fully establish when they were first posted or who made them, but they are definitely fake, and it only took me a couple of minutes to confirm it.
In both cases, I ran the photos through Google’s reverse image search tool. For the Bezos debunk, I found photographs of him in a similar background environment and wearing the exact same outfit (with, yes, no hair) that included a watermarked image credit at the bottom left. Searching for the credit then led me to the original photographs in their unaltered state, which were taken in 2023. Finding the original tressless images of Statham was even easier — the reverse image search immediately surfaced watermarked versions of the originals, which were snapped by a paparazzo in 2011.
There’s other evidence too if you know what to look for. The main flag is that it’s probably impossible for Bezos and Statham to be realistic candidates for hair replacement surgery anyway; it requires you to have enough “donor” hair to sacrifice from the back and sides of your head to then replant closer to your desired hairline. You can technically take it from other places (or even other people), but doing so is incredibly rare due to undesirable results and rejection concerns. Transplant patients also typically experience some pretty dramatic facial swelling for the first week or so, which Bezos shows no signs of. Wigs, toupees, and other hair systems can also be used as nonpermanent hair restoration solutions, but as someone who used to make and install them professionally, it would be an astounding whoopsie for someone as rich and connected as Bezos to go this route and still end up looking like a Chia Pet.
This isn’t the first time photo-manipulated fakery has fooled people across social media, and with ongoing generative AI advancements, it probably won’t be the last. Previous incidents gave us the viral swagged-out pope, and recent trends have seen paparazzi photographs of celebrities like Callum Turner, Harry Styles, and Noah Schnapp being manipulated to remove their shirts. These kinds of edits are typically designed to rack up likes, reposts, and other engagement — they play into our fascination with celebrities’ lives with fabricated situations that are just outlandish enough to be believable, grab our attention, and be shared around as the latest hot gossip by those who are fooled, or who simply don’t care to verify the facts.
If you’re ever unsure if there’s fakery afoot with images of famous faces, just remember that most of the convincing edits (AI or otherwise) are based on real photos that you can hunt down to verify the original source.

Orbital Matter 3D printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
20:57:17 UTC
05:57:17 KST

A satellite built by the German startup Orbital Matter 3D-printed a half-meter long beam out of a custom plastic material, in what executives called a first for a free-flying spacecraft in orbit, and a step toward constructing large structures in space.
The company’s small satellite, Replicator 2, was launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission this summer, with four of the company’s 3D printers onboard. Each printer can create a rigid, cylindrical beam by extruding coils of resin that are cured by an ultraviolet light, which the company analogizes to cement and water.
This technology matters because future spacecraft will need to be larger in order to generate more electrical power and radiate a more heat into the vacuum of space, particularly if they’re going to serve as orbital data centers. But they’ll still need to fit into the tight confines of the fairing on top of the rocket that carries them into orbit. If spacecraft are able to construct their own structures in orbit, the power and heat-dissipation challenges may get a lot easier to solve.
“Replicator 2 is the first proof that we can simply build the array in space, at whatever size the mission demands,” said Jakub Stojek, CEO and co-founder of Orbital Matter. The company is partnering with the European Space Agency and Thales Alenia, a leading European satellite builder, with which it collaborated on Replicator 2.
Today’s large structures in space are origami projects — large solar arrays or telescope mirrors are folded up and then deployed on orbit. That’s a tricky engineering project, and so the idea of making and assembling those structures in space is appealing. NASA has funded some efforts at the idea, notably a mission with the company Redwire that 3D-printed structural beams in a vacuum chamber in 2023 but never got off the ground.
Two of Orbital Matter’s printers are designed to deploy a flexible solar array, but an anomaly led one of the printers to fail. Still, the boom that was created successfully deployed the solar array, and is an important proof of concept. Previous 3D-printing efforts in microgravity were limited to the pressurized environment onboard the International Space Station.
“That’s why we put so many printers on this single satellite. We preferred to learn in orbit and adapt the software as needed rather than waste years testing every possibility on the ground,” Orbital Matters CTO Robert Ihnatisin told TechCrunch.
The boom’s length is limited by the amount of resin carried onboard the satellite, and the company’s engineers believe that 100 meter booms are feasible. For comparison, SpaceX’s Starlink V2 satellites — among the most powerful mass-produced satellites in orbit — uses solar arrays that are 20 meters long.
Orbital Matter was co-founded in 2022 by Ihnatsin, who previously worked at 3D-printing company FormLabs, and Stojek, and raised a $3 million seed round.
Now, Orbital Matter is working on another demonstration mission, scheduled for launch in 2028, that will test a larger version of its printer on a bigger satellite that the company hopes will deploy a solar array that can generate 5 kw of power. That will be a “stepping stone” toward larger deployments of 100+ KW per wing by 2030.
The company is also collaborating with satellite builders that are considering incorporating its PADS (printer-assisted deployment system) into their spacecraft to extend solar panels, antennas, or other components.

The Pnyx and the Agora (2016)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
20:49:11 UTC
05:49:11 KST

The Pnyx and the Agora
Richard Sennett
THE PNYX AND THE AGORA
I am not going to speak about the present, but about the past: about the foundations on which our democracy is based. These foundations were rooted in cities, in their civic spaces. We need to remember this history to think about how democratic cities should be made today.
A democracy supposes people can consider views other than their own. This was Aristotle’s notion in the Politics. He thought the awareness of difference occurs only in cities, since the every city is formed by synoikismos, a drawing together of different families and tribes, of competing economic interests, of natives with foreigners.
“Difference” today seems about identity -- we think of race, gender, or class. Aristotle’s meant something more by difference; he included also the experience of doing different things, of acting in divergent ways which do not neatly fit together. The mixture in a city of action as well as identity is the foundation of its distinctive politics. Aristotle’s hope was that when a person becomes accustomed to a diverse, complex milieu he or she will cease reacting violently when challenged by something strange or contrary. Instead, this environment should create an outlook favourable to discussion of differing views or conflicting interests. Almost all modern urban planners subscribe to this Aristotelian principle. But if in the same space different persons or activities are merely concentrated, but each remains isolated and segregated, diversity loses its force. Differences have to interact.
Classical urbanism imagines two kinds of spaces in which this interaction could occur. One was the pnyx, an ampitheatre in which citizens listed to debates and took collective decisions; the other was the agora, the town square in which people were exposed to difference in a more raw, unmediated form.
The Pnyx was a bowl-shaped, open-air theatre about ten minutes’ walk from the central square of Athens. Chiselled out of a hill, the Pnyx in form resembled other Greek theatres, and like them originally provided space for dancing and plays. In the Sixth and Fifth Centuries BC, Athenians put this ordinary theatre to a different use, in seeking for order in their politics. Speakers stood in the open, round space on a stone platform called a bema, so that they could be seen by everyone in the theatre; behind the speaker the land dropped away, so that words seemed to hover in the air between the mass of five to six thousand bodies gathered together and the empty sky; the sun from morning to late afternoon struck the speaker’s face so that nothing in his expression or gestures was obscured by shadow. The audience for this political theatre sat around the bowl in assigned places, men sitting with others who belonged to the same local tribe. The citizens watched each other’s reactions as intently as the orator at the bema.
People sat or stood in this relation for a long time -- as long as the sunlight lasted. The theatrical space thus functioned as a detection mechanism, its focus and duration meant to get beneath the surface of momentary impressions. And such a disciplinary space of eye, voice, and body had one great virtue: through concentration of attention on a speaker and identification of others in the audience who might call out challenges or comments, the ancient political theatre sought to hold citizens responsible for their words.
In the Pnyx, two visual rules thus organized the often raucous meetings at which people took decisions: exposure, both of the speaker and of the audience to one another, and fixity of place, in where the speaker stood and the audience sat. These two visual rules supported a verbal order: a single voice speaking at any one time.
The other space of democracy was the Athenian agora. The town square consisted of a large open space crossed diagonally by the main street of Athens; at the sides of the agora were temples and buildings called stoas, the latter sheds with an open side onto the agora. A number of activities occurred simultaneously in the agora -- commerce, religious rituals, casual hanging out. In the open space lay also a rectangular law court, surrounded by a low wall, so that citizens banking or making an offering to the gods, could also follow the progress of justice. The stoa helped resolve this confusion; as one moved inside the building out of the open space, one moved from a public realm in which citizens freely intermingled into more private spaces. The rooms at the back of the stoas were used for dinner parties and private meetings. Perhaps the most interesting feature of the stoa was the transition space just under the shelter of the roof on the open side; here one could retreat yet keep in touch with the square.
The Athenian agora made differences among male citizens interact in two ways. First, in the open space of the agora there were few visual barriers between events occurring at the same time, so that men did not experience physical compartmentalization. As a result, in coming to the town square to deal with a banker, you might be suddenly caught up in a trial occurring in the law court, shouting out your own opinion or simply taking in an unexpected problem. Secondly, the agora established a space for stepping back from engagement. This occurred at the edge, just under the roof of the stoa on its open side; here was a fluid, liminal zone of transition between private and public.
These two principles of visual design, lack of visual barriers but a welldefined zone of transition between public and private, shaped people’s experience of language. The flow of speech was less continuous and singular than in the Pnyx; in the agora, communication through words became more fragmentary, as people moved from one scene to another. The operations of the eye were correspondingly more active and varied in the agora than in the Pnyx; a person standing under the stoa roof looked out, his eye searching, scanning. In the Pnyx the eye was fixed on a single scene, that of the orator standing at the bema; at most, the observer scanned the reactions of people sitting elsewhere, fixed in their seats.
This ancient example illustrates how the making of theatres and town squares can be put to democratic use. The theatre organizes the sustained attention required for decision-making; the square is a school for the often fragmentary, confusing experience of diversity. The square prepares people for debate; the theatre visually disciplines their debating.
This is, of course, in principle. Throughout their long history, these two urban forms have been put to many divergent or contrary uses. We need only think of the Nazi spectacles in Germany to summon an image of theatrically-focused attention dedicated to totalitarian ends.
Yet the most urgent social requirement for democratic deliberation today is that people concentrate rather than “surf” social reality. It is for this reason that I’ve come to believe that designers need to pay attention to the architecture of theatres as possible political spaces. Live theatre aims at concentrating the attention of those within it. To achieve sustained attention, to commit people to one another even when the going gets rough or becomes boring, to unpack the meaning of arguments, all require a disciplinary space for the eye and the voice.

Subvocal raised $1.3M. A developer recreated it with AirPods in 9 minutes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
20:40:00 UTC
05:40:00 KST

A macOS prototype that tests whether AirPods Pro head-motion data (CMHeadphoneMotionManager) carries enough information to turn silently mouthed words into text.
It doesn't use a language model. It's a small-vocabulary template recognizer plus a statistical test that tells you whether the signal is real.
brew install xcodegen   # once
xcodegen generate
open Subvox.xcodeproj   # ⌘R
Or from the command line:
xcodebuild -project Subvox.xcodeproj -scheme Subvox -derivedDataPath build -allowProvisioningUpdates build
open build/Build/Products/Debug/Subvox.app
xcodebuild -project Subvox.xcodeproj -scheme Subvox -derivedDataPath build test
Requires macOS 14+, AirPods Pro or another headphone that supports head tracking, connected as the Mac's audio output. On first launch, grant Motion. The mic and speech prompts only appear when you start the mic.
- Segmentation (CaptureController). Space-hold, or an energy trigger above a calibrated noise floor with pre-roll and hangover.
- Features (MotionFeatures). Per frame: user acceleration (3), rotation rate (3), and attitude change since the start of the segment (3). Each channel is mean-centered, and quiet lead-in and lead-out frames are trimmed.
- Matching (DTW, TemplateClassifier). Each channel is z-scaled across the training set. Matching is 1-nearest-neighbour per word, using dynamic time warping with a Sakoe–Chiba band. A segment is rejected if the best distance is above max distance or the margin to the runner-up is below min confidence.
- Is it real? (Evaluation). The leave-one-out accuracy is compared with the same procedure run on shuffled labels. If p < 0.05, the motion stream distinguishes your words better than chance.
Use Record Session in the toolbar or on the Sensors screen. Recordings go to ~/Documents/Subvox/Sessions/<timestamp>-<condition>/:
- motion.csv: every motion sample. t is seconds from session start.
- audio.caf: microphone audio, if the mic is running.
- events.csv: every Space-held segment, with its label or prediction.
- meta.json: condition, prompt, and the audio start offset for aligning audio with motion.
Suggested runs: the same 5-word script under Normal speech, Whisper and Silent mouthing, 10 reps each. Then, in Train, compare the Evaluate results across feature sets.
The training set lives at ~/Library/Application Support/Subvox/dataset.json.
- Headphone motion is processed and low-rate (roughly 25 Hz on AirPods). The speech-detecting accelerometer and the inward mic are not exposed. Expect jaw and head movement, not vocal vibration.
- Templates are user- and session-specific. Re-seating the AirPods can shift the signal.
- Choosing AirPods as the mic input switches them to the Bluetooth headset (HFP) profile.

I Dumped Apple's Fucking Word List

~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db
Lexicon.framework
Content note: this article prints the words uncensored, slurs included, because the article is about what Apple flags.
Nick posted this, I asked where it lives, and he answered. So I had Claude open mine.
$ sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db .schema CREATE TABLE properties (ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, key, value, UNIQUE (key)); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "vword_usage" ( ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, app TEXT, -- app identifier recipient TEXT, -- recipient identifier vword TEXT, -- vulgar word word_reading TEXT, -- the reading form of a word (relevant for Japanese) usage_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0, last_use_timestamp REAL DEFAULT 0, -- last use timestamp (seconds since the reference date) journaled ); CREATE UNIQUE INDEX app_recipient_vword_word_reading_idx ON vword_usage(app, recipient, vword, word_reading);
So the keyboard can know that you say fuck in Messages to one particular friend, but not in Mail to your boss. The unique index is on (app, recipient, word, reading), so that is the granularity.
Mine is empty: no rows, a properties table holding only version = 2, and a modification date in April 2024.
At WWDC in June 2023, Craig Federighi announced the iOS 17 autocorrect rewrite with this line: "In those moments where you just want to type a ducking word, well, the keyboard will learn it, too." (TechCrunch, NPR)
These function names from the macOS shared library cache show how the keyboard uses the database:
TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_app_id(CFString) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_recipient_ids(vector<string>) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::increment_usage_count(word, reading, recipients) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::decrement_usage_count(...) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect(word, app, recipients) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect_somewhere(word, reading) KB::FilterNonVulgarIfTopCandidateVulgar::filter_candidates(...) KB::Candidate::every_vulgar_word_is_allowlisted(VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper*, ...)
Plus log strings like Passing recipient IDs to the vulgar word usage database wrapper; number of IDs: %lu.
A _KSUserWordsSynchroniser sharedAcrossLanguagesVulgarWordUsageValue symbol suggests it syncs between devices like your other learned words.
Claude tried to fill it, using agent-desktop to open a new TextEdit document and type well fuck this shit, damn it., first as a text insert, then as individual key presses. Nothing changed: no row, no log line, and the file's modification date stayed in 2024.
On Hacker News, swiftcoder reported that neither the database nor the ~/Library/Keyboard folder exists on their macOS Tahoe install. dr_pardee had the same problem, saw that macOS was trying to write the file and failing, and had Claude work out why. The prompt they used is in their gist.
The cause is a missing folder. AppleSpell, the background service behind autocorrect, opens ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db the first time a text field asks it for predictions in a given language. SQLite creates a database file when it's missing, but not the folder it lives in. Without ~/Library/Keyboard, the open fails with "no such file or directory", AppleSpell logs a com.apple.libsqlite3 error naming the path, and it carries on without the database. There's no visible error, so the feature stays off on that Mac without anyone noticing.
To get the file, create the folder, restart AppleSpell and type a sentence in a native app such as TextEdit:
mkdir -p ~/Library/Keyboard kill -9 $(pgrep AppleSpell) # per the gist, a plain kill is ignored; macOS relaunches it on demand
On my Mac the folder already existed (it dates from 2023), so the database was created normally in April 2024. The gist also explains why mine is empty: a row is only written when autocorrect offers to replace a vulgar word and you keep the original. A correctly spelled swear word never gets a correction, so there is nothing to count, which fits my TextEdit test where every word was spelled correctly.
The database only counts words that are already marked as vulgar somewhere else, so the next step was finding that list.
Searching the dyld shared cache for "vulgar" turned up a C API with an LX prefix (LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCreate, LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCanAutocorrect, …) and, more usefully, two functions on dictionary entries:
_LXEntryGetCategoryFlags _LXEntryGetMetaFlags
LX is Lexicon.framework, a private framework that reads the per-language dictionaries under /System/Library/LinguisticData/. Every word in those dictionaries is an LXEntry with two 32-bit flag fields. If the vulgarity rating is anywhere, it's in those bits.
NSSpellChecker, UITextChecker, NaturalLanguage and UILexicon don't expose vulgarity. SensitiveContentAnalysis covers images and video, not text. The only places "profanity" shows up on developer.apple.com are App Store age ratings and review guidelines.
Lexicon has no headers, but the C functions are exported, and their signatures are easy to guess because they follow CoreFoundation conventions. This program opens the dictionary for a locale, walks every entry, and prints both flag fields:
// lx.c — dump every word in a system lexicon with its flags. // clang -O1 -o lx lx.c -F/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks -framework Lexicon -framework CoreFoundation #include <CoreFoundation/CoreFoundation.h> #include <stdbool.h> #include <stdio.h> typedef const void *LXLexiconRef, *LXCursorRef, *LXEntryRef; extern CFStringRef kLXLexiconLocaleKey; LXLexiconRef LXLexiconCreate(CFDictionaryRef options, CFErrorRef *error); LXCursorRef LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(LXLexiconRef); void LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXCursorRef, void (^)(LXEntryRef, bool *stop)); CFStringRef LXEntryCopyString(LXEntryRef); uint32_t LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(LXEntryRef); uint32_t LXEntryGetMetaFlags(LXEntryRef); int main(int argc, char **argv) { CFStringRef locale = CFStringCreateWithCString(NULL, argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "en_US", kCFStringEncodingUTF8); const void *keys[] = {kLXLexiconLocaleKey}, *values[] = {locale}; CFDictionaryRef options = CFDictionaryCreate(NULL, keys, values, 1, &kCFTypeDictionaryKeyCallBacks, &kCFTypeDictionaryValueCallBacks); LXLexiconRef lexicon = LXLexiconCreate(options, NULL); if (!lexicon) return 1; LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(lexicon), ^(LXEntryRef entry, bool *stop) { char word[512] = ""; CFStringRef s = LXEntryCopyString(entry); if (s) { CFStringGetCString(s, word, sizeof word, kCFStringEncodingUTF8); CFRelease(s); } printf("%08x\t%08x\t%s\n", LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(entry), LXEntryGetMetaFlags(entry), word); }); }
$ ./lx en_US | wc -l 199019 $ ./lx en_US | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "fuck" || $3 == "table" || $3 == "Trump"' 00000000 00800002 fuck 00000000 00000000 table 00002000 02000081 Trump
The same thing in Swift, loading the functions at runtime with dlopen and dlsym so you don't need to link against a private framework. It prints only words that carry one of the three tiers:
// lexflags.swift — swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags && ./lexflags en_US import Foundation let lexicon = dlopen("/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/Lexicon.framework/Lexicon", RTLD_NOW)! func sym<T>(_ name: String, as _: T.Type) -> T { unsafeBitCast(dlsym(lexicon, name)!, to: T.self) } typealias LXRef = UnsafeRawPointer let create = sym("LXLexiconCreate", as: (@convention(c) (CFDictionary, UnsafeMutablePointer<Unmanaged<CFError>?>?) -> LXRef?).self) let rootCursor = sym("LXLexiconCreateRootCursor", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> LXRef?).self) let enumerate = sym("LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef, @convention(block) (LXRef, UnsafeMutablePointer<Bool>) -> Void) -> Void).self) let copyString = sym("LXEntryCopyString", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> Unmanaged<CFString>?).self) let metaFlags = sym("LXEntryGetMetaFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self) let category = sym("LXEntryGetCategoryFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self) let localeKey = dlsym(lexicon, "kLXLexiconLocaleKey")!.load(as: CFString.self) let locale = CommandLine.arguments.dropFirst().first ?? "en_US" guard let lex = create([localeKey: locale] as CFDictionary, nil), let root = rootCursor(lex) else { fatalError("could not open lexicon for \(locale)") } let tiers: [(UInt32, String)] = [(0x0080_0000, "vulgar"), (0x0100_0000, "offensive"), (0x0200_0000, "sensitive")] enumerate(root) { entry, _ in let meta = metaFlags(entry) guard let tier = tiers.first(where: { meta & $0.0 != 0 })?.1, let word = copyString(entry)?.takeRetainedValue() else { return } print(tier, String(format: "%05x", category(entry)), word, separator: "\t") }
Both are read-only. They open the same dictionary the keyboard uses and print it.
Apple doesn't document these flags, so every meaning below is inferred: Claude grouped words by bit and read samples until each group's theme was obvious. The system code helps with one of them. An enum case called offensiveVulgarSensitive sits right next to the vulgar-word code, and three adjacent meta bits match it.
0x00800000
0x01000000
0x02000000
In en_US a word has at most one tier: they never overlap. Out of 199,019 entries, 4,271 have one.
Roughly: vulgar is swearing and sex slang, offensive is slurs aimed at groups of people, and sensitive is everything a keyboard shouldn't offer you unprompted: mild swears, insults, drugs, weapons, extremism, disease and bodily functions.
The other field is a topic bitmask, and a word can have several topics:
0x00100
0x00200
0x00400
0x00800
0x01000
0x02000
0x04000
0x08000
0x10000
0x20000
0x40000
The topic flags and the tiers are independent. 2,052 English words have a topic but no tier: gay, fat, God, Allah and sex are all tagged "sensitive context" but are not vulgar, offensive or sensitive. My guess is the topic is a hint ("be careful how you rank this") and the tier is the rule.
The lower meta bits are dull: proper nouns, abbreviations, camel-case brand names like iMac and tvOS.
Next to the expected orgy, sext and merde:
blocklist.dat
The sensitive tier has 109 capitalized words. Here is all of it:
Al-Qaeda, Al-Qaida, Aryan, Aryans, Auschwitz, Bacchus, Beelzebub, Birkenau, Brave(s), Buchenwald, Chief(s), Chippendale(s), Christ-y, Christer(s), Crip(s), Dachau, Eichmann, Frenchier, Gentile(s), Gestapo(s), Goebbels, Goering, Hamas, Hezbollah, Himmler, Hitler, Hitlerian, Hitlerism, Hitlerite(s), Hitlerjugend, Hooters, Isis, Islamophobe(s), Islamophobic, Jehovah(s), Jewfro(s), Jezebel(s), Kalashnikov(s), Kristallnacht, Kuomintang, Londonderry, Luftwaffe, Mao, Mauthausen, Mickie(s), Mollie(s), Mongol(s), Mossad, Nazi(s), Nazism, Osama, Pornhub, Quaalude(s), Reich, Reichsmark, Reichstag, Sachsenhausen, Satan, Satanism, Shoah, Sinophobe(s), Sinophobic, Sodom, Stasi, Taliban, Treblinka, Trump, Trumps, Unabomber, Uzi(s)
(Plurals and possessives folded for brevity.)
Every other real person on that list is dead, and nearly all of them are Nazi officials, dictators or terrorists. Trump is the only living exception:
category meta word 00002000 02000081 Trump sensitive tier + politics topic 00002000 02000081 Trumps 00002000 02000081 Trump's 00000000 00000000 trump (the card-game word: clean) 00000000 00000000 trumped
For comparison:
en_GB matches en_US. Other languages differ: the German dictionary has Trump clean (and puts Hitler in the offensive tier), and Swedish flags Putin as sensitive.
What the flag does matters here. As far as I can tell, a sensitive word is one the keyboard shouldn't suggest on its own. You can still type it and it won't be corrected away. It stays out of the QuickType bar unless you're already typing it, which is much milder than a ban.
There is a plausible reason Apple would want that for one specific name. In February 2025, iPhone dictation briefly showed "Trump" when people said "racist". It went viral, and Apple called it a "phonetic overlap" in the speech model and shipped a fix within a day (9to5Mac). The dictionary files on my Mac are from July 2025. A rule that keeps the name out of unprompted suggestions would stop that kind of thing from happening again through the keyboard.
Because I'm Norwegian and had to check:
Every party gets the politics topic and none gets a tier. The only Norwegians in the sensitive tier are a mass murderer and a Nazi collaborator.
The same three tiers exist in every European dictionary we tried, Cyrillic included. The counts are entries, not lemmas, so heavily inflected languages like Polish and Russian look much worse than they are: every case and conjugation of a swear word is a separate entry.
The bits don't seem to mean the same thing everywhere. Arabic and Hebrew return hundreds of thousands of "sensitive" entries, so those dictionaries probably reuse the bits for something else, so they're left out. Korean, Catalan and Hungarian return nothing, and Japanese crashes the dumper.
Samples from Norwegian, since that's what I type in when I'm not typing English:
There is a second, separate filter. Every English language model has a blocklist.bundle, and there's a qp_blocklist.bundle for QuickPath, the swipe keyboard:
/System/Library/LinguisticData/RequiredAssets_en.bundle/AssetData/en.lm/ ├── blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat} └── qp_blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat}
blocklistidmap.dat is a 20-byte header followed by (lexicon token ID, class ID) pairs of 32-bit integers. Mapping the token IDs back through the dictionary gives 2,544 words in 930 classes. Most classes are inflection groups:
931 fuck | fucked | fucking | fucks 1181 molest | molestation | molested | molester | molesting 1514 died | dies | dying 1611 Holocaust | holocaust | holocausts 1614 denied | denies | deny | denying 923 Semite | Semites | Semitic 1487 ghetto | ghettoes | ghettos 1720 animals | brown | cats
blocklist.dat is a packed trie over those class IDs, so it blocks sequences: "deny" followed by "Holocaust", and whatever 1720 pairs with. A class that puts brown next to animals and cats suggests the list targets specific phrasings rather than single words, though which phrasings can't be told without decoding the trie. The runtime check is LMLanguageModelTokenSequenceIsBlocklisted in LanguageModeling.framework. Claude got far enough to learn that its fourth and fifth arguments include an output pointer, but its probe still crashes intermittently, so the actual phrases haven't been read yet. That's for a follow-up.
# Your own learned-swears database (probably empty on a Mac) sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db 'select * from vword_usage' # Build the Swift version from above and filter by tier swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags ./lexflags en_US | awk -F'\t' '$1 == "vulgar" {print $3}' | sort -u | less ./lexflags nb_NO | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "faen" || $3 == "helvete" || $3 == "idiot"'
If you'd rather not build anything, the gist has every tiered word for 15 locales as TSV, plus the code and a script that regenerates them. It's a snapshot of macOS 15.6 and won't be kept up to date.

Content note: this article prints the words uncensored, slurs included, because the article is about what Apple flags.
Nick posted this, I asked where it lives, and he answered. So I had Claude open mine.
$ sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db .schema CREATE TABLE properties (ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, key, value, UNIQUE (key)); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "vword_usage" ( ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, app TEXT, -- app identifier recipient TEXT, -- recipient identifier vword TEXT, -- vulgar word word_reading TEXT, -- the reading form of a word (relevant for Japanese) usage_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0, last_use_timestamp REAL DEFAULT 0, -- last use timestamp (seconds since the reference date) journaled ); CREATE UNIQUE INDEX app_recipient_vword_word_reading_idx ON vword_usage(app, recipient, vword, word_reading);
So the keyboard can know that you say fuck in Messages to one particular friend, but not in Mail to your boss. The unique index is on (app, recipient, word, reading), so that is the granularity.
Mine is empty: no rows, a properties table holding only version = 2, and a modification date in April 2024.
At WWDC in June 2023, Craig Federighi announced the iOS 17 autocorrect rewrite with this line: "In those moments where you just want to type a ducking word, well, the keyboard will learn it, too." (TechCrunch, NPR)
These function names from the macOS shared library cache show how the keyboard uses the database:
TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_app_id(CFString) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_recipient_ids(vector<string>) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::increment_usage_count(word, reading, recipients) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::decrement_usage_count(...) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect(word, app, recipients) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect_somewhere(word, reading) KB::FilterNonVulgarIfTopCandidateVulgar::filter_candidates(...) KB::Candidate::every_vulgar_word_is_allowlisted(VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper*, ...)
Plus log strings like Passing recipient IDs to the vulgar word usage database wrapper; number of IDs: %lu.
A _KSUserWordsSynchroniser sharedAcrossLanguagesVulgarWordUsageValue symbol suggests it syncs between devices like your other learned words.
Claude tried to fill it, using agent-desktop to open a new TextEdit document and type well fuck this shit, damn it., first as a text insert, then as individual key presses. Nothing changed: no row, no log line, and the file's modification date stayed in 2024.
On Hacker News, swiftcoder reported that neither the database nor the ~/Library/Keyboard folder exists on their macOS Tahoe install. dr_pardee had the same problem, saw that macOS was trying to write the file and failing, and had Claude work out why. The prompt they used is in their gist.
The cause is a missing folder. AppleSpell, the background service behind autocorrect, opens ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db the first time a text field asks it for predictions in a given language. SQLite creates a database file when it's missing, but not the folder it lives in. Without ~/Library/Keyboard, the open fails with "no such file or directory", AppleSpell logs a com.apple.libsqlite3 error naming the path, and it carries on without the database. There's no visible error, so the feature stays off on that Mac without anyone noticing.
To get the file, create the folder, restart AppleSpell and type a sentence in a native app such as TextEdit:
mkdir -p ~/Library/Keyboard kill -9 $(pgrep AppleSpell) # per the gist, a plain kill is ignored; macOS relaunches it on demand
On my Mac the folder already existed (it dates from 2023), so the database was created normally in April 2024. The gist also explains why mine is empty: a row is only written when autocorrect offers to replace a vulgar word and you keep the original. A correctly spelled swear word never gets a correction, so there is nothing to count, which fits my TextEdit test where every word was spelled correctly.
The database only counts words that are already marked as vulgar somewhere else, so the next step was finding that list.
Searching the dyld shared cache for "vulgar" turned up a C API with an LX prefix (LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCreate, LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCanAutocorrect, …) and, more usefully, two functions on dictionary entries:
_LXEntryGetCategoryFlags _LXEntryGetMetaFlags
LX is Lexicon.framework, a private framework that reads the per-language dictionaries under /System/Library/LinguisticData/. Every word in those dictionaries is an LXEntry with two 32-bit flag fields. If the vulgarity rating is anywhere, it's in those bits.
NSSpellChecker, UITextChecker, NaturalLanguage and UILexicon don't expose vulgarity. SensitiveContentAnalysis covers images and video, not text. The only places "profanity" shows up on developer.apple.com are App Store age ratings and review guidelines.
Lexicon has no headers, but the C functions are exported, and their signatures are easy to guess because they follow CoreFoundation conventions. This program opens the dictionary for a locale, walks every entry, and prints both flag fields:
// lx.c — dump every word in a system lexicon with its flags. // clang -O1 -o lx lx.c -F/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks -framework Lexicon -framework CoreFoundation #include <CoreFoundation/CoreFoundation.h> #include <stdbool.h> #include <stdio.h> typedef const void *LXLexiconRef, *LXCursorRef, *LXEntryRef; extern CFStringRef kLXLexiconLocaleKey; LXLexiconRef LXLexiconCreate(CFDictionaryRef options, CFErrorRef *error); LXCursorRef LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(LXLexiconRef); void LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXCursorRef, void (^)(LXEntryRef, bool *stop)); CFStringRef LXEntryCopyString(LXEntryRef); uint32_t LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(LXEntryRef); uint32_t LXEntryGetMetaFlags(LXEntryRef); int main(int argc, char **argv) { CFStringRef locale = CFStringCreateWithCString(NULL, argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "en_US", kCFStringEncodingUTF8); const void *keys[] = {kLXLexiconLocaleKey}, *values[] = {locale}; CFDictionaryRef options = CFDictionaryCreate(NULL, keys, values, 1, &kCFTypeDictionaryKeyCallBacks, &kCFTypeDictionaryValueCallBacks); LXLexiconRef lexicon = LXLexiconCreate(options, NULL); if (!lexicon) return 1; LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(lexicon), ^(LXEntryRef entry, bool *stop) { char word[512] = ""; CFStringRef s = LXEntryCopyString(entry); if (s) { CFStringGetCString(s, word, sizeof word, kCFStringEncodingUTF8); CFRelease(s); } printf("%08x\t%08x\t%s\n", LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(entry), LXEntryGetMetaFlags(entry), word); }); }
$ ./lx en_US | wc -l 199019 $ ./lx en_US | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "fuck" || $3 == "table" || $3 == "Trump"' 00000000 00800002 fuck 00000000 00000000 table 00002000 02000081 Trump
The same thing in Swift, loading the functions at runtime with dlopen and dlsym so you don't need to link against a private framework. It prints only words that carry one of the three tiers:
// lexflags.swift — swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags && ./lexflags en_US import Foundation let lexicon = dlopen("/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/Lexicon.framework/Lexicon", RTLD_NOW)! func sym<T>(_ name: String, as _: T.Type) -> T { unsafeBitCast(dlsym(lexicon, name)!, to: T.self) } typealias LXRef = UnsafeRawPointer let create = sym("LXLexiconCreate", as: (@convention(c) (CFDictionary, UnsafeMutablePointer<Unmanaged<CFError>?>?) -> LXRef?).self) let rootCursor = sym("LXLexiconCreateRootCursor", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> LXRef?).self) let enumerate = sym("LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef, @convention(block) (LXRef, UnsafeMutablePointer<Bool>) -> Void) -> Void).self) let copyString = sym("LXEntryCopyString", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> Unmanaged<CFString>?).self) let metaFlags = sym("LXEntryGetMetaFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self) let category = sym("LXEntryGetCategoryFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self) let localeKey = dlsym(lexicon, "kLXLexiconLocaleKey")!.load(as: CFString.self) let locale = CommandLine.arguments.dropFirst().first ?? "en_US" guard let lex = create([localeKey: locale] as CFDictionary, nil), let root = rootCursor(lex) else { fatalError("could not open lexicon for \(locale)") } let tiers: [(UInt32, String)] = [(0x0080_0000, "vulgar"), (0x0100_0000, "offensive"), (0x0200_0000, "sensitive")] enumerate(root) { entry, _ in let meta = metaFlags(entry) guard let tier = tiers.first(where: { meta & $0.0 != 0 })?.1, let word = copyString(entry)?.takeRetainedValue() else { return } print(tier, String(format: "%05x", category(entry)), word, separator: "\t") }
Both are read-only. They open the same dictionary the keyboard uses and print it.
Apple doesn't document these flags, so every meaning below is inferred: Claude grouped words by bit and read samples until each group's theme was obvious. The system code helps with one of them. An enum case called offensiveVulgarSensitive sits right next to the vulgar-word code, and three adjacent meta bits match it.
0x00800000
0x01000000
0x02000000
In en_US a word has at most one tier: they never overlap. Out of 199,019 entries, 4,271 have one.
Roughly: vulgar is swearing and sex slang, offensive is slurs aimed at groups of people, and sensitive is everything a keyboard shouldn't offer you unprompted: mild swears, insults, drugs, weapons, extremism, disease and bodily functions.
The other field is a topic bitmask, and a word can have several topics:
0x00100
0x00200
0x00400
0x00800
0x01000
0x02000
0x04000
0x08000
0x10000
0x20000
0x40000
The topic flags and the tiers are independent. 2,052 English words have a topic but no tier: gay, fat, God, Allah and sex are all tagged "sensitive context" but are not vulgar, offensive or sensitive. My guess is the topic is a hint ("be careful how you rank this") and the tier is the rule.
The lower meta bits are dull: proper nouns, abbreviations, camel-case brand names like iMac and tvOS.
Next to the expected orgy, sext and merde:
blocklist.dat
The sensitive tier has 109 capitalized words. Here is all of it:
Al-Qaeda, Al-Qaida, Aryan, Aryans, Auschwitz, Bacchus, Beelzebub, Birkenau, Brave(s), Buchenwald, Chief(s), Chippendale(s), Christ-y, Christer(s), Crip(s), Dachau, Eichmann, Frenchier, Gentile(s), Gestapo(s), Goebbels, Goering, Hamas, Hezbollah, Himmler, Hitler, Hitlerian, Hitlerism, Hitlerite(s), Hitlerjugend, Hooters, Isis, Islamophobe(s), Islamophobic, Jehovah(s), Jewfro(s), Jezebel(s), Kalashnikov(s), Kristallnacht, Kuomintang, Londonderry, Luftwaffe, Mao, Mauthausen, Mickie(s), Mollie(s), Mongol(s), Mossad, Nazi(s), Nazism, Osama, Pornhub, Quaalude(s), Reich, Reichsmark, Reichstag, Sachsenhausen, Satan, Satanism, Shoah, Sinophobe(s), Sinophobic, Sodom, Stasi, Taliban, Treblinka, Trump, Trumps, Unabomber, Uzi(s)
(Plurals and possessives folded for brevity.)
Every other real person on that list is dead, and nearly all of them are Nazi officials, dictators or terrorists. Trump is the only living exception:
category meta word 00002000 02000081 Trump sensitive tier + politics topic 00002000 02000081 Trumps 00002000 02000081 Trump's 00000000 00000000 trump (the card-game word: clean) 00000000 00000000 trumped
For comparison:
en_GB matches en_US. Other languages differ: the German dictionary has Trump clean (and puts Hitler in the offensive tier), and Swedish flags Putin as sensitive.
What the flag does matters here. As far as I can tell, a sensitive word is one the keyboard shouldn't suggest on its own. You can still type it and it won't be corrected away. It stays out of the QuickType bar unless you're already typing it, which is much milder than a ban.
There is a plausible reason Apple would want that for one specific name. In February 2025, iPhone dictation briefly showed "Trump" when people said "racist". It went viral, and Apple called it a "phonetic overlap" in the speech model and shipped a fix within a day (9to5Mac). The dictionary files on my Mac are from July 2025. A rule that keeps the name out of unprompted suggestions would stop that kind of thing from happening again through the keyboard.
Because I'm Norwegian and had to check:
Every party gets the politics topic and none gets a tier. The only Norwegians in the sensitive tier are a mass murderer and a Nazi collaborator.
The same three tiers exist in every European dictionary we tried, Cyrillic included. The counts are entries, not lemmas, so heavily inflected languages like Polish and Russian look much worse than they are: every case and conjugation of a swear word is a separate entry.
The bits don't seem to mean the same thing everywhere. Arabic and Hebrew return hundreds of thousands of "sensitive" entries, so those dictionaries probably reuse the bits for something else, so they're left out. Korean, Catalan and Hungarian return nothing, and Japanese crashes the dumper.
Samples from Norwegian, since that's what I type in when I'm not typing English:
There is a second, separate filter. Every English language model has a blocklist.bundle, and there's a qp_blocklist.bundle for QuickPath, the swipe keyboard:
/System/Library/LinguisticData/RequiredAssets_en.bundle/AssetData/en.lm/ ├── blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat} └── qp_blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat}
blocklistidmap.dat is a 20-byte header followed by (lexicon token ID, class ID) pairs of 32-bit integers. Mapping the token IDs back through the dictionary gives 2,544 words in 930 classes. Most classes are inflection groups:
931 fuck | fucked | fucking | fucks 1181 molest | molestation | molested | molester | molesting 1514 died | dies | dying 1611 Holocaust | holocaust | holocausts 1614 denied | denies | deny | denying 923 Semite | Semites | Semitic 1487 ghetto | ghettoes | ghettos 1720 animals | brown | cats
blocklist.dat is a packed trie over those class IDs, so it blocks sequences: "deny" followed by "Holocaust", and whatever 1720 pairs with. A class that puts brown next to animals and cats suggests the list targets specific phrasings rather than single words, though which phrasings can't be told without decoding the trie. The runtime check is LMLanguageModelTokenSequenceIsBlocklisted in LanguageModeling.framework. Claude got far enough to learn that its fourth and fifth arguments include an output pointer, but its probe still crashes intermittently, so the actual phrases haven't been read yet. That's for a follow-up.
# Your own learned-swears database (probably empty on a Mac) sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db 'select * from vword_usage' # Build the Swift version from above and filter by tier swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags ./lexflags en_US | awk -F'\t' '$1 == "vulgar" {print $3}' | sort -u | less ./lexflags nb_NO | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "faen" || $3 == "helvete" || $3 == "idiot"'
If you'd rather not build anything, the gist has every tiered word for 15 locales as TSV, plus the code and a script that regenerates them. It's a snapshot of macOS 15.6 and won't be kept up to date.

Apple opens the door to a nightmare world of always-listening tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
20:25:05 UTC
05:25:05 KST

Watch what you say: Apple opens the door to a nightmare world of always-listening tech
Apple this week announced plans to roll out "always-listening" features for newer Apple Watches. One of the features, Live Rewind, lets you "go back in time" and replay the most recent 15 seconds of ambient audio as a text transcript. The other feature, Siri Recap, listens throughout the day and summarizes your conversations as high-level notes into a written report on your iPhone.
Apple claims these features are helpful to "jog" your memory. The massive trade-off is that your Apple Watch is always listening to you and anyone else within earshot while the feature is enabled.
Here's the relevant section from Apple's live event:
Given these features we're bound to be controversial, it's clear that Apple put thought into the security and privacy guardrails before shipping these features (which may still change). The tech giant says on its support page that the always-listening tech doesn't record or store audio, and that the recaps are end-to-end encrypted so that any summarized data is inaccessible to anyone else, not even Apple. And, its security documentation [PDF] detailing how the features work is worth reading as well.
What is more concerning to me, to underscore on a point I made in a Bluesky post, is that Apple is opening the door to a world where other companies, device makers, and app developers try to recreate or rival Apple's technology and do a far shoddier job, all the while creating a worse surveillance monster and introducing new security and privacy risks along the way.
So far there have been a few companies and startups that made always-listening devices, like pendants, often including AI. Apple by comparison is one of the largest technology companies in the world and its global reach means millions of people will get these features and switch them on. Apple's market dominance, coupled with its decision to make always-listening tech, sets a precedent that signals it's OK for other companies to follow suit and normalize this intrusive tech. It also implies that there is money to be made in developing this technology, making it a space ripe for disruption (or exploitation) by profiteers.
Bloomberg ($) reports lawyers are already finding that Apple's always-listening tech is at odds with the law in several U.S. states. Some states require all parties' consent before being recorded, setting up the feature for potential legal battles down the line. This comes amid the rise of smart camera-enabled "pervert glasses" like those made by Meta and Snap, which have supercharged abuse and harassment against people by recording them without consent.
~this week in security~ is my weekly cybersecurity newsletter and blog supported by readers like you. Please consider signing up for a paid subscription starting at $10/month for access to exclusive articles, analysis, and more.

Recent stories include: How residential proxy networks are hiding hackers in your home | The top highlights from Black Hat, Def Con, and BSides Las Vegas 2026 | When AI chatbots and LLMs get legal, check your privilege | Vigilantism comes for Flock
Privacy for me, but not for thee?
While Apple has emphasized security and privacy features for its own users, it hasn't explained how people opt out of its customers' recordings.
I chatted this week with Em, a digital privacy and security technologist, activist, and author of the Control Alt Delete blog, and whose work you have no doubt seen while she wrote for Privacy Guides. Em told me that these new Apple features follow a "recent trend of gadgets that are constantly collecting information from surroundings, including from people who aren't wearing or buying these gadgets themselves," like smart glasses and speakers.
Em said that while anyone can make notes of every conversation they have, this kind of technology "normalizes it happening at all time and in every context."
"Even if Apple seems to have put some thought into protecting the privacy and consent of the people using the Apple Watch, this technology doesn't do much to protect the privacy and consent of everyone interacting with people using it," Em told me.
I also asked Thorin Klosowski, a senior security and privacy activist at Electronic Frontier Foundation, for his thoughts and he said similarly that Apple's approach is largely about protecting its customers' data but does little for anyone else.
"Increasingly we’re seeing tech companies frame privacy this way — as personal responsibility — but it has never been just about that, it’s a collective effort that relies as much on personal choice as it does social contracts," said Klosowski. He added that we should all be free to converse without fear of tech documenting everything that's being said. "Especially when combined with all the other similar devices we’re seeing, whether that’s pendants or glasses or rings, there is absolutely a risk of normalization here."
EFF's privacy litigation director Adam Schwartz added that since there's no practical means for people to consent or decline recording, "we suggest people should think twice before using this technology, out of respect to the conversational privacy of others."
For its part, Apple says on its support page that users should "consider those around you where conversations may be private or sensitive." The broader message Apple seems to be sending is: Prepare for a world where everyday devices are always listening in.

Apple starts giving Siri AI access to third-party apps
